INJECTION, POWDER, LYOPHILIZED, FOR SOLUTION
Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia (SAB) in Adults:
667 mg every 6 hours on day 1 to 8, followed by every 8
hours from day 9 onwards over 2-hour infusion
ABSSSI and CABP in Adults: 667 mg every 8 hours over 2
hour infusion
CABP in Pediatric Patients:
Adolescents: 12 to less than 18 years of age: 13.3 mg/kg (up
to 667 mg) every 8 hours over 2-hour infusion
Infants and children: 3 months and less than 12 years
old: (b) (4) mg/kg (up to 667 mg) every 8 hours over 2 hour
infusion
Note: 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent
to 500 mg of ceftobiprole. For pediatric patients: 13.3 mg/kg
is equivalent to 10 mg/kg of ceftobiprole. (b) (4) mg/kg of
ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to (b)
(4) mg/kg of
ceftobiprole. Dosing adjustments for each indication are
based on renal function

susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gramnegative microorganisms:
Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible and
methicillin-resistant isolates), Streptococcus pyogenes,

Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella
pneumoniae

I. Executive Summary
1. Summary of Regulatory Action
New drug application (NDA) 218275 for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection was
submitted by Basilea Pharmaceutica International Ltd, Allschwil (Applicant) for the following
indications:
1. Treatment of adult patients with Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (SAB), including those
with right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE)
2. Treatment of adult patients with acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI)
3. Treatment of adult and pediatric patients (greater than or equal to 3 months to less than
18 years of age) with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP)
The application was reviewed by the multidisciplinary review team. The review team has
recommended approval, and I, the signatory for this application, concur with this
recommendation.
Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is a cephalosporin antibacterial drug which exerts its antibacterial
activity by binding to penicillin-binding proteins and inhibiting synthesis of the bacterial cell
wall. Ceftobiprole medocaril is the prodrug that rapidly converts to its active moiety,
ceftobiprole. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is the salt form of ceftobiprole medocaril;
ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is used interchangeably with ceftobiprole throughout this review.
Ceftobiprole demonstrated in vitro and clinical activity against gram-positive and gram-negative
bacteria including methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) and methicillin-resistant S. aureus
(MRSA), Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae,
Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Klebsiella pneumonia and Escherichia coli.
The Applicant submitted a single, phase 3, randomized, double-blinded, active-controlled,
noninferiority trial in adults for each of the indications (SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP) that
demonstrated noninferiority to the comparators. Additionally, the Applicant submitted a phase 3,
randomized, active-controlled trial in pediatric subjects with CABP and hospital-acquired
bacterial pneumonia (HABP) and a phase 3 trial in adults with HABP and ventilator-associated
bacterial pneumonia (VABP). Data from the pediatric CABP/HABP trial were primarily used to
support the safety of ceftobiprole in pediatric subjects with CABP with efficacy extrapolated
from the adult CABP trial. Indications for HABP/VABP in adults and HABP in pediatric
subjects were not sought in this application and the data from the HABP/VABP subjects
informed safety assessments.
The safety database consisted of 464 subjects who received at least one dose of ceftobiprole in
phase 1 studies, and 1315 total subjects who received at least one dose of ceftobiprole at the tobe-marketed dose in the phase 3 trials. Overall, the safety findings observed with ceftobiprole
were similar to other FDA-approved cephalosporins. The risks can be mitigated through labeling
and further evaluated during routine pharmacovigilance.

34

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
The overall benefit-risk profile is favorable to support approval of ceftobiprole for the treatment
of:
1. Adult patients with SAB, including those with right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE),
caused by methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates
2. Adult patients with ABSSSI caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive
and gram-negative microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible and
methicillin-resistant isolates), Streptococcus pyogenes, and Klebsiella pneumoniae
3. Adult and pediatric patients (3 months to less than 18 years old) with CABP caused by
susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms:
Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus
influenzae, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae
The drug product established name and strength will be expressed in terms of the salt (i.e.,
ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, 667 mg/vial) and labeling will include a statement
stating that 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole (the
active metabolite). This is an exception to the USP Salt Policy to eliminate having three
different names/strengths in labeling (i.e., based on the prodrug, salt form, and active
metabolite), thereby reducing the possibility for medication errors and harmonizing the US FDA
labeling with existing medical literature and product labeling from other countries.
For detailed information supporting the basis for this approval, please refer to the reviews
included in this interdisciplinary assessment and the product quality review.

In both adults and children, CABP is a serious
Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) is generally
infection that causes significant morbidity and
defined as an infection of the lung parenchyma in patients
without recent healthcare exposure. The microbiology of CABP mortality and may be caused by a variety of
typically includes S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. pneumoniae, pathogens.
S. aureus, and Enterobacterales. The rise in the incidence of
antibacterial resistance necessitates the use of broader
spectrum antibacterial drugs for treatment. Despite treatment,
CABP continues to have significant morbidity and mortality with
mortality rates ranging from 5.1% to 36.5% depending on the
severity at presentation, age, co-morbidities, and level of care
required (Fine et al. 1996, Peters et al. 2022) (Fine et al. 1996;
Peters et al. 2022)).
Community-acquired pneumonia, both bacterial and viral, is the
most common cause of death in children under 5 years of age
globally, causing nearly 15% of deaths in this age group (World
Health Organization). In the US, CABP is among the most
common causes of hospitalization in children of all ages with an
annual incidence rate of approximately 15.7 hospitalizations per
10,000 children (Jain et al. 2016)(Jain et al. 2015).
Initial treatment of CABP is empiric and is tailored to risk factors
and severity of illness at presentation. FDA approved
antibacterial drugs include beta-lactams, cephalosporins,
macrolides, and fluoroquinolones with oral and parenteral
formulations.
In pediatric patients, treatment of mild to moderate CABP in the
outpatient setting involves empiric coverage of the most
common causative organism, S. pneumoniae. For hospitalized
patients, use of ampicillin demonstrates similar outcomes when
compared to broader regimens (Messinger et al. 2017), but
additional antibacterial coverage including cephalosporins and
macrolides are recommended in patients with history of allergic
reactions, recent influenza infection, or history of infection with
MDR organisms.

There are many antibacterial drugs approved
for treatment of CABP. However, with
increasing antibacterial resistance, adverse
reactions, including hypersensitivity, treatment
options may be limited in some patients.

2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
All three of the proposed indications (SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP) are serious and often lifethreatening infections with significant morbidity and mortality. While there are multiple
antibacterial drugs currently approved to treat ABSSSI and CABP, the continued evolution of
antibacterial resistance mechanisms, drug-drug interactions, and adverse effects of available
antibacterial drugs can limit treatment options. There is an urgent need to develop antibacterial
drugs which cover both gram-negative and gram-positive organisms, especially MRSA, which is
a major cause of hospital and community-acquired infections worldwide . Current treatments for
MRSA infections have certain limitations (e.g., vancomycin is associated with nephrotoxicity
and the need for drug monitoring, linezolid has certain drug-drug interactions and toxicities,
daptomycin does not penetrate the lung parenchyma, and ceftaroline is not FDA-approved for
difficult to treat infections such as bacteremia and RIE). Approved treatments for SAB, including
RIE due to MRSA are especially limited.
Ceftobiprole, an advanced generation cephalosporin antibacterial drug would provide an
effective treatment option with a favorable safety profile for the indications sought (SAB,
ABSSSI, and CABP). The Applicant submitted data demonstrating safety and effectiveness for
all three indications.
Trial BPR-CS-009 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to daptomycin ± aztreonam in
the treatment of subjects with SAB, including those with RIE, caused by methicillin-susceptible
and methicillin-resistant isolates in regard to the primary endpoint of overall success based on
data review committee assessment at the post-treatment evaluation visit in the modified intent-totreat population (ceftobiprole 69.8%, daptomycin 68.7% [difference 2.0%; 95% confidence
interval (CI): -7.1, 11.1]), which met the prespecified 15% noninferiority (NI) margin.
Trial BPR-CS-008 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam
in the treatment of subjects with ABSSSI with respect to the primary endpoint of early clinical
response in the intent-to-treat population (ceftobiprole 91.3%, vancomycin plus aztreonam
88.1% [difference 3.3%; 95% CI: -1.2, 7.8]), which met the prespecified 10% NI margin.
Trial CAP-3001 demonstrated that ceftobiprole is noninferior to ceftriaxone ± linezolid in the
treatment of adult subjects with CABP. In the intent-to-treat population, the clinical cure rate in
the ceftobiprole group was 76.4% compared with the comparator group at 79.3% with a
treatment difference of -2.9%, 95 CI (-9.3, 3.6), which met the prespecified 10% NI margin.
Efficacy for CABP in the pediatric population was extrapolated from the adult CABP Trial.
The safety database for ceftobiprole was adequate for the proposed dosing regimens, intended
subject populations, and respective indications. Generally, the Applicant provided data
demonstrating that the safety of ceftobiprole was similar to the active comparator in each trial.
Overall, ceftobiprole has a favorable safety profile, and safety findings can be adequately
addressed in labeling and by routine pharmacovigilance.

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Based on review of all available efficacy and safety data, NDA 218275 for ceftobiprole provides
substantial evidence of effectiveness and a favorable benefit-risk profile for the treatment of the
following indications:
1. Treatment of adult patients with SAB, including those with right-sided infective endocarditis,
caused by methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates
2. Treatment of adult patients with ABSSSI caused by susceptible isolates of the following
gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillinsusceptible and methicillin-resistant isolates), Streptococcus pyogenes, and Klebsiella
pneumoniae
3. Treatment of adult and pediatric patients (3 months to less than 18 years old) with CABP
caused by susceptible isolates of the following gram-positive and gram-negative
microorganisms: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-susceptible isolates), Streptococcus
pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Escherichia coli, and
Klebsiella pneumoniae

Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)

II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
3. Introduction
Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection (Zevtera) is a cephalosporin antibacterial drug that
binds to penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits their transpeptidase activity. The active
ingredient (drug substance), ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, is a salt of a prodrug, ceftobiprole
medocaril, and the active metabolite is ceftobiprole. The dosage form of the drug product is a
powder for injection. Ceftobiprole is currently approved in several countries outside of the US
for the treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) and hospital-acquired
bacterial pneumonia (HABP).
Ceftobiprole was submitted under new drug application (NDA) 022132 for treatment of
complicated skin and skin structure infections by the previous Applicant, Johnson and Johnson
Pharmaceutical Research & Development LLC (J&J) on May 18, 2007. NDA 022132 received
an Approvable Letter on March 17, 2008, a Complete Response Letter on November 21, 2008,
and a Complete Response Letter on December 28, 2009. The Clinical Deficiencies cited in these
letters concerned studies BAP 00154 and BAP 00414 which are not included in this new NDA
218275. Ownership of NDA 022132 was transferred back to Basilea Pharmaceutica Ltd. on
January 24, 2011.
Ceftobiprole medocaril for injection was granted Qualified Infectious Disease Product
designation for the CABP, acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI), and
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (SAB) indications on July 20, 2015, August 7, 2015, and
December 8, 2017, respectively. Refer to Section 12 for a more detailed regulatory summary.
In this NDA submission, the proposed indications are for the treatment of adult patients with
SAB, including right-sided infective endocarditis (RIE), ABSSSI, and CABP and for treatment
of pediatric patients 3 months to less than 18 years old with CABP. For current available
therapies and typical pathogens for each indication, refer to Section 2.1.
All three indications were supported by phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, active
controlled noninferiority (NI) trials which met their respective primary endpoints within the
prespecified NI margins. Refer to Section 6 and 7 for reviews of efficacy and safety for each
trial.

46

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
The proposed dosing regimen is ceftobiprole 500 mg every 6 hours on Days 1 to 8, followed by
every 8 hours from Day 9 up to 42 days for SAB and 500 mg every 8 hours for 5 to 14 days for
ABSSSI and CABP with dosing adjustments based on renal function. The initial proposal by the
Applicant was based on the strength of the amount of the “active moiety/metabolite” as 500 mg
ceftobiprole/vial.
During the NDA review, the OPQ team recommended that the drug product established name
and strength be revised following the USP Salt Policy to express the amount of the prodrug
neutral form (i.e., ceftobiprole medocaril for injection, 646 mg/vial). In response, the Applicant
requested exemption from the USP Salt Policy following the example of a previously approved
product which was also a salt of a prodrug, Cresemba (isavuconazonium sulfate), for which the
strength is expressed in terms of the salt in approved labeling.
The clinical team and the Division of Medication and Error Prevention Analysis (DMEPA)
agreed with the Applicant that an exception to the USP Salt Policy would eliminate having three
different names/strengths in labeling (i.e., based on the prodrug, salt form, and active
metabolite), thereby reducing the possibility for medication errors and also harmonizing the US
FDA labeling with existing medical literature and product labeling from other countries. Upon
further discussion of the drug product name and strength between the Office of New Drugs
(OND) and Office of Policy and Pharmaceutical Quality (OPPQ) teams, a consensus was
reached that the drug product established name and strength should be expressed in terms of the
salt (i.e., ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, 667 mg/vial) and labeling would include a
statement stating that 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of
ceftobiprole. For details regarding this decision, refer to the Memorandum filed in DARRTS on
3/21/24 by Jibril Abdus-Samad, OPQ/OPPQ/COSS.

3.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
The primary evidence of effectiveness and safety of ceftobiprole for the proposed indications of
the treatment of SAB and ABSSSI in adults, and CABP in adult and pediatric patients were
provided in five clinical trials. Four of the trials were submitted for efficacy evaluation of
ceftobiprole. The HABP/ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia (VABP) trial was submitted
to support the safety evaluation. All five studies were randomized, double-blind, activecontrolled, multicenter, phase 3 studies. The active control and the ceftobiprole dosing used in
each study varied based on the clinical condition being treated. The endpoint evaluations in each
trial were also adjusted based on the clinical indication. Additional data from post-marketing
surveillance from other countries along with a review of literature publications were evaluated to
support the safety evaluation. See Section 7.3 for further details.
Key review issues that were identified during the review are addressed in greater detail in
Sections 6.3 for efficacy and Section 7.7 for safety. Overall, the submitted clinical trials were
adequate for the safety and efficacy evaluation of ceftobiprole. Table 5 provides an overview of
the clinical trials relevant to the review of ceftobiprole’s efficacy and safety.

5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics,
and Clinical Pharmacology
5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential
Effectiveness
Nonclinical Ceftobiprole PK/PD Information
Several studies were conducted to examine the nonclinical pharmacokinetics (PK)/
pharmacodynamics (PD) of ceftobiprole in murine thigh and pneumonia models. Percent of time
that free-drug concentrations remain above the minimum inhibitory concentration (%fT>MIC)
was best correlated with ceftobiprole efficacy, indicating that antibacterial activity of
ceftobiprole is time dependent, similar to other beta-lactams (see Section 14.1.1 for more
information).
53
Integrated Review Template, version 3.0 (05/25/2022)

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Identification of PK/PD Target
An efficacy study was performed in neutropenic thigh-infected mice given single subcutaneous
doses (0.2 mL/ dose) of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (10, 40, and 160 mg/kg). A sigmoid
dose-response model derived from the four-parameter Hill equation was used to calculate the
dose of ceftobiprole producing a net bacteriostatic effect and 1-log10 kill over 24 hours. The free
time above MIC (fT > MIC) values for each static and 1-log kill dose were estimated from PK
and MICs. Ceftobiprole was tested against a total of 14 gram-positive strains and five strains of
gram-negative bacteria, including E. coli, K. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa and E. cloacae (see
Section 14.1.1 for more information). The results of %fT > MIC to achieve bacteriostasis, 1log10 kill and 2-log kill are presented in Table 7.
Table 7. Summary Statistics for Ceftobiprole Free-Drug Plasma %T>MIC Targets Associated With
Net Bacterial Stasis and 1- and 2-log10 CFU Reductions From Baseline in a Neutropenic Murine
Thigh Infection Model

Source: Craig 2008
Abbreviations: CFU, colony forming unit; MIC, minimum inhibitory concentration

Since free-drug plasma %T>MIC targets from this study were only reported for net bacterial
stasis and a 2-log10 colony forming unit (CFU) reduction from Baseline, free-drug plasma
%T>MIC targets associated with a 1-log10 CFU reduction from baseline were linearly
interpolated by averaging the targets for net bacterial stasis and a 2-log10 CFU reduction from
Baseline.
Based on these results, the Applicant chose ceftobiprole bactericidal (1-log kill) %fT>MIC
values of 30% and 50% for the treatment of infections caused by gram-positive and gramnegative pathogens, respectively.

Clearance

5 L/hr

Half-life

The terminal half-life of ceftobiprole is approximately 3 hours, ranging from 2.4
to 4.11 hours across the phase 1 studies.

Metabolic pathway(s)

Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is the active pharmaceutical ingredient.
Ceftobiprole medocaril is the prodrug of the active form, ceftobiprole.
Conversion from ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to ceftobiprole occurs rapidly
and is mediated by non-specific plasma esterases.
Ceftobiprole undergoes minimal metabolism to an open-ring metabolite which is
microbiologically inactive. Systemic exposure of the open-ring metabolite is
approximately 4% of the parent exposure.

Primary excretion
pathways (% dose)

The main route of elimination of ceftobiprole is by renal excretion, by glomerular
filtration. Following single dose administration, approximately 89% of the
administered dose is recovered in the urine as active ceftobiprole (83%), the
open-ring metabolite (5%) and ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (<1%; Study CSI1004).

No clinically significant differences in the PK of ceftobiprole were observed in
adults based on body weight. Dose adjustment is not needed.

Dosage in Pediatric Patients with CABP
The recommended dosage in pediatric subjects with CABP is outlined in Table 11. Evidence of
effectiveness for the proposed ceftobiprole dosage in CABP pediatric patients ages 3 months and
older is based on safety and PK data in pediatric patients as well as extrapolation of effectiveness
from adult CABP patients. Because CABP is pathophysiologically similar in adults and pediatric
patients aged 3 months and older, the efficacious ceftobiprole exposures in adults are expected to
also be effective in pediatric patients. Population PK analyses demonstrate that estimated
ceftobiprole exposures resulting from the proposed dosage in pediatric CABP patients are similar
to the efficacious exposures in adults, thus enabling extrapolation of effectiveness from adults to
pediatric patients. Additionally, supportive evidence of effectiveness for the proposed dosage is
provided by the results of probability of PK/PD target attainment analysis (see Section 14.5 for
more information).

6.2. Clinical Studies/Trials Intended to
Demonstrate Efficacy
6.2.1. SAB, Trial BPR-CS-009
6.2.1.1. Design, Trial BPR-CS-009
Trial BPR-CS-009 was conducted from August 2018 to March 2022. The trial protocol was
reviewed as a special protocol assessment (SPA) under investigational new drug application
(IND) 64407. This was a randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, parallelarm, multi-center trial in adult hospitalized subjects with SAB, including infective endocarditis
(IE), which was conducted in two parts. Part 1 enrolled an initial cohort of subjects (Cohort 1)
for a maximum treatment duration of 28 days as animal studies had indicated the potential of an
increased risk of convulsions with prolonged ceftobiprole treatment duration (> 4 weeks) and no
prior clinical studies of ceftobiprole with this treatment duration had been conducted. Based on a
safety evaluation of Cohort 1, the Data and Safety Monitoring Board decided that it was safe to
proceed to Part 2. Part 2 allowed a longer treatment duration of up to 42 days and the inclusion
of subjects with more difficult to treat infections such as osteomyelitis and epidural or cerebral
abscess who were excluded from Cohort 1. Subjects with left-sided infective endocarditis (LIE)
diagnosed after randomization were also permitted to continue in the trial.
Following a screening period of up to 72 hours, subjects were randomized 1:1 to receive
intravenous (IV) ceftobiprole or daptomycin ± aztreonam. The randomization was stratified by
Trial site, dialysis status, and prior antibacterial treatment use within 7 days before
randomization. Following the completion of treatment, visits were scheduled at end-of-treatment
(EOT) (within 72 hours of the last Trial drug administration), Day 35 (± 3 days), Day 42 (± 3
days), and at post-treatment evaluation (PTE) on Day 70 (± 5 days) post-randomization. Note
that the Day 35 and Day 42 visits could have been active treatment periods for subjects in Part 2
59

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
requiring up to 42 days of treatment. The total duration of the Trial for each subject was
approximately 10 weeks.
A total of 390 subjects were planned to be randomized, and a total of 390 subjects were actually
randomized and comprised the intent-to-treat (ITT) population (ceftobiprole n = 192; comparator
n = 198). An independent blinded data review committee (DRC) comprising six infectious
diseases experts was assembled to review detailed subject profiles, including imaging and
microbiological and laboratory results, of all subjects in the ITT population, to assess the
baseline categories of complicated SAB, the response outcome for the primary endpoint, and the
secondary endpoints of microbiological outcomes and death attributed to SAB.
Primary Endpoint
Overall success assessed by the DRC at the PTE visit assessed in the modified intent-to-treat
population.
Overall success was defined as all of the following criteria being met:
1. Subject alive at Day 70 (± 5 days) post-randomization
2. No new metastatic foci or complications of the SAB infection
3. Resolution or improvement of SAB-related clinical signs and symptoms
4. Two negative blood cultures for S. aureus (without any subsequent positive blood culture for
S. aureus):
•

At least one while the subject was on active study treatment; AND

•

Confirmed by at least one subsequent negative blood culture for S. aureus
a. Either in the period between 7 days after the EOT Visit and the PTE Visit
b. Or at the PTE Visit

Treatment failure was defined as any of the following:
1. Premature discontinuation of study treatment due to DRC assessed lack of efficacy or for
adverse events (AEs) that represented manifestation of disease progression or relapse, at any
time between first dose of study drug and the PTE visit.
2. Development of new metastatic or other complications related to SAB between Day 8 and
the PTE visit.
3. SAB relapse/reinfection based on evidence from a blood culture positive for S. aureus (after
documented clearance of S. aureus from the bloodstream and clinical improvement) between
the EOT and PTE visits.
4. Receipt of systemic non-study antibacterial treatment, other than those permitted under the
protocol, for the treatment of SAB. This included subjects who were prematurely
discontinued from study therapy due to an AE, but who required continuation of antibacterial
treatment for SAB.
5. Treatment of infections other than SAB with systemic non-study antibacterial treatment
which was potentially effective against S. aureus, and which was considered by the DRC to

60

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
have a relevant impact on the primary endpoint in accordance with guidelines provided in the
protocol.
6. Death for any reason between first administration of study drug and the PTE visit.
7. Indeterminate outcome, defined as any data needed to determine whether the outcome was
success or failure was missing at the PTE visit, including but not limited to:
•

Missing PTE visit, or missing key data to evaluate the primary endpoint

•

Lost-to-follow-up, or subjects who withdrew consent prior to the PTE visit

•

Subjects not meeting the criteria for success or failure, or subjects not meeting all criteria
for overall success

8. Requirement for systemic antibacterial treatment for SAB beyond EOT.
Secondary Endpoints
1. All-cause mortality assessed at Day 70 (PTE Visit) in the mITT population (ITT subjects
who received any dose of study medication, and had a blood culture positive for S. aureus at
Baseline).
2. Microbiological eradication assessed by the DRC at Day 70 (PTE Visit) in the mITT
population.
3. The overall success rate in the ITT, mITT, and clinically evaluable (CE) populations:
•

At the EOT and PTE (ITT and CE populations only) visits

•

At the EOT and PTE visits, for RIE versus non-IE SAB

•

At the EOT and PTE visits, by renal-function status

4. Development of new metastatic foci or other complications of SAB after Day 7 were
assessed in the mITT and CE populations.
5. Time to S. aureus bloodstream clearance in the mITT and CE populations, defined as the
elapsed time (days) from randomization to bloodstream clearance, with bloodstream
clearance defined as the occurrence of two consecutive study days with blood-culturenegative assessments for S. aureus; bloodstream clearance in subjects with intermittent
positive on treatment blood cultures started after the last positive blood culture. Subjects with
S. aureus relapse or reinfection as per DRC assessment were not considered as bloodstream
clearance.
6. Safety and tolerability.
7. Pharmacokinetics.
6.2.1.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial BPR-CS-009
The trial enrolled adult subjects with complicated SAB, defined as subjects with at least one
positive blood culture for S. aureus at Baseline, signs and symptoms of bacteremia (fever,
white blood cell [WBC] count, tachycardia, and/or hypotension), and one of the following
underlying conditions or complications: chronic intermittent hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis,
61

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
persistent SAB, definitive native-valve RIE, ABSSSIs, or metastatic infections of native tissue
(e.g., septic arthritis, septic/suppurative thrombophlebitis, visceral abscess, septic pulmonary
emboli).
Subjects with osteomyelitis or cerebral/epidural abscess were to be enrolled in Part 2 only.
Subjects who received treatment with potentially effective anti-staphylococcal systemic
antibacterial treatment for more than 48 hours within 7 days before randomization were excluded
from the trial unless they met the criteria for persistent SAB.
Inclusion Criteria
Subjects meeting all of Inclusion Criteria 1 – 5 and at least one of Inclusion Criteria 6 – 11 were
eligible for enrollment:
1. Male or female ≥18 years of age.
2. Informed consent signed by the subject (or by their legally acceptable representative, if
appropriate) indicating that they understood the purpose of, and procedures required for, the
trial and were willing to participate in the trial.
3. SAB, based on at least one positive blood culture obtained within the 72 hours prior to
randomization:
•

Identified by culture laboratory report, or

•

Positive diagnostic test for S. aureus (e.g., polymerase chain reaction [PCR], tube
coagulase test and fluorescent in situ hybridization) obtained from a blood culture.

At least one of the following signs or symptoms of bacteremia within the 72 hours prior to
randomization (may be based on measurements obtained before or after informed consent but
within the 72 hours prior to randomization):
1. Fever >38°C / 100.4°F measured orally, >38.5°C / 101.3°F measured tympanically, >37.5°C
/ 99.5°F measured by axillary method, or >39°C /102.2°F measured rectally
2. WBC count ˃10.0 x 10⁹/L or <4.0 x10⁹/L, or >10% immature neutrophils (bands)
3. Tachycardia (heart rate >90 beats per minute [bpm])
4. Hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] <90 mm Hg)
5. Required duration of study antibacterial treatment ≤42 days.
6. SAB in subjects undergoing chronic intermittent hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.
7. Persistent SAB: documented failure of bloodstream clearance, defined as a positive blood
culture for S. aureus within the 72 hours prior to randomization, after prior appropriate antistaphylococcal treatment (except failure under daptomycin therapy) of at least 3 complete
days.
8. Other forms of complicated SAB, including the following:
•

ABSSSIs

•

Metastatic infection of native tissue. Examples include but were not limited to:

9. Septic arthritis or bacterial joint infection/empyema
62

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
10. Septic or suppurative thrombophlebitis
11. Visceral soft-tissue abscesses requiring ≤42 days of study antibacterial treatment
12. Septic pulmonary emboli/infarction
13. Definite native-valve RIE by Modified Duke’s Criteria.
Prohibited Concomitant Medications
Concomitant systemic antibacterials that provide activity against S. aureus were prohibited
during the period from randomization up to the PTE visit. The use of non-study antibacterial
treatment during the trial was not necessarily considered to be an outcome of ‘failure’. The
significance of concomitant potentially effective non-study antibacterial treatment (except
aztreonam, metronidazole, nitrofurantoin, and oral vancomycin) was assessed in accordance with
the guidelines provided in the clinical study report (CSR) to determine whether the treatment had
an impact on the primary endpoint.
Permitted Antibacterial Treatments
The following concomitant antibacterial medications were permitted:
1. In the daptomycin treatment arm, aztreonam using a standard-dose regimen at the site for
coverage of gram-negative infections (i.e., for polymicrobial bloodstream infections, or
gram-negative non-bloodstream infections). Subjects randomized to the ceftobiprole arm
who were considered to require coverage against gram-negative infections received dummy
treatment with placebo so that blinding was maintained during the active treatment phase.
2. In both treatment arms:
•

Nitrofurantoin for urinary tract infections

•

Metronidazole using a standard-dose regimen at the site for coverage of anaerobic
infections

•

Oral vancomycin was considered a non-systemic antibiotic and was permitted for use at
any time during the trial.
6.2.1.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial BPR-CS-009

Disposition of Subjects
The disposition of subjects is described in Figure 1. A total of 390 subjects were randomized to
receive either the ceftobiprole (n = 192) or daptomycin (n = 198) treatment. Three subjects did
not receive study treatment (1 in ceftobiprole arm and 2 in the daptomycin arm). Two subjects,
both in the ceftobiprole arm, were determined by central laboratory results not to have a
confirmed positive blood culture for S. aureus at Baseline.

Baseline demographic and disease characteristics
As shown in Table 13, the baseline demographic and disease characteristics in the mITT
population were generally balanced across the treatment arms. Subjects in the mITT were mostly
White (96%), European (93%) or male (69%) with a median age of 58 years. Approximately 8%
of subjects were Hispanic or Latino. Of note, 54% of subjects had a fever at baseline, 13% were
on chronic dialysis and 40% had an abnormal WBC at baseline. Prior antibacterial medication
use was common at 70% and concomitant (allowed) antibacterial medication use was also
common using aztreonam (34%) or metronidazole (6%).
Reviewer Comments
The large percentage of White subjects (96%) may limit the generalizability of the trial’s
findings to other races.

Analysis Sets
The analysis sets defined in the trial were as follows:
ITT Population
All randomized subjects.
The Safety Population
All randomized subjects who received at least one dose of study drug.
mITT Population
ITT subjects who received any dose of study medication, and who had a blood culture positive
for S. aureus at baseline.
CE Population
Protocol-compliant ITT subjects who complied with important aspects of the study.
Sample Size Determination
The sample size estimate was based on:
•
•
•
•

A point estimate for overall success of 40% in each treatment arm in the mITT
population
One-sided alpha level of 0.025
Power of >80%
Non-inferiority margin of 15% for the between-arm difference in the primary endpoint

With these assumptions, enrollment of 175 subjects per treatment arm (total of 350 subjects) was
required for the mITT population. Assuming that approximately 90% of subjects in the ITT
population had confirmed SAB and therefore were to be included in the mITT population, it was
necessary for 195 subjects per arm (total of 390 subjects) to be randomized and receive Trial
treatment.
Statistical Methods
Primary Analysis
The Trial was designed to determine whether ceftobiprole was non-inferior to daptomycin for the
primary outcome measure of overall success at the PTE Visit at Day 70 (± 5 days) after
randomization, in the mITT population. The specified NI margin was 15%.
Reviewer Comments
This 15% NI margin was based on 7 studies from the pre-penicillin era reporting clinical
outcome (survival) in untreated subjects with SAB which combined suggested all-cause mortality
(ACM) of 76% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 71%, 79%) as well as 3 studies of mortality in
SAB subjects receiving antibacterial treatment which suggested an ACM of 16% (95% CI: 12%,
20%). The M1 is estimated to be 51% for ACM. The protocol stated that “An estimation of M1
for an overall success endpoint is not possible, as this was not reported in the historical studies,
68

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
which considered survival to be success” but that “the mortality data suggest that M1 for a
clinical/overall success outcome for SAB would similarly be very large, i.e., in the range of 50%,
when outcomes are compared for untreated subjects and subjects who received effective
antibacterial treatment.” The NI margin of 15% was chosen based on clinical judgement. With a
sample size of 250–350 subjects (in the mITT population), an NI margin of 15% would allow for
the determination of noninferiority only if the point estimate between ceftobiprole and
daptomycin is <5%.
The difference in the percentage of responders (i.e., subjects with overall success at PTE)
(ceftobiprole arm minus the comparator arm) was determined, and a two-sided 95% CI for the
difference was computed, with adjustment for actual dialysis status, and prior antibacterial
treatment use (defined as receipt of medications within 7 days prior to randomization that were
categorized as potentially effective systemic antibacterial treatments). Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel
(CMH) weights were used for the stratum weight in the calculation of the CI. The non-inferiority
hypothesis test was a one-sided hypothesis test performed at the 2.5% level of significance. If the
lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the difference in response rates in the mITT population
was greater than −15%, the noninferiority of ceftobiprole to daptomycin therapy was concluded.
Secondary Analyses
Secondary analyses considered the above approach for overall success assessed by the DRC at
the EOT visit in the ITT and CE populations. All-cause mortality was assessed in the mITT and
ITT populations and time to death was calculated using Kaplan-Meier methods. Survival rates
(event-free probability estimates) at Day 28 and Day 70 in the ITT and mITT populations were
provided and associated two-sided 95% CIs were calculated using the Greenwood formula. The
hazard ratio for all-cause mortality and associated 95% CI were provided using a Cox
proportional-hazard model, with treatment and actual stratum (dialysis status and prior
antibacterial treatment use) as covariates. S. aureus clearance was analyzed in a similar manner
as all-cause mortality.
6.2.1.4. Results of Analyses, Trial BPR-CS-009
Primary and Key Secondary Endpoint Analyses
Table 15 shows the results from the primary analysis and reasons for failure. For the primary
endpoint of overall success at the PTE visit at Day 70 (± 5 days) after randomization in the mITT
population, noninferiority was demonstrated with an adjusted difference (Ceftobiprole –
Daptomycin) of 2.0% with a lower 95% confidence limit of -7.1% which exceeded the prespecified NI margin of -15%. Similar findings were observed when considering the primary
endpoint in the CE population.
Reasons for failure were generally similar between the treatment arms; however, there was a
lower proportion of failures due to ‘Requirement for systemic antibacterial treatment for SAB
beyond protocol-defined maximum study treatment duration’ in the ceftobiprole arm, 9/57
(15.2%) vs. 15/62 (24.2%). A slightly lower proportion of failures due to SAB
relapse/reinfection was also observed in the ceftobiprole arm, 2/57 (3.5%) vs. 4/62 (6.5%). The
most common reason for treatment failure in both treatment arms was ‘Treatment of SAB with
systemic non-study antibacterial treatment, other than those permitted under the protocol’ which

was more common in the ceftobiprole arm accounting for 20/57 (39.1%) versus 19/61 (30.6%) of
failures.

Subgroup Analyses
Subgroup analyses for the primary endpoint, ‘overall success based on DRC assessment at the
PTE visit’ by gender, race and ethnicity are shown in Table 17. Treatment differences tended to
be more favorable in ceftobiprole subjects among subjects who were 18-34 years, male, White
and Hispanic/Latino. There were a few other notable findings. Among subjects 18 to 34 years of
age, overall success rates were 17/20 (85%) versus 11/19 (57.9%) which showed a nominally
significant treatment difference of 26.7% (95 CI: 0.4, 53.0) favoring ceftobiprole. Also, among
non-White subjects, overall success rates were 0/5 (0%) for subjects in the ceftobiprole arm
versus 5/6 (66.7%) for subjects in the daptomycin arm which showed a nominally significant
treatment difference of -55.6% (95 CI: -100.0, -10.5) favoring daptomycin.
Reviewer Comments
The small number of non-White subjects combined with the nominally significant difference in
non-White subjects favoring daptomycin may make generalizing trial results to non-White
subjects more difficult. Of note, this difference was likely due to the small sample size and
random variation since the subjects’ reasons for failure were often not directly related to a lack
of treatment effect.

Conclusions
Trial BPR-CS-009 met its primary objective of demonstrating noninferiority for the pre-specified
primary endpoint of overall success based on DRC Assessment at the PTE (Day 70) Visit. Key
secondary endpoints also appeared to be generally consistent with noninferiority. Overall, there
were no major concerns regarding the evidence of effectiveness.
Minor concerns are related to subject selection with approximately 96% of subjects being
‘White,’ which may limit the generalizability of efficacy findings to other races. There were also
less favorable treatment differences in a few subgroups receiving ceftobiprole (‘non-White’,
75

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
‘U.S.’, ‘MRSA’ and ‘polymicrobial BSIs’), although sample sizes tended to be small. Findings
of large regional differences in clinical overall success rates at PTE (e.g., Ukrainian vs. ExUkrainian sites) may also limit generalizability. Although the high success rates at the Ukrainian
sites did not positively affect the estimated treatment difference in this trial, they could affect the
assumptions used in the justification of the NI margin (see 6.3 for more details).

6.2.2. ABSSSI, Trial BPR-CS-008
6.2.2.1. Design, Trial BPR-CS-008
Trial BPR-CS-008 was conducted from August 2018 to March 2022. The protocol was reviewed
as a SPA under IND 64407. The design of pivotal trial BPR-CS-008 was based on the current
FDA Guidance for Industry Acute Bacterial Skin and Skin Structure Infections: Developing
Drugs for Treatment, October 2013, including with respect to the efficacy endpoints, timing of
assessments, and statistical considerations.
This was a randomized, double-blind, active-controlled, parallel-arm, multicenter trial in adult
hospitalized subjects to establish the safety and efficacy of ceftobiprole compared with
vancomycin plus aztreonam in the treatment of ABSSSIs. The trial had a noninferiority design,
with vancomycin plus aztreonam selected as an established comparator regimen. Vancomycin,
recognized in current guidelines as the standard treatment for ABSSSI, is effective against grampositive bacteria, including MRSA. Aztreonam was added to vancomycin due to its efficacy
against gram-negative bacteria.
Trial BPR-CS-008 was conducted in three phases:
1. Pre-treatment: Screening and baseline, duration up to 24 hours.
2. Active treatment: Randomization and at least 5 days, and up to 10 days, of study drug
administration. Study treatment could be extended up to 14 days if required.
3. Post-treatment: An EOT visit within 24 hours after last treatment, a test-of-cure (TOC) visit
15 – 22 days after randomization and at least 5 days after EOT, and a last follow-up visit 28 –
35 days after last treatment. In addition, survival status (Alive; Dead; Lost to Follow-up) was
to be verified for evaluation of all-cause mortality. Survival status (by telephone or visit) was
to be obtained at Day 28 (± 2 days).
The total duration of the study for each subject was approximately 5 – 7 weeks.
The selected ceftobiprole dose was the dose approved for the HABP and CABP indications in
non-U.S. countries: 500 mg administered as a 2-hour IV infusion every 8 hours, to be adjusted
for subjects with moderate or severe renal impairment (500 mg of ceftobiprole is equivalent to
667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium). The dose of vancomycin was 1,000 mg or 15 mg/kg
administered as a 2-hour IV infusion every 12 hours; this could be modified for renal function.
The dose of aztreonam was 1,000 mg per 0.5-hour IV infusion every 12 hours, to be adjusted for
subjects with severe renal impairment; the need for treatment with aztreonam was to be
reassessed at the 72-hour study Visit.

76

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Other design considerations:
•
•

Primary measurement of the target lesion size was to be performed using a flexible ruler,
measuring longest length, and maximum width perpendicular to the length.
Measurements were to be performed at Screening (prior to randomization and within the 6
hours prior to first dose of study drug), twice on Day 2, Day 3, and Day 4, and once on
Day 8, and the EOT, TOC, and last follow-up visits. On days when two measurements were
obtained, the measurements were to be taken at least 8 hours apart. Infection-site assessment
includes incision/drainage, erythema, heat/localized warmth, pain/tenderness to palpation,
fluctuance, and swelling/induration.

•

A digital photograph was to be obtained at Screening, at the early clinical response
assessment (48–72 hours after first treatment), and at the EOT and TOC Visit, for each
subject (primary ABSSSI lesion), and was to be used for documentation purposes and as
source data. Digital photography was not to be used for the measurement of the ABSSSI
lesion size area; the determination of the ABSSSI lesion size area was to be solely based on
the ruler measurements.

•

Clinical success was to be assessed by the investigator using a four-point scale relative to the
baseline assessment: cured, improved, stable, or worsened. In case of worsened (e.g.,
bacteremia, osteomyelitis, amputation), signs and symptoms needed to be documented as
AEs.

•

Concomitant antibacterial therapies, other drug therapies, and non-drug procedures were to
be assessed at all scheduled study visits.

•

Survival status (by telephone or visit) was to be obtained at Day 28.

The primary objective for Trial BPR-CS-008 was to demonstrate the non-inferiority of
ceftobiprole to vancomycin plus aztreonam in subjects with ABSSSI with respect to early
clinical response based on percent reduction in lesion size at 48 – 72 hours after first treatment in
the ITT population.
The main secondary objective was to demonstrate the non-inferiority of ceftobiprole to
vancomycin plus aztreonam in subjects with ABSSSI with respect to investigator-assessed
clinical success at the TOC visit 15 – 22 days after randomization in the ITT and Clinically
Evaluable populations.
Primary Endpoint
Early clinical response based on percent reduction from baseline in lesion size at 48 – 72 hours
after first study-drug administration, measured in subjects who did not receive rescue therapy,
and were alive. A clinical response was defined as a percentage reduction in lesion size greater
than or equal to 20 percent compared to baseline.
The Main Secondary Endpoint
Investigator-assessed clinical success at the TOC visit 15 – 22 days after randomization, and at
least 5 days after the EOT, assessed in the ITT and CE populations.

6.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial BPR-CS-008
The eligible subject population for trial BPR-CS-008 included adults who were diagnosed with
ABSSSI (cellulitis/erysipelas, major cutaneous abscess, wound infection) with regional or
systemic signs of infection, who were hospitalized (in a hospital or equivalent medical
confinement or clinical research unit) and required IV antibacterial treatment. Subjects with
other forms of ABSSSI or uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections were excluded, as
were those with infections related to prosthetic devices, or infections which required more than
two surgical interventions.
Subjects who had received any systemic antibacterial treatment within 14 days, or topical
antibacterial on the primary lesion within 96 hours, before first infusion of study drug, were also
excluded.
The minimum lesion size had to be 75 cm2 using standardized measurements (longest length of
the lesion by widest width perpendicular to that length) with a flexible plastic ruler. The
proportion of subjects with major cutaneous abscesses was also not to exceed 30% of the total
subject population included.
Inclusion Criteria
Subjects meeting all of the following:
1. Male or female, aged ≥18 years.
2. Diagnosis of ABSSSI, meeting at least one of the definitions in (a) to (c) below. Local
symptoms must have started within the 7 days prior to the Screening visit.
3. Cellulitis/erysipelas, defined as a diffuse skin infection characterized by all of the following
within 24 h:
a. Rapidly spreading areas of erythema, edema, and/or induration with a minimum total
lesion surface area of 75 cm².
b. No collection of pus apparent upon visual examination.
c. At least two of the following local signs of infection:
•

•

clinical research unit) until completion of the early-clinical-response assessment for the
primary endpoint.
19. Informed consent signed by the subject, or their legally acceptable representative if
appropriate, indicating that they understand the purpose of, and procedures required for, the
trial, and are willing to participate.

Prohibited Concomitant Medications
Concomitant systemic antibacterial drugs were prohibited during the trial up to the TOC visit,
with the following exceptions:
1. Vancomycin PO 125 mg or 250 mg every 6 hours, fidaxomicin PO 200 mg q12h, or
metronidazole IV or PO 500 mg q8h, in both treatment arms, for the treatment of Clostridium
difficile infections.
2. Metronidazole IV as adjunctive therapy in both treatment arms for coverage of anaerobic
bacteria.
3. Nitrofurantoin at any time during the trial in both treatment arms as it does not achieve
therapeutic blood levels.
All NSAIDs were prohibited until 72 hours after start of treatment, and were then permitted only
after early clinical response had been determined.
The administration of steroids (>40 mg per day prednisolone, or equivalent), or
immunosuppressants was prohibited between administration of first study drug and the TOC
Visit.
Chronic systemic therapy with calcineurin-inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, or cyclosporin),
mycophenolate mofetil or mycophenolate sodium, azathioprine, sirolimus, and topical
antibacterial drugs on the primary lesion was prohibited from randomization to the TOC Visit.
Non-Drug Adjunctive Therapy
Adjuvant surgical treatment was recognized as appropriate and necessary for adequate treatment
of wound infections and abscesses. Subjects were evaluated at Screening to determine whether
more than one intra-operative surgical intervention was required. Those expected to require more
than two surgical interventions in the operating room for the ABSSSI were to be excluded from
the trial.
When indicated, the initial surgical procedure was to be performed before randomization, and
subsequent procedures performed no later than 48 hours after the start of treatment.
Adjunctive therapies permitted for the treatment of ABSSSI at any time were debridement at the
bedside, topical solutions, including antiseptic agents such as povidone-iodine (topical solutions
did not contain anti-microbial agents), and local bedside wound care in accordance with hospital
protocols.

receive trial treatment (1 in ceftobiprole arm and 2 in the vancomycin plus aztreonam arm). In

Baseline Demographic and Disease Characteristics
As shown in Table 26, the baseline demographic and disease characteristics in the mITT

of subjects had diabetes mellitus at baseline, 35% of subjects had fever at baseline, 16% had
CrCL <80 mL/min and 35% had abnormal WBC at baseline. Systemic prior antibacterial

Analysis Populations
The ITT Population
Included all randomized subjects, analyzed according to the treatment they were randomized to
receive, and if different, not according to what they actually received.
The Microbiological ITT Population
Was the subset of subjects in the ITT population who had causative (i.e., infecting) pathogens
identified by the central microbiology laboratory from skin lesion or blood cultures; local
laboratory identification results were only used if the corresponding causative pathogen was not
available for identification by the central laboratory. Subjects with no pathogens isolated at
Baseline (microbiologically non-evaluable) were excluded from the microbiological ITT (microITT) population.
CE Population
Was the subset of subjects in the ITT population who complied with important aspects of the
trial until the TOC visit, i.e., with no major protocol deviations (e.g., a completed response
outcome assessment, and no concomitant systemic antibacterial treatment or topical antibacterial
applied to the primary lesion).
The Microbiologically Evaluable Population
Was the subset of subjects in the micro-ITT population who were also in the CE population.
Analysis at each time point was performed on subjects with available response at that time point
(excluding those with microbiological response of ‘Not Evaluable’ or missing).
Sample Size Determination
A sample size of 674 subjects (337 per arm) provided at least 90% power to reject the
null hypothesis (H0) against the alternative hypothesis (HA) at the one-sided alpha level of
0.025 as follows, using a two-arm large-sample normal approximation test of Proportions.
Early clinical response rates of an at least 20% reduction in lesion area size (primary
endpoint) and clinical cure rates at the TOC visit (main secondary endpoint) were based on
recent phase 3 studies in ABSSSI. The sample size estimate was based on a point estimate for
early clinical response of 80% in each treatment arm in the ITT and CE population, a one-sided
alpha level of 0.025, a non-inferiority margin of 10 percentage points for the between-arm
difference of the primary endpoint.
Data Monitoring and Interim Analyses
Investigators, Applicant employees, and others involved in the conduct and analysis of the Trial
(with the exception of the unblinded pharmacist or delegate) remained blinded to the treatment
codes and interim analysis results until all monitoring decisions were made, and the database
locked for the final analysis.
A blinded interim analysis for sample size re-estimation assessed whether the initial sample size
estimate was adequate for evaluating the primary endpoint, and to select a larger sample size if
warranted.
84

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
The blinded interim analysis was performed in November 2018, and was based on pooled
information across the two treatment arms when early clinical response data were available for
60% of the subjects planned to be randomized (approximately 404 subjects). The number and
percentage of responders and non-responders based on the primary Endpoint (and Clinical
Success / No-Success based on the main secondary endpoint) were provided.
Reviewer Comments:
The interim analyses appeared to be conducted appropriately and there were no major concerns.
Note that no statistical adjustment was required, and the sample size specified in the protocol
remained unchanged after the blinded review of the primary and secondary endpoints.
Statistical Methods
Trial BPR-CS-008 was designed to determine whether ceftobiprole was non-inferior to
vancomycin plus aztreonam for both the primary endpoint of early clinical response and the main
secondary endpoint of investigator-assessed clinical success at the TOC visit. The main primary
analysis was based on the ITT population consisting of all randomized subjects. The weighted
difference in percentage of responders at 48–72 h (ceftobiprole arm minus the vancomycin plus
aztreonam arm), and the 95% CI for the weighted difference was computed using CMH weights
method adjusted for geographical region (North America and Europe), and actual type of
ABSSSI.
The non-inferiority hypothesis test was a one-sided hypothesis test performed at the 2.5% level
of significance. If the lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI for the difference in response rates
(ceftobiprole minus vancomycin plus aztreonam) in the ITT population was greater than -10%,
the non-inferiority of ceftobiprole to vancomycin plus aztreonam would be concluded. If noninferiority was declared at the one-sided significance level of 0.025, then the difference would be
tested for superiority. Superiority would be declared if the lower limit of the two-sided 95% CI
exceeded 0 (or equivalently p-value less than 0.05 using CMH test). The same analysis was
repeated on the CE population.
Reviewer Comments
The overall data from two studies by Snodgrass in 1937, both of which compared ultraviolet
light against a sulfonamide antibacterial drug, in subjects with cellulitis/erysipelas for an
outcome of cessation of spread of lesion at 48-72 hours, support a treatment difference of 18%.
Because this is thought to be conservatively estimated at 18 percent for antibacterial drugs in the
treatment of ABSSSI for the endpoint based on lesion size assessment, further discounting of the
treatment effect may not be necessary and thus M1 is estimated to be 18 percent. These scientific
data provide support for the selection of a noninferiority margin of 10 percent that preserves
some of M1 based on an endpoint of lesion size assessment. Refer to the ABSSSI Guidance2 for
further details on the justification of a 10% NI margin for ABSSSI.
The main secondary analysis was based on the weighted difference in percentage of clinical
success at the TOC visit (ceftobiprole arm minus the vancomycin plus aztreonam arm), and the

Treatment, October 2013

6.2.2.4. Results of Analyses, Trial BPR-CS-008
Primary Analysis
As shown in Table 27, ceftobiprole met the primary objective of this trial by demonstrating the
non-inferiority of ceftobiprole (greater than the pre-specified 10% non-inferiority margin) to
vancomycin plus aztreonam for the primary endpoint of early clinical response based on a 20%
or more reduction from baseline in lesion size at 48–72 hours after start of trial drug
administration. In the ITT population (primary analysis population), 306 subjects (91.3%) in the
ceftobiprole arm were responders (95% CI: 87.8, 94.1) versus 303 (88.1%) subjects in the
vancomycin plus aztreonam arm (95% CI: 84.2, 91.3). The proportion difference (ceftobiprole
minus vancomycin plus aztreonam) was 3.3% (95% CI: −1.2, 7.8). Since −1.2% (the lower limit
of this 95% CI) exceeded the required NI limit of −10%, non-inferiority was demonstrated.
There were 29 (8.7%) and 41 (11.9%) non-responders in the ceftobiprole and vancomycin plus
aztreonam arms, respectively. The most common reason for non-responders at 48-72 hours after
start of treatment was <20% reduction from baseline in surface area of primary lesion which
included 65.5% of ceftobiprole non-responders and 70.7% of vancomycin plus aztreonam nonresponders. In general, there were no notable treatment differences regarding the reasons for
non-response.

Secondary Analyses
As shown in Table 28, the main secondary endpoint was also supportive of non-inferiority in the
primary analysis. The proportion of clinical successes at TOC was slightly higher in the
ceftobiprole arm versus vancomycin plus aztreonam arm, 302/335 (90.1%) versus 306/344
(89.0%), respectively. The proportion difference (ceftobiprole minus vancomycin plus
aztreonam) was 1.0% (95% CI: −3.5, 5.6). There were no concerns related to reasons for
nonclinical success which were mostly comparable between arms.
There were 33 (9.9%) and 38 (11.0%) nonclinical successes at TOC in the ceftobiprole and
vancomycin plus aztreonam arms, respectively. The most common reason for nonclinical success
was ‘Missing assessment at TOC’ which occurred in 60.6% of ceftobiprole non-successes and
60.5% of vancomycin plus aztreonam non-successes. In general, there were no notable treatment
differences regarding the reasons for non-success. A slightly greater proportion of subjects in the
vancomycin plus aztreonam arm were non-successes due to ‘Unplanned surgical procedure for
the ABSSSI after start of therapy and prior to TOC’ (13.2% versus 6.1%) and there were 2
(5.2%) of non-successes due to ‘death prior to TOC’ in the vancomycin plus aztreonam arm
versus 0 (0.0%) in the ceftobiprole arm.

Conclusions
Trial BPR-CS-008 met its primary objective of demonstrating non-inferiority for the primary
endpoint. In general, primary and secondary efficacy findings tended to numerically favor
ceftobiprole to vancomycin plus aztreonam. Early clinical response appeared to be sustained at
later timepoints. Overall, there are no major concerns with the evidence of effectiveness.
Minor concerns were that over 95% of subjects in the ITT population were White, which may
(b) (4)
limit the generalizability of findings to other races.

6.2.3. CABP, Trial CAP-3001
6.2.3.1. Design, Trial CAP-3001
This was a randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial of ceftobiprole versus ceftriaxone with or
without linezolid designed to assess the efficacy and safety of ceftobiprole in adult subjects with
CABP requiring hospitalization. The trial was conducted from June 2006 to July 2007.

91

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
The primary objective of this trial was to demonstrate the noninferiority of ceftobiprole
compared with ceftriaxone with or without linezolid with respect to the clinical cure rate at the
TOC visit in subjects hospitalized with CABP.
The secondary objectives were to compare the following in hospitalized CABP subjects after
treatment with ceftobiprole versus treatment with the comparator:
•
•
•
•

The microbiological eradication rate at the TOC Visit
The clinical cure rate and the microbiological eradication rate at the TOC Visit of subjects
who required mechanical ventilation within the first 48 hours of enrollment
The clinical and microbiological relapse rates at the late follow-up visit
The 30-day pneumonia-specific mortality rates.

Since many subjects in this trial would not require hospitalization for the entire duration of
antibacterial therapy, a switch from IV study drugs to oral cefuroxime axetil (500 mg every
12 hours) was allowed after a minimum of 3 days of IV therapy, but only for those subjects who
met all protocol-specified criteria for improvement and were candidates for hospital discharge.
The use of cefuroxime axetil was consistent with the recommendation of practice guidelines.
All subjects continued to receive intravenous therapy while hospitalized and trial sites were
encouraged to keep subjects on IV therapy as long as appropriate in order to maximize the
number of subjects receiving a full course of IV study medication. In addition, subjects with a
positive blood culture at baseline were required to receive IV study drug for a minimum of
5 days pending results of repeat blood cultures.
The total duration of study drug therapy (IV plus oral) for all subjects was a minimum of 5 days
and a target of 7 days. If in the investigator’s opinion a subject required additional days of study
therapy, the duration of the therapy could have been extended up to a maximum of 10 days.
Therapy could have been further extended to a maximum of 14 days.
At the discretion of the investigator, subjects were allowed to receive study drug infusions as
outpatients or through a home-care agency, provided they met all other protocol requirements,
but all IV study drug infusions had to be administered and monitored by a qualified nurse, a
qualified member of the trial staff, or an infusion specialist. No concomitant administration of
antibacterial treatments was permitted. The treatment and follow-up schedules are summarized in
Figure 4.

An independent data monitoring committee (IDMC) was established to monitor data on an
ongoing basis to ensure the continuing safety of subjects enrolled in this trial and the efficacy of
93

Reference ID: 5357793

the study drug. The IDMC included independent experts, not affiliated with the Applicant, in
internal medicine, critical care medicine, infectious diseases, and biostatistics. The IDMC could
call upon experts in other specialties to attend IDMC meetings to provide information regarding
unanticipated findings or issues. The committee met on 3 occasions (14 October 2006,
23 January 2007, and 24 May 2007) to review data collected in this Trial and made
recommendations after each review to continue conduct of the trial as planned.
6.2.3.2. Eligibility Criteria, Trial CAP-3001
Approximately 670 subjects hospitalized with CABP severe enough to require treatment with
IV antibacterials for at least 3 days, were to be enrolled to achieve 532 (266 in each treatment
arm) clinically evaluable subjects. In total, 666 subjects at 103 sites worldwide were randomly
assigned centrally in a 1:1 ratio to treatment with either ceftobiprole (500 mg every 8 hours as a
120-minute IV infusion) or ceftriaxone (2 g once daily as a 30-minute IV infusion) with or
without linezolid (600 mg every 12 hours as a 60-minute IV infusion). Subjects were stratified
by the Pneumonia Outcomes Research Team (PORT) Severity Index (PSI) score at
randomization (PSI ≤90 versus PSI ≥91), and by the need for anti-staphylococcal therapy
(linezolid or placebo) based on signs, symptoms, and medical history at enrollment.

Inclusion Criteria
Subjects meeting all the following:
•

Men or women, 18 years of age or older who provided written informed consent.

•

Women must have been postmenopausal (for at least 1 year), surgically sterile or
practiced an effective method of birth control.

•

Subjects had a diagnosis of CABP severe enough to require hospitalization and treatment
with IV antibacterial drugs for at least 3 days (72 hours), defined as meeting all the
following criteria:

•

Subjects had a diagnosis of CABP severe enough to require hospitalization and treatment
with IV antibacterials for at least 3 days (72 hours), defined as meeting all of the
following criteria (must meet a, b, c, d, and e):
a) Clinical diagnosis of acute bacterial pneumonia acquired in the community. Subjects
must have resided in the community (i.e., not in a chronic care facility such as a
nursing home or rehabilitation facility) and must not have been hospitalized during
the 14 days before the onset of symptoms of pneumonia. Residence in an assistedliving facility where the subject had regular access to the community was allowed.
b) Clinical signs or symptoms of acute bacterial pneumonia with at least 2 of the
following criteria:
 Cough (new or increased over usual state)
 Production of purulent sputum or a worsening in the character of sputum
 Auscultatory findings on pulmonary examination of rales or evidence of
pulmonary consolidation (dullness on percussion, bronchial breath sounds, or
egophony)
 Dyspnea or tachypnea (respiratory rate ≥20 breaths per minute), that was new or
worse than usual state
 New onset hypoxemia on room air (PO2 <60 mm Hg on arterial blood gas or O2
saturation <90% by pulse oximetry), or respiratory failure that required
mechanical ventilation.
c) New radiographic infiltrates (not related to another disease process) consistent with
the diagnosis of bacterial pneumonia
d) Fever or leukocytosis/leukopenia (temporally associated with the onset of pneumonia
symptoms)
 Fever (in the absence of antipyretics) defined as an axillary temperature >37.5°C,
an oral temperature >38°C, a tympanic temperature >38.5°C, a rectal temperature
>39°C, or hypothermia, defined as a rectal body temperature of <35°C
 Leukocytosis defined as an elevated total peripheral WBC count ≥10 x 109/L or
≥15% immature neutrophils (bands), regardless of total peripheral white count; or
leukopenia with total WBC ≤4.5 x 109/L
e) Severity of pneumonia required IV antibacterial therapy

6.2.3.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Trial CAP-3001
Disposition of Subjects
A total of 706 subjects were enrolled into this trial, Figure 5. Sixty-eight subjects were not
included in the ITT analysis set (i.e., the ITT population of all randomized subjects) including 40
subjects who were screen failures and 28 subjects who were randomly assigned to treatment with
ceftobiprole (14 subjects) or ceftriaxone with or without linezolid (14 subjects) at site 5060023.
A total of 638 subjects were randomized to receive either the ceftobiprole (n = 314) or
ceftriaxone with or without linezolid (n = 324) treatment.
One subject was randomly assigned to the comparator arm but was treated with ceftobiprole.
As shown in Table 32, a total of 532 of 638 (83%) of ITT subjects completed the study. Of the
17% of subjects who discontinued the study, the main reasons for study discontinuation were
subjects having AEs (5%) or being lost to follow-up (3%). Overall, there were no notable
imbalances between the treatment arms regarding reasons for discontinuation from the study.

Baseline Demographic and Disease Characteristics
As shown in Table 33, the baseline demographic characteristics in the ITT population were
generally balanced across the treatment arms. Overall, subjects had a median age of 56 years and
tended to be males (57%), White (62%) or not Hispanic or Latino (75%). Approximately 13% of
subjects were from North American sites and 41% were from European sites. Disease
characteristics were also balanced across the treatment arms. Overall, 22% of subjects had a
PSI ≥ 91, 49% had a PORT Risk Class of ≥ III and 54% had systemic inflammatory response
syndrome (SIRS) at baseline. Concomitant use of linezolid was observed in 11% of subjects. The
percentage of ITT subjects with a valid pathogen at baseline was 29%.

Sample Size Determination
The sample size was determined to show the noninferiority of ceftobiprole compared with
ceftriaxone with or without linezolid in terms of the clinical cure rate at the TOC visit.
The sample size calculation was based on the following assumptions for the ITT analysis set:
•
•
•
•
•

The clinical cure rate is 70% in both treatment arms,
The non-inferiority margin is 10%,
The power (1-β) is 80%,
The level of significance is 2-sided 5%,
The clinically evaluable rate is 80%.

Based on the above, 670 subjects needed to be randomly assigned to treatment, providing 335
subjects in each treatment arm.
Efficacy Analysis Sets
•

ITT Analysis Set: included all subjects randomly assigned to treatment.

•

mITT Analysis Set: a subset of the ITT analysis set that included all ITT subjects who had a
valid pathogen at Baseline.

•

Clinically Evaluable Analysis Set: a subset of the ITT analysis set that included all the ITT
subjects who received at least 48 hours of Trial medication but excluded those subjects with
a derived clinical outcome of Not Evaluable at the TOC Visit. The derived clinical outcome
was based on clinical assessment and evaluability of a subject, whereas the clinical outcome
collected in the electronic case report form was based on the investigator’s assessment.

•

Clinically Evaluable Analysis Set at the Late Follow-Up Visit: included all clinically
evaluable subjects with a derived clinical outcome of cure at the TOC visit and who were
clinically evaluable at the late follow-up visit.

•

Microbiologically Evaluable Analysis Set: a subset of the mITT analysis set that included
all mITT subjects who were also clinically evaluable subjects, excluding those with a
microbiological outcome of ‘Not Evaluable’ at the TOC Visit.

•

Microbiologically Evaluable Analysis Set at the Late Follow-Up Visit: included all
microbiologically evaluable subjects with a microbiological outcome of eradication or
presumed eradication at the TOC visit and who were microbiologically evaluable at the late
follow-up visit.

•

Safety Analysis Set: The safety analysis set is a subset of the ITT analysis set and included
all the subjects in the ITT analysis set who were exposed to any Trial medication.

Derived Clinical Outcome at the TOC Visit
In the ITT and mITT analyses subjects whose clinical outcomes were assessed as
‘Not Evaluable’ by the investigator were considered failures. Subjects who were considered
clinically cured by the investigator at the TOC Visit but received effective concomitant therapy
for any reason, were also considered failures in the ITT and mITT analyses.

Cure
A subject was considered a ‘derived clinical cure’ at the TOC visit if the clinical outcome at the
TOC visit was cure and the subject was not a ‘derived failure’ as defined below.
Failure
A subject was considered a clinical failure at TOC if he or she took study medication for at least
48 hours and met any of the following criteria:
•
•
•
•
•
•

Clinical outcome at the TOC visit was failure
Subject withdrew from the treatment because of a treatment-related adverse event
Subject died due to pneumonia after 48 hours of treatment
Subject withdrew from the Trial due to lack of efficacy
Subject missed a TOC visit assessment and the final clinical assessment before the TOC visit
was ‘Unchanged’ or ‘Worsened from Baseline’,
Subject received non-study systemic antibiotics for treatment of pneumonia prior to the TOC
Visit.

Subjects who withdrew from treatment because of an adverse event but received a full course of
therapy (5 to 14 days) were regarded as clinical cures if the clinical outcome at the TOC Visit
was cure.
Non-evaluable
A subject was considered ‘non-evaluable’ at the TOC visit if the following criteria were
satisfied:
•
•

Subject did not meet the criteria for cure or failure (as defined above), and
Subject had missing TOC visit or the investigator’s assessment of the clinical outcome at the
TOC visit was ‘Not Evaluable’.

Evaluability at the TOC Visit
A subject was deemed clinically evaluable at the TOC visit unless he or she met any of the
following criteria:
• Clinical Diagnosis Unconfirmed: Per the investigator, the inclusion criterion related to a
diagnosis of CABP was not satisfied.
• Community-Acquired Pneumonia Unconfirmed: The baseline infiltrate was not consistent
with pneumonia by central x-ray evaluation.
• Mortality:
 Early Mortality: The subject died within 48 hours after the first infusion.
 Unrelated Mortality: The mortality was unrelated to pneumonia and the last clinical
assessment was not worsened, and the subject had no treatment-related adverse event, did
not withdraw due to lack of efficacy, and had no TOC visit.
 Effective Concomitant Therapy: The subject took a systemic antibacterial drug
(administered for a reason other than CABP), against gram-positive or gram-negative
pathogens. Subjects who received a concomitant medication with purely anaerobic (e.g.,
metronidazole), anti-fungal, or antiviral activity were considered evaluable. Subjects who
received non-absorbable antibacterial drugs s (e.g., oral vancomycin, neomycin) or
topical antibacterial drugs were also evaluable.
 Other Protocol Violations: The presence of neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count
≥0.5x109/L).
 Resistant to Study Drugs:
i.
Subjects whose cultures yielded pathogens resistant to both treatment arms of the trial
based on central laboratory results (MIC values ≥ 16 mg/mL), or
ii.
Subjects who withdrew due to “resistant organism at baseline” based on local
laboratory results.
•

Inappropriate Clinical Evaluation:
 The subject did not meet the definition of failure and the TOC visit was not completed 6
to 21 days following the last dose of study drug.

•

Course Too Short:
 The subject took study medication for less than 48 hours, or
 The subject had a clinical outcome of ‘Cure’ at the TOC visit but took study medication
for less than 120 hours, or
 The subject took less than 80% of scheduled IV study medication.

•

Missing TOC Visit: Subjects who missed the TOC visit and did not meet the definition of
cure or failure.

Derived Clinical Outcome at the Late Follow-Up Visit
Clinical Relapse
A subject was considered a clinical relapse at the late follow-up visit if the subject was an
evaluable cure at the TOC visit and any of the following applied:
• The outcome at the late follow-up visit was relapse, or
• The subject died due to pneumonia prior to the late follow-up visit, or
• The subject took effective concomitant therapy for pneumonia between the TOC visit and
the late follow-up visit.
Evaluability at the Late Follow-Up Visit
A subject was considered clinically evaluable at the late follow-up visit if the following criteria
were met:
• The subject was evaluable and had a clinical outcome of cure at the TOC visit.
• The subject did not take effective concomitant therapy for a reason other than pneumonia
during the period between the TOC and late follow-up visits, OR the subject took
effective concomitant therapy for a reason other than pneumonia and was a clinical
relapse at the late follow-up visit.
• The subject had a clinical evaluation at the late follow-up visit or the subject died of
pneumonia prior to the late follow-up visit.
Microbiological Outcome at the TOC Visit
Microbiological outcome at the subject level was not directly collected in the electronic case
report form, but was obtained through a combination of the clinical assessment, infection
symptoms, and the microbiological assessment at the baseline, TOC, and late follow-up visits.
For all subjects with a valid pathogen at baseline, the microbiological outcome at the TOC visit
was derived following the mapping shown in Table 34 below.

Microbiological Evaluability at the TOC Visit
A subject was considered microbiologically evaluable at the TOC visit if the following criteria
