•
•

Subject was clinically evaluable at the TOC visit
Subject had a valid pathogen isolated at baseline. To be considered valid, a pathogen must
have met the following isolation criteria:
 Tracheal aspirate, bronchoalveolar lavage, PBS, or other
 Expectorated samples with less than 10 squamous epithelial cells and greater than 25
leukocytes/lpf.

Primary Efficacy Analysis
The primary efficacy analysis was performed on the clinically evaluable and the ITT co-primary
analysis sets. The primary efficacy endpoint was the clinical cure rate at the TOC visit, defined
as the ratio of the number of subjects who had a derived clinical outcome of cure at the TOC
visit to the total number of the subjects in the analysis set under consideration.
The hypotheses tested were:
H0: The clinical cure rate of the ceftobiprole arm is more than 10% inferior to that of the
ceftriaxone with or without linezolid arm.
H1: The clinical cure rate of the ceftobiprole arm is no more than 10% inferior to that of the
ceftriaxone with or without linezolid arm.
A 2-sided 95% confidence interval based on the Normal approximation for the difference of two
binomial proportions was calculated for the between-treatment difference (ceftobiprole minus
ceftriaxone with or without linezolid) at the TOC Visit. Noninferiority of ceftobiprole compared
with ceftriaxone with or without linezolid was concluded if the lower limit of this confidence
interval was greater than or equal to –10%.
Secondary Efficacy Analyses
The secondary efficacy endpoints were tested using a step-down hierarchical procedure in the
following order:
1) microbiological eradication rate at the TOC visit,
2) clinical cure rate at the TOC visit for subjects who had a PSI score ≥91,
3) the 30-day pneumonia-specific mortality rates.
The microbiological eradication rate at the TOC Visit was defined as the ratio of the number of
subjects with a microbiological outcome of Eradication or Presumed Eradication at the TOC visit
to the total number of subjects in the analysis set under consideration at the TOC visit. This
analysis was performed on the microbiologically evaluable analysis set.
The clinical cure rate for subjects who had a PSI score ≥91 was defined as the ratio of the
number of subjects with PSI score ≥91 who had a clinical outcome of cure at the TOC visit to the
total number of the subjects with a PSI score ≥91 in the analysis set under consideration. The
analysis of the clinical cure rate for subjects who had a PSI score ≥91 was performed on the
clinically evaluable and ITT analysis sets.
Noninferiority hypotheses similar to the primary hypothesis were tested for the microbiological
eradication rate and the clinical response rate in subjects with a PSI score ≥91.
103

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
The 30-day pneumonia-specific mortality rate was defined as the ratio of the number of deaths
due to pneumonia to the total number of subjects in the analysis set under consideration. This
analysis was performed on the clinically evaluable and ITT analysis sets.
Given the limited sample sizes for these tests, a 15% noninferiority margin was used to test all
secondary hypotheses. This was documented prior to database lock, but was not prespecified in
the protocol or the analysis plan. The 2-sided 95% confidence interval was computed in the same
way as for the primary efficacy analysis.
6.2.3.4. Results of Analyses, Trial CAP-3001
Primary Efficacy Analysis
The protocol specified two co-primary endpoints to be analyzed in the primary efficacy analysis,
which included the clinical cure rate at the TOC visit in the CE and ITT populations. For both
co-primary endpoints, treatment differences were shown to satisfy a 10% NI margin based on the
respective lower confidence limits exceeding -10% (Table 35). In the clinically evaluable
analysis set, the clinical cure rate at the TOC visit was 86.6% (ceftobiprole) versus 87.4%
(comparator), a treatment difference of -0.8% (95% CI: -6.9, 5.3) which indicated NI since the
lower bound of -6.9% exceeded a -10% limit. In the ITT analysis set, the clinical cure rate at the
TOC visit was 76.4% (ceftobiprole) versus 79.3% (comparator), a treatment difference of -2.9%
(95% CI: -9.3, 3.6) which indicated NI since the lower bound of -9.3% exceeded the -10% limit.

The secondary efficacy endpoints were tested using a step-down hierarchical procedure in the

Findings for key secondary endpoints were generally consistent with the non-inferiority finding
in the primary analysis.

Reviewer Comments
The Applicant cannot demonstrate non-inferiority for these endpoints due to uncertainty
regarding the NI margin. The specified NI margin for the above secondary endpoints has not
been scientifically justified and therefore the interpretation of findings for these endpoints may
not be clear unless superiority is shown. These endpoints were therefore considered to be
descriptive.

Conclusions
Based on findings from the re-analyses which followed the guidelines of the CABP 2020
Guidance, Trial CAP-3001was considered to provide an adequate level of evidence provided
there is support from positive trial findings in the other two indications (SAB and ABSSSI). See
Section 6.3.1 for further details on the re-analyses.
There were no other major concerns. Minor concerns related to there being very few subjects
from U.S. sites included in the Day 3 mITT population (i.e., 7 subjects in the ceftobiprole arm
and 10 in the ceftriaxone arm). In addition, only 3 of these 7 subjects (43%) had an early clinical
success compared to 7 of 10 (70%) in the ceftriaxone arm.

6.2.4. Community-Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia, Trial
BPR-PIP-002
BPR-PIP-002 was a multicenter, randomized, investigator-blind, active-controlled trial
conducted in pediatric subjects ages 3 months to less than 18 years with CABP or HABP
requiring hospitalization and treatment with IV antibacterial drugs. The primary objective of this
trial was to evaluate the safety of ceftobiprole. The trial was not powered for comparative
inferential efficacy analysis, and no efficacy endpoint was identified as primary.
Randomization was stratified by 4 age groups (3 months to <2 years; 2 years to <6 years;
6 years to <12 years; 12 years to <18 years) and by diagnosis of HABP or CABP. Subjects were
randomized 2:1 within each group to receive either ceftobiprole or the comparator which was an
107

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
IV standard-of-care cephalosporin with optional antibacterial coverage for MRSA (ceftazidime
with or without vancomycin for subjects with HABP; ceftriaxone with or without vancomycin
for subjects with CABP) for 7-14 days. Subjects were to receive IV antibacterial treatment for at
least 3 days but then could be switched to oral antibacterial drugs if clinical improvement criteria
for IV to oral switch were met. Ceftobiprole was administered at a dose of 10-20 mg/kg IV every
8 hours, age-adjusted for dose and infusion duration (maximum daily dose was 1500 mg).

For all subjects who discontinued Trial drug, AE monitoring was to be continued up to and

The primary endpoint was analysis of AEs on the first 3 days of Trial treatment, at the EOT,
TOC and last follow-up visits, though AEs were assessed for the full study period. Secondary
endpoints included clinical response at Day 4 and EOT visits, and clinical cure rates at the TOC
and last follow-up visits in the ITT and CE populations, and microbiological eradication rates at
the TOC and last follow-up visits. Clinical response was assessed by the blinded investigator at
Day 4 and EOT as cured (no signs or symptoms of pneumonia), improved (clinically relevant
improvement in signs and symptoms), unchanged (no or minor change from baseline) or
worsened (clinically relevant increased in severity of signs and symptoms). Clinical cure was
assessed by the blinded investigator at the TOC Visit and defined as signs and symptoms of
pneumonia normalized or improved to an extent that further antibiotic therapy was not necessary,
and stabilization or improvement of chest X-rays post-baseline if these were available.
Pharmacokinetic assessments were also performed.
The Trial population consisted of 138 subjects (94 in the ceftobiprole arm, 44 in the comparator
arm), of which 94.7% and 100% respectively, completed Trial treatment. Of the subjects in the
ceftobiprole arm, 18 were ages 12 to <18 years old, 27 were 6 to <12 years old, 37 were
2 to <6 years old, and 12 were aged 3 months to <2 years. The majority of subjects (94.2%) had
CABP, and only 6 subjects had a pathogen identified at baseline. Subjects with ventilatorassociated HABP were excluded from the Trial. The median duration of exposure to IV
treatment was similar for the ceftobiprole and comparator arms (6 versus 7 days respectively) as
was the median duration of exposure to oral treatment (5 days in each arm).
The clinical response was determined at study Day 4, the EOT visit (7-14 days after
randomization), and at the TOC Visit (7-14 days after the EOT visit). The ITT population
included all subjects who were randomized.
In the ITT population, the clinical response rates in the ceftobiprole and comparator arms were
respectively 95.7% and 93.2% on Day 4 (between-arm difference 2.6% [95% confidence interval
CI: 5.5, 14.7]), 96.8% and 100% at the EOT visit (between-arm difference -3.2% [95% CI: -9.1,
5.5]), and 90.4% and 97.7% at the TOC visit (between-arm difference -7.3% [95% CI: -15.7,
3.6]).

6.3. Key Efficacy Review Issues
6.3.1. Re-Analysis of Trial CAP-3001
Issue
CAP-3001 was conducted prior to the CABP Guidance of 2020 and was not designed to assess
an early clinical success endpoint (Day 4) in an appropriate Trial population (e.g., PORT Risk
Class ≥ III) in which a non-inferiority margin could be scientifically justified. Therefore, the
Applicant provided several post-hoc re-analyses which considered new analysis populations,
endpoints, and selection criteria which closely followed those outlined in the CABP Guidance4.
Background
Since Trial CAP-3001 was conducted from June 2006 to July 2007, i.e., before the current FDA
CABP Guidance for Industry was issued in June 2020, the Applicant included CSR Addendum 2
in this NDA submission. Addendum 2 included additional post-hoc analyses that were performed
after completion of the original CSR (dated November 3, 2009). These new analyses shown in
the tables below were taken directly from Addendum 2 of the CSR. These analyses were critical
in assessing the overall evidence obtained from this Trial and the Trial’s ability to meet the
current recommendations for CABP trials outlined in the FDA Guidance.
The endpoints and Trial populations specified in the re-analysis were similar to those described
in the Guidance. The primary endpoint in Trial CAP-3001 was clinical cure at the TOC visit
which clearly differed from the endpoint of clinical success at Day 4 stipulated in the current
guidance. Therefore, the re-analyses considered an early clinical response endpoint at Day 3
(prior to IV to oral switch) which resembled the Guidance endpoint at Day 4, as shown in Table
39. There were also differences in the Trial populations of CAP-3001 and the Guidance. The
Applicant modified the analysis populations to be more consistent with the FDA Guidance.
There were also differences between the original entry criteria of CAP-3001 and those outlined
in the Guidance are shown in Table 40.

FDA guidance for CABP “Community- Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia: Developing Drugs for
Treatment, June 2020” (U.S. Department of Health Human Services) (FDA 2020)
4

111

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Analysis Populations for the Re-analysis
In total, four analysis populations were used for the re-analyses using the primary endpoint
stipulated in the 2020 FDA CABP guidance:
•

The ‘Day 3-ITT population’ comprised all randomized subjects who had at least two of the
following symptoms at baseline: tachypnea, cough, production of purulent sputum, or chest
pain. Subjects were analyzed according to the study medication assigned at randomization.

•

The Day 3-modified ITT population comprised the subset of subjects in the Day 3-ITT
population who met all of the following additional criteria: 1. At least one of new-onset
hypoxemia, rales or pulmonary consolidation, and leukocytosis or leukopenia. 2. At least two
of fever, hypothermia, hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea.

•

The Day 3-mITT population was the subset of the Day 3-ITT subjects who had a valid
pathogen at baseline.

•

The Day 3-modified mITT population was the subset of the Day 3-modified ITT subjects
who had a valid pathogen at baseline.

The Baseline demographic and disease characteristics in the ‘Day 3-ITT population’ and the
‘Day 3-modified ITT population’ are shown in Table 39.
Primary Efficacy Analysis in Re-analysis
The re-analysis was performed to determine whether ceftobiprole is non-inferior to ceftriaxone ±
linezolid for the primary endpoint of clinical success at Day 3. Analysis of the primary endpoint
was based on the Day 3-ITT population and the Day 3-modified ITT population.
A two-sided 95% confidence interval using the Normal approximation to the difference of two
binomial proportions, was calculated for the between-treatment difference (ceftobiprole minus
ceftriaxone ± linezolid) at the TOC Visit.
The result for the primary endpoint of the re-analysis was interpreted in the context of a 12.5%
non-inferiority margin, i.e., non-inferiority of ceftobiprole compared with ceftriaxone with or
without linezolid was interpreted if the lower limit of this confidence interval was greater than or
equal to −12.5%.
The same subgroup analyses were performed for the re-analysis of the primary endpoint in
accordance with the 2020 FDA CABP guidance as described for the pre-specified primary
endpoint of derived clinical cure at the TOC Visit (CAP-3001 CSR Appendix 2.2.1.1). The
exception is the subgroup analysis by oral switch status, as none of the subjects in the Trial had
switched to oral therapy at the Day 3 assessment.
Reviewer Comments
The 12.5% NI margin mentioned above was chosen by the Applicant to be wider than the 10% NI
margin for the original primary analysis to account for additional variability from having to
reduce the size of the analysis populations to be consistent with the guidelines for populations
specified in the 2020 CABP Guidance. However, since a NI margin of 10% was satisfied in the
re-analyses for early clinical success in the Day 3 ITT and Day 3 mITT populations (as
discussed later in this section), this change in the margin did not impact conclusions.

Secondary and other efficacy analyses
For all secondary and other analysis included in the re-analysis, a two-sided 95% confidence
interval using the Normal approximation to the difference of two binomial proportions was
calculated for the between-treatment difference (ceftobiprole minus ceftriaxone ± linezolid).
Analyses of the secondary and other endpoints were descriptive with no testing against an
interpretative non-inferiority margin.

Assessment
Baseline Demographic and Disease Characteristics
Baseline demographic and disease characteristics for Day 3 ITT population and Day 3-modified
ITT are shown in Table 41. In the Day 3 ITT population, the median age was 56 years, 62% of
subjects were White, 66% were not Hispanic or Latino, 87% were from ex-U.S. sites, 29% had a
valid pathogen at baseline, 22% of subjects had PORT Risk Class ≥ IV and 31% had SIRS at
baseline. Compared to the Day 3 ITT population, the Day 3-modified ITT included older
subjects (median age of 67 versus 56 years) and a greater percentage of subjects with PORT Risk
Class ≥ IV (50% vs. 22%) or SIRS (65% vs. 31%). This would be expected given that the Day 3modified ITT population excluded a large number of lower risk subjects with PORT Risk
Classes of I and II (i.e., approximately 51% of the Day 3 ITT population).
In general, there were no major imbalances between the treatment arms in either of these
populations which would raise serious concerns. However, in the Day 3-modified ITT
population, a slightly lower percentage of subjects with PORT Risk Class ≥ IV observed in the
ceftobiprole arm (45% versus 54%).

Main Efficacy Results
The main efficacy results of the Applicant’s re-analysis are presented in Table 42,. For the
clinical success at Day 3 endpoint in the Day 3 ITT population, success rates were 71.0%
(ceftobiprole) versus 71.1% (ceftriaxone), a treatment difference (ceftobiprole – ceftriaxone) of 0.1% (95% CI: -7.2, 7.1). For the clinical success at Day 3 endpoint in the Day 3 modified-ITT
population, success rates were 71.1% (ceftobiprole) versus 67% (ceftriaxone), a treatment
difference (ceftobiprole – ceftriaxone) of 4.5% (95% CI: -8.8, 17.7). Treatment differences in
these analyses were more favorable than those in the originally specified primary analysis of
clinical cure rates at TOC (Table 42). These findings appeared to be consistent with the finding
of non-inferiority within a 10% NI margin observed in the original primary analysis.
Findings for other efficacy endpoints also tended to be comparable between the treatment arms
and generally consistent with non-inferiority. A notable finding was that in the Day 3-modified
ITT population, the 28-day ACM rate was observed to be substantially lower in the ceftobiprole
arm (2.1%) compared to the ceftriaxone arm (7.8%) with a treatment difference of -5.7% (95%
CI: -11.9, 0.5) which approached nominal significance in favor of the ceftobiprole arm.

Subgroup Analysis Results
As shown in Table 43, analyses of subgroups in the re-analysis were limited due to the reduced
sample size, especially in the Day 3-modified ITT population. There were no nominally

population. However, there were some notable findings in this population. For example,
ceftobiprole tended to have greater efficacy in more severe cases of CABP. For example, in
subjects with PORT classes of ≥ IV, response rates at Day 3 were 77.3% (ceftobiprole) versus
61.2% (ceftriaxone) whereas comparisons among subjects with PORT classes of III were 66.2%
versus 73.0%, respectively. Subgroup comparisons also favored the ceftobiprole arm in subjects
with gram-positive pathogens at baseline (13/18 (72.2%) versus 6/14 (42.9%) with pronounced
differences also observed for the Day 3 ITT population.
A more detailed comparison of clinical efficacy in subjects with gram-positive and gramnegative causative pathogens is shown in Table 44. Clinical success rate in infections due to
Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most commonly isolated pathogen, was higher in the ceftobiprole
as compared to ceftriaxone group, 27/33 (81.8%) versus 27/41 (65.9%), respectively. Among
gram-negative pathogens, E. coli, K. pneumonia, H. influenzae, and H. parainfluenzae occurred
in sufficient numbers of subjects across the treatment arms and will be included in the indication
for CABP in labeling.

Conclusions
Trial CAP-3001, as originally designed, met its primary objective. When reviewing this Trial
under current FDA guidance recommendations, Trial CAP-3001 was considered to have major
limitations. However, although the re-analysis was conducted in a post-hoc manner and involved
limited sample sizes, findings appeared to be consistent with the assumption of non-inferiority.
Findings in the re-analysis showed that treatment differences tended to favor ceftobiprole when
considering an earlier time point (i.e., Day 3) as well as a population that excluded subjects with
PORT Risk Classes of 1 or 2 (i.e., Day 3 mITT). Positive findings for the CAP-3001 Trial are
considered adequate as evidence of effectiveness for the CABP indication provided they are
supported by positive findings for the studies of the SAB and ABSSSI indications.

6.3.2. Clinical Success in Ukrainian Versus NonUkrainian Sites in Trial BPR-CS-009
Issue
In Trial BPR-CS-009, it was observed that sites in Ukraine showed substantially higher overall
success rates compared to sites in other countries. Due to large site-specific efficacy and fewer
AEs, these sites were identified for inspection but could not be inspected due to the current travel
restrictions to Ukraine. Thus, in addition to clinical site inspections, an Applicant inspection was
also conducted (see Section 10 for details), and higher overall success in Ukraine was evaluated
in further detail.
Background
There may be limitations with generalizing Trial findings across different geographical regions.
Overall response rates in non-Ukrainian countries may be lower than rates observed in the
Trial BPR-CS-009, which included Ukrainian sites with high response rates. Ukraine was
also the highest-enrolling country in the Trial, with 46.5% of subjects (180/387) in
the mITT population. This may also have implications for the assumptions used in justifying the
non-inferiority margin since the subject populations of Ukraine may not be appropriate for
inclusion due to inherently lower risk factors and more effective therapeutic interventions
compared to those of the assumed study population.
Based on post-hoc analyses, subjects enrolled in Ukraine were younger and had a more favorable
distribution of Baseline categories for complicated SAB, e.g., the percentage of subjects on
chronic dialysis was 0.6% (1/180) in Ukraine compared to 23.2% (48/207) in other countries,
and there were no subjects with LIE from Ukraine vs 4.8% (10/207) in other countries.
Therapeutic interventions with the potential for achieving source control for SAB were
performed more often within 72 hours before, or within 7 days after, randomization, in subjects
from Ukraine than in other countries, e.g., in 70.5% for abdominal abscesses in Ukraine
compared to 9.1% in abdominal abscesses in other countries, and in 67.9% (74/109) in
ABSSSIs/soft tissue infections in Ukraine compared to 30.5% (30/128) in other countries. (Table
45).

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275

Assessment
Significantly higher overall success rates based on DRC at the PTE visit were observed in
Ukraine (86.7%, 156/180 across treatment arms) versus other countries excluding Ukraine
(54.1%. 112/207 across treatment arm). The rate difference (Ukraine – non-Ukraine) was highly
significant at 86.7% versus 54.1%, difference favoring Ukraine by 32.6% (95% CI: 23.9, 40.8),
p<0.0001.
As shown in Table 45, treatment comparisons of overall success rates based on DRC assessment
at PTE were 74/88 (84.1%) vs. 82/92 (89.1%) in Ukraine versus 58/101 (57.4%) versus 54/106
(50.9%) in other countries (excluding Ukraine). Since comparisons in Ukraine were less
favorable for the ceftobiprole arm, the inclusion of Ukrainian sites likely did not positively
influence the overall finding of non-inferiority.
Conclusion
As noted above, concerns were lessened since the between-arm difference was not more
favorable in Ukraine versus the other countries. However, real life comparisons of rates may be
lower than what was observed in this Trial due to the high rates observed in Ukraine, therefore
comparisons of rates in the potential labeling should describe the strong differences in overall
success rates between Ukrainian and non-Ukrainian sites.

7. Safety (Risk and Risk Management)
7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Nonclinical Data
The nonclinical safety profile of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium has been explored in single and
repeat-dose studies in mice, rats, dogs, rabbits and monkeys for up to 3 months duration; in vitro
and in vivo genotoxicity studies; reproductive and developmental toxicity studies including
fertility studies in male and female rats, embryofetal developmental studies in rats and monkeys,
and pre- and post-natal developmental toxicity study in rats; and PK and toxicokinetic studies to
support ceftobiprole medocaril sodium development and to compare PK in animals and humans.
The target organs of toxicity that may be relevant to human risks are described below.
Injection Site Reactions, Thrombi, Emboli, Convulsions, Mortality
Thrombi formation at the injection site was a consistent finding in toxicological studies across
species, including rats, marmosets and dogs with severity increasing with dosing duration. In 24- and 13-week studies in rats, marmosets, and dogs, injection site findings included thrombus
formation, accumulation of inflammatory cells, thickening of the vascular wall in the periphery
of the dosing catheter, granulomas, edema/hemorrhage and/or necrosis of tissues around the
catheter. No other significant toxicities were observed in 2-week studies in rats and in 4-week
studies in rats and marmosets administered ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (at doses up to
360 mg/kg/day (1.4-times the maximum recommended human dose [MRHD] based on body
surface area [BSA] comparisons) and 200 mg/kg/day respectively, (0.75 times the MRHD, based
on BSA comparisons). However, in the 13-week studies in the rats and marmosets at similar
doses to those used in shorter term studies, convulsions and mortality were observed (≥50 mg/kg
in marmosets, 0.2 times the MRHD; ≥250 mg/kg in rats, 0.94 times the MRHD, based on BSA
comparisons). Thrombi/emboli were seen in marmosets in several tissues distal to the site of
injection, including in skeletal muscle, heart, and lungs, that were attributed to the cause of
mortality at all doses tested. In the rat 13-week study, mortality was primarily attributed to
kidney failure (see kidney toxicity information below). Although no seizures or thrombi (except
at the injection site) were reported in the dog 13-week study (up to 32 mg/kg/day, 0.4 timed the
MRHD, based on BSA comparisons), the dosing catheter in many animals did not remain patent
for the duration of the study and was found to be filled with fibrin, erythrocyte clumps and
inflammatory cell infiltrate. In mice, tonic/clonic convulsions were observed after ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium was administered as a single intravenous dose at ≥250 mg/kg (0.75 times the
MRHD, based on BSA comparisons).
Kidney Toxicity
No significant kidney toxicities were observed in 2- or 4-week studies in rats or in 4-week
studies in marmosets. However, in a 13-week rat study at doses up to 750 mg/kg/day in males
(2.8 times the MRHD, based on BSA comparisons) and 376 mg/kg/day in females (1.42 time the
MRHD, based on BSA comparisons), significant kidney toxicity (dose dependent increases in
tubular/duct eosinophilic bodies, and presence of foreign material) was observed at
≥250 mg/kg/day potentially due to precipitation of test article; kidney interstitial fibrosis
(moderate) was observed in males at the high dose. Mortality was observed at ≥250 mg/kg/day,
124
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
primarily on study Days 34 to 87 and attributed to kidney failure due to obstruction with foreign
material. Mice administered a single dose of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium intravenously at
≥250 mg/kg showed kidney tubules deposits (moderate to marked), dilation, congestion,
degeneration of distal tubules and necrosis. In this study the lethal dose in mice was ≥500 mg/kg
(0.94 the MRHD based on BSA comparisons).
Hypersensitivity
In a 2-week dog study, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium administered intravenously at
≥50 mg/kg/day (0.6 times the MRHD based on BSA comparisons) induced a histaminergic
reaction (reddening of the skin, face edema, injection of the oral mucosa, vomiting and
salivation) primarily associated with a relatively short infusion time (30 minutes). Findings
significantly decreased with a longer infusion time (2 hours) for the high and medium dosed
animals. These finding correlated with a dose dependent increase in plasma levels of histamine
that returned to control levels after approximately 4 hours from start of infusion. In a 13-week
dog study, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium administered intravenously at up to 32 mg/kg/day (0.4
times the MRHD based on BSA comparisons) caused sporadic reddening of the gums of some
dogs primarily during the first 3 weeks of dosing. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium administered to
guinea pigs by the intravenous or subcutaneous route, at a dose up to 100 mg/kg (0.5 times the
MRHD based on BSA comparisons), showed moderate antigenic potential.

7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
Ceftobiprole is a cephalosporin antibacterial drug. In general, cephalosporins have a favorable
safety profile and have been well-tolerated with extensive use worldwide. Common adverse
reactions associated with their use include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rash.
Labeled Warnings and Precautions across the five generations of cephalosporins include serious
hypersensitivity/anaphylactic reactions, Clostridioides difficile associated diarrhea, neurotoxicity
including seizures and encephalopathy, development of drug-resistant bacteria with prolonged or
inappropriate use, and laboratory-based abnormalities such as direct Coombs’ test
seroconversion and decrease in prothrombin activity. Almost all cephalosporins require dose
adjustment in subjects with impaired renal function. The second generation cephalosporins carry
a risk of hearing loss in pediatric subjects while third generation cephalosporins such as
ceftriaxone may interact with calcium containing products, or cause pancreatitis, biliary sludge,
gallbladder pseudolithiasis, and hemolytic anemia. Third and fourth generation cephalosporins
have rarely been associated with electrolyte derangements including hyponatremia and
hyperkalemia.
Reported post-marketing adverse events for cephalosporins include serum sickness-like reaction,
acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis. A few cases of
neonatal death in subjects receiving ceftriaxone in conjunction with calcium-containing fluids
have been reported. Hepatotoxicity or drug induced liver injury due to cephalosporins are
uncommon with the exception of ceftriaxone which as noted above can cause biliary sludge
related to the formation of ceftriaxone-calcium salt. Finally, there have been reports of lifethreatening or fatal occurrences of encephalopathy, myoclonus and seizures related to cefepime
use. This was primarily observed in subjects with renal impairment who exceeded recommended
dosages but have also occurred in subjects in whom doses were appropriately adjusted.
125
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Given its drug class, the risks and safety concerns for ceftobiprole are anticipated to be similar to
those associated with cephalosporins already on the market as summarized above. Adverse
events of special interest monitored by the Applicant during the clinical development program of
ceftobiprole included hypersensitivity/anaphylactic reaction, C. difficile colitis, convulsions,
acute renal failure, increased hepatic enzymes, hyponatremia, nausea, vomiting, and thrombosis.

7.3. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Identified
Through Postmarket Experience
A review of the literature regarding the postmarketing experience for ceftobiprole yielded a
retrospective case series conducted in Italy reporting on 29 patients who received ceftobiprole; 2
patients developed myoclonus and 1 patient developed a rash that were attributed to ceftobiprole
(Durante-Mangoni et al. 2020). No deaths occurred in patients while receiving ceftobiprole.
Another published case reported agranulocytosis in a patient receiving ceftobiprole after DRESS
associated with vancomycin and rifampin (Wendland et al. 2011). After discontinuation of
ceftobiprole, the patient’s neutrophils recovered without further issues. The Applicant has also
submitted postmarketing surveillance data in their application highlighting cases of serious
hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, urticaria, and angioedema.
The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System was also queried for AEs reported with ceftobiprole.
Upon review, AEs that were deemed potentially related to ceftobiprole were leukopenia,
encephalopathy, rash, agranulocytosis, hyponatremia, and seizures.
Review of the labeling from Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia did not identify any
new safety issues. Safety issues and adverse reactions reported in the ex-US labeling were
derived from the clinical studies covered in this review. No additional postmarketing experiences
were identified.

7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
Please see the discussion in Section 3.2 for a description of the clinical trials and any other data
used in the review of safety and whether the trials submitted were fit for purpose. The studies
submitted for safety were analyzed individually as described in this section. Pooling of safety
results was not deemed to be appropriate given clinically distinct subject populations and
differences in study design and conduct across pivotal trials. No major data quality or integrity
issues were identified that would preclude performing a safety review for this NDA. There were
no major identified issues with respect to recording, coding and categorizing AEs. A few
preferred terms (PTs) were reclassified based on the verbatim terms. The clinical data scientist
performed standard safety analyses including Food and Drug Administration Medical Dictionary
for Regulatory Activities queries (FMQs) to determine safety signals, and additional analyses as
requested by the clinical team. The clinical review team performed a grouped query (GQ)
analysis for selected treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) to evaluate potential splitting
of similar AEs and these are discussed in the TEAE section of each indication. Review of subject
narratives and graphical subject profiles (created using JMP clinical version 17) were used in
some instances to help determine causality. AE and TEAE are used interchangeably in this
review.
126
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Safety evaluations included recording of AEs, vital signs (including electrocardiogram results),
and collection of laboratory parameters. For all studies, AEs included any untoward medical
occurred associated with the use of the drug in humans, whether or not considered drug related.
An AE could arise with any use of the drug (e.g., off-label use, use in combination with another
drug) and with any route of administration, formulation, or dose, including an overdose. If there
was a suspicion that a GQ was related to ceftobiprole, subject narratives and graphical subject
profiles (created using JMP clinical version 17) were used to help determine causality.
For Trial BPR-CS-009, AEs were collected continuously from the start of first dosing up to and
including the scheduled PTE visit (Day 70 ± 5 days post-randomization). For Trial BPR-CS-008,
AEs were collected continuously from start of first dosing up to and including the scheduled last
follow-up visit (28-35 days after last treatment). The Medical Dictionary for Regulatory
activities (MedDRA) version 24.0 was used for both Trials. In order to assess severity, a 3-point
grading scale was used (mild, moderate, severe). For Trial CAP-3001, AEs were collected from
the time of informed consent up to completion of the last trial-related procedure. For BAP
248307, AEs were collected from the first study related procedure up to the last trial-related
procedure. MedDRA version 10.0 was used for studies CAP-3001 and BAP 248307. For Trial
BPR-PIP-002, AEs were collected continuously from time of first study drug administration up
to and including the scheduled last follow-up visit (28-35 days after EOT). MedDRA version
22.1 was used for this Trial.

7.6. Safety Results
7.6.1. SAB, Trial BPR-CS-009
7.6.1.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, Trial BPR-CS-009
As shown in Table 47 the overall incidence of TEAEs was 63.4% in the ceftobiprole arm and
59.1% in the daptomycin arm. Most of the TEAEs in the ceftobiprole arm were of moderate
severity and there were slightly fewer severe TEAEs as compared to the daptomycin arm. There
was an overall lower incidence of SAEs in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the daptomycin
arm, respectively (18.8% versus 22.7%). The number of deaths and TEAEs leading to
discontinuation were similar between treatment arms.
There were four subjects in the ceftobiprole arm and none in the comparator arm with TEAEs
leading to dose modification of the study drug. In the ceftobiprole arm, two subjects each
required dose reduction and dose interruption, described below:

7.6.1.2. Deaths, Trial BPR-CS-009
There were no imbalances in TEAEs leading to death between the treatment arms (17/191
(8.9%) in the ceftobiprole and 18/198 (9.1%) in the daptomycin arm). In both arms, the most
commonly reported TEAE leading to death was multiple organ dysfunction syndrome and septic
shock.
None of the TEAEs leading to death were assessed as drug related by the investigator or by the
FDA reviewer upon a detailed review of the case narratives. The case narratives and subject
profiles suggested that the deaths appeared to be related to underlying comorbidities and
complications arising from the underlying infection, which is not unexpected for subjects with
SAB. A meta-analysis performed in 2022 estimated that the all-cause mortality rate of SAB in a
total of 341 studies (536,791 subjects, spanning from January 1, 1991 to May 7, 2021) was
10.4% (95% CI, 9.0%–12.1%) at 7 days, 13.3% (95% CI, 11.1%–15.8%) at 2 weeks, 18.1%
(95% CI, 16.3%–20.0%) at 1 month, 27.0% (95% CI, 21.5%–33.3%) at 3 months, and 30.2%
(95% CI, 22.4%–39.3%) at 1 year (Bai et al. 2022).
The mortality rate in the BPR-CS-009 trial of 8.9% at Day 70 was less than what was seen in the
meta-analysis by Bai et al. described above, possibly due to mortality being assessed in a clinical
trial setting.

7.6.1.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial
BPR-CS-009
The incidence of SAEs was lower in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the daptomycin arm
(18.8% versus 22.7%). Most SAEs occurring in both arms were related to the Infections and
Infestations system organ class (SOC) (9.4% in the ceftobiprole versus 12.6% in the daptomycin
arm). Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome was the only SAE that had a greater than 1% risk
difference in the ceftobiprole arm versus the daptomycin arm. After reviewing the narratives of
the subjects who experienced an SAE of multiple organ dysfunction syndrome while on
(b) (6)
ceftobiprole (
), none of these SAEs appeared to be drugrelated, or due to failure of treatment with ceftobiprole.
Additional SAEs were evaluated to determine relatedness to ceftobiprole, and selected SAEs are
described below by SOC. The FDA reviewer agreed with the investigator that two SAEs (seizure
and leukopenia) could have been related to ceftobiprole. There were two additional SAEs (tonicclonic seizure and cutaneous vasculitis) may also have been related to ceftobiprole, and the FDA
reviewer’s causality assessment for these selected SAEs is noted below:

Day 18, ceftobiprole was discontinued due to leukopenia. The subject was switched to

Nervous System Disorders
As described below, two subjects in the ceftobiprole arm, who had no past medical history of

Cephalosporins can precipitate seizures and seizures are noted as warnings in the labeling of

seizures and other central nervous system disorders in the warnings section of labeling as
proposed by the Applicant.

(b) (6)

In both arms, the number of subjects who had AEs leading to treatment discontinuation was
comparable (9.4% in the ceftobiprole arm and 9.1% in the daptomycin arm). The most common

7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial BPR-CS009
TEAEs occurred in 63.4% of the subjects in the ceftobiprole arm and 59.1% in the daptomycin
arm with a risk difference of 4.3%. The GQs demonstrating a risk difference of at least 4% or
higher in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the daptomycin arm were nausea, vomiting,
hypokalemia, pneumonia, and diarrhea; these are described below. Hypokalemia is discussed in
the laboratory Section 7.6.1.6. Although the GQ of bacterial infections were common in both
arms, it was not considered an adverse reaction as they were likely related to underlying medical
conditions and was not caused by ceftobiprole.

139
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Gastrointestinal Symptoms
Most TEAEs of either nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea were of mild to moderate severity and did
not lead to discontinuation. About half of the TEAEs of nausea or vomiting were related to
ceftobiprole by the investigator.
There were no reports of diarrhea associated with Clostridioides difficile. Gastrointestinal
symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are often considered common adverse
reactions associated with antibacterial drugs, and are proposed by the Applicant in Section 6 of
labeling.
Pneumonia
The narrow FMQ of pneumonia encompassed the PTs of pneumonia, pneumonia staphylococcal,
pneumonia aspiration, lung abscess, pneumonia pseudomonal, pneumonia viral, and infectious
pleural effusion. Although the number of subjects with pneumonia was higher in the ceftobiprole
arm compared to the daptomycin arm [16 (8.4%) versus 5 (2.5%)], review of subject profiles and
narratives did not reveal a link between ceftobiprole and the PTs in the narrow FMQ. Out of the
16 subjects with FMQs of pneumonia, 2 were due to aspiration and 1 was due to a viral cause. In
most of the cases the subjects had comorbidities which made pneumonia more likely to occur
(presence of endotracheal tube, immunosuppression, prolonged hospitalization). There was also
no information about the pathogen except in 4 cases, where all but one of the pathogens isolated
was gram negative. The subject with a S. aureus pneumonia is described below:
•

(b) (6)

One subject,
, had an AE of pneumonia staphylococcal on Day 7. The subject
was on cefazolin for 6 days for persistent SAB prior to randomization. After 6 days of
ceftobiprole, the subject experienced an SAE of respiratory failure and MSSA was isolated
from lavage from the endotracheal tube; ceftobiprole was discontinued and changed to
imipenem-cilastatin. The AEs of pneumonia staphylococcal and respiratory failure were
resolved 2 days later. Overall, given that the AE occurred even after 6 days of cefazolin and
6 days of ceftobiprole but resolved after 2 days of imipenem-cilastatin suggests either a
source control issue or an issue related to incomplete duration of treatment. This subject was
considered a treatment failure due to use of non-study antibacterial drugs.

Analysis of the following adverse events of special interest were performed as these AEs have
been observed with use of other cephalosporins or noted in the nonclinical studies using
ceftobiprole: renal impairment, leukopenia, liver enzyme increased, thrombosis, rash,
hypersensitivity reactions, and seizure. Leukopenia and liver enzyme increased are discussed in
the laboratory section. Thrombosis will be discussed in Section 7.7.2, key safety review issues.
Renal Impairment
There were 13 subjects (6.8%) who experienced AEs related to the GQ of renal impairment
(renal impairment, blood creatinine increased, creatinine renal clearance decreased, acute kidney
injury, and oliguria) in the ceftobiprole arm, and there was a similar frequency in the daptomycin
arm. Although none appeared to have a definitive association between renal impairment and
(b) (6)
ceftobiprole, there was a possible association in 2 subjects (
.
Blood creatinine increased was proposed by the Applicant in labeling, and a few additional PTs
noted in this section will be added.
•

(b) (6)

Subject
is an 82-year-old male with a medical history of cellulitis and
creatinine renal clearance decrease. As he finished his 28-day course of ceftobiprole, his
140

creatinine slowly increased and on the final day of ceftobiprole, the creatinine was measured
at 1.81 mg/dL (1.37 mg/dL on Day 1). Concomitant medications which could have also
caused the increase in creatinine included metamizole and omeprazole. Overall, the
contribution of ceftobiprole cannot be completely excluded. However, there were
confounding factors such as history of renal impairment, advanced age, and concomitant

(b) (6)
Subject
is a 66-year-old male with a medical history of diabetes mellitus and

medications included omeprazole, furosemide, and ketoprofen. On Day 29, his creatinine
improved to 1.1 mg/dL. Although there were confounding factors such as concomitant
medications and underlying comorbidities which could have caused the increase in
creatinine, the contribution of ceftobiprole cannot be completely excluded.

7.6.1.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial BPR-CS-009
Chemistry
Chemistry findings between the two arms were similar with exception of decreased potassium,
elevated chloride, elevated random glucose, elevated albumin and elevated blood urea nitrogen
(BUN) which had more than a 2% risk difference of occurring in the ceftobiprole arm than in the
daptomycin arm. None of the differences in the chemistry findings, with exception to
hypokalemia, were felt to be directly due to ceftobiprole given that chemistry derangements are

143
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
common in critically ill subjects. There were no laboratory measurements for lipase, amylase,
phosphate, magnesium, calcium, and bicarbonate.
Hypokalemia
There was a greater frequency of AEs of blood potassium increased (GQ of hypokalemia) in the
ceftobiprole arm as compared with the daptomycin arm, as shown in Table 52 above; this
correlated with an increased number of subjects in the ceftobiprole arm with low potassium
values as noted in the table below. Hypokalemia could be explained by increased gastrointestinal
losses caused by diarrhea and vomiting; both of which were higher in the ceftobiprole arm. As
such, hypokalemia will be added to the Applicant’s proposed labeling as an adverse reaction.
Moreover, in the ceftobiprole arm, there were 14 subjects with a low potassium value of level 3.
In contrast, 9 subjects in the daptomycin arm had the same level with a risk difference of 2.8%,
higher in the ceftobiprole arm. Subject profiles were evaluated for cardiac events that could be
associated with hypokalemia. Upon examination of the 14 subjects, two subjects had AEs related
to cardiac arrythmias, atrial fibrillation and arrhythmia, described below:
•

Subject
reported an AE of arrhythmia on Day 12. The subject had a medical
history of hypertension, myocardial ischemia, myocardial infarction, diabetes mellitus, renal
failure, cardiac ventricular thrombosis, decubitus ulcer, intermittent hypokalemia,
intermittent hypernatremia, and atrial fibrillation. The nadir for potassium measurement
occurred on Day 3 where it was measured at 2.3 mmol/L and the subject was given
potassium chloride. On Day 12, the subject experienced an SAE of arrhythmia and despite
cardiopulmonary resuscitation and adrenaline, the subject died. No potassium level was
recorded on this day with the last potassium level of 3.2 mmol/L being recorded on Day 7.

•

Subject
reported an AE of atrial fibrillation on Day 5. The subject had a
medical history of atrial fibrillation, venous thrombosis, and aortic valve sclerosis. The
lowest potassium measurement occurred on Day 21 where it was measured at 2.8 mmol/L.
The subject did not receive any potassium supplementation for hypokalemia but was on a
standing order of electrolyte replacement (calcium chloride, magnesium chloride, potassium
chloride and sodium chloride).

Subject profiles with a low hemoglobin level 3 (i.e., decreased by >2 g/dL from Baseline) were
examined for any possible signals of drug-induced hemolytic anemia which has been seen with
other cephalosporins or other causes of drug related anaemia such as bone marrow suppression.
No subjects had any significant patterns in hemoglobin values or laboratory abnormalities
(increased lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, increased bilirubin) to suggest drug-induced
hemolytic anemia; or chronology to suggest bone marrow suppression. In 11 of these subjects,
the level 3 decrease in hemoglobin occurred after ceftobiprole was discontinued while 14
occurred within 7 days of starting ceftobiprole. Four subjects required transfusions. For most of
the subjects, the hemoglobin initially decreased but increased while on ceftobiprole treatment
without the need for transfusions. Overall, no subjects exhibited a decrease in hemoglobin to
suggest ceftobiprole as a cause. Furthermore, when comparing subjects who experienced the AE
of anaemia in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the daptomycin arm, both arms experienced the
same number of AEs (13.1%). By the PTE, both arms had similar mean change from Baseline.

7.6.1.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial BPRCS-009
Overall, the number of subjects in the four screening quadrants for drug-induced liver injury
(DILI) were generally balanced between the two treatment arms. There were no identified cases
of Hy’s law in the ceftobiprole treatment arm.
(b) (6)

One subject (
) in the ceftobiprole arm, represented by a blue dot in Figure 7, was
in the potential Hy’s Law quadrant but did not meet the criteria for Hy’s Law as he did not have
an alkaline phosphatase level of less than 2x the upper limit of normal. Also, prior to being
randomized to ceftobiprole, the subject already had elevated liver enzymes (AST >3x upper limit
of normal [ULN] and total bilirubin >5x ULN).
Graphical profiles of subjects noted in the cholestasis and temple’s corollary quadrants were
reviewed and elevated liver tests did not appear to be solely attributed to ceftobiprole.

•

Subject
had a medical history significant for hypertension, chronic cardiac
failure, chronic pancreatitis, stage 5 chronic kidney disease with an AV fistula, who
developed ALT and AST ≥10x ULN. On Day 14, peak values of 755 U/L (baseline of 5 U/L)
for ALT, 960 U/L for AST (baseline of 11U/L), 170 U/L for alkaline phosphatase (baseline
of 59 U/L), and 64 U/L for gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) (baseline of 13 U/L). On
Day 21, all liver related lab values decreased while on ceftobiprole (AST was 50 U/L and
ALT 238 U/L). If the elevations were caused by ceftobiprole, it would be expected that there
would be continued elevation or worsening of the liver enzymes. According to the
investigator and FDA Reviewer, the transaminase elevation was less likely due to
ceftobiprole. However, since there were no other apparent causes of the laboratory
abnormalities, such as concomitant medications or other infection besides the primary
infection, drug-induced transaminitis could not be fully excluded.

to decrease on Day 13 and normalized by Day 41. The FDA reviewer agrees with the
investigator that it is probable that ceftobiprole could have caused elevations of the liver
enzymes given the temporal association.

7.6.1.9. Subgroup Analyses, Trial BPR-CS-009
Several subgroups were examined based on demographic variables. For most subgroups, the
percent of AEs occurred at similar rates. However, there was a higher percentage of AEs in
subjects ≥65 years old in the ceftobiprole arm as compared to the daptomycin arm. There was
also a higher percentage of AEs seen in subjects ≥65 years old compared to subjects ≤65 years
old within the group of subjects receiving ceftobiprole, however, the types of AEs seen were
similar. A similar trend was seen among subjects ≥75 years old, however, the size of this
subgroup was small. In the subgroup of subjects ≥75 years old, there was a similar frequency of
SAEs (seven subjects in the ceftobiprole arm (41%) experienced 13 SAEs while 10 subjects in
the daptomycin arm (48%) experienced 19 SAEs). In terms of mortality, there were 6 deaths in
the ceftobiprole arm (35%) compared to 7 deaths in the daptomycin arm (33%). The FDA
reviewer agrees with the investigator that none of these SAEs or deaths in the ceftobiprole arm
could be attributed to the drug.
In addition, the majority of subjects were White, non-Hispanic or Latino, and from outside of the
US. The frequency of AEs in these subgroups was similar to the frequency of AEs occurring in
the entire safety population. The other demographic groups were too small to make any
conclusions regarding safety, but no major differences are anticipated.

7.6.2. Acute Bacterial Skin/Soft Tissue Infection, Trial
BPR-CS-008
7.6.2.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, Trial BPR-CS-008
The overall incidence of TEAEs was 44.3% in the ceftobiprole arm and 38.3% in the
vancomycin and aztreonam arm. Most TEAEs in the ceftobiprole arm were mild or moderate,
and there were fewer severe TEAEs as compared to the vancomycin and aztreonam arm
(2.7% versus 7.0%). There was a lower incidence of SAEs in the ceftobiprole versus the
vancomycin and aztreonam arm (1.8% and 3.5%, respectively). Treatment discontinuation due
to TEAEs was also lower in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the vancomycin and aztreonam
arm (1.8% versus 2.9%).
Five subjects in each arm had interruptions of their respective treatment. In the ceftobiprole
arm, the AEs leading to interruption were blood creatinine increased in two subjects and the
following in one subject each: pruritus, vomiting, and both headache and nausea. None were
SAEs and all subjects recovered.

The following subjects in the ceftobiprole arm had SAEs. SAEs related to AEs of special interest
such as pneumonia and thromboembolism are also discussed in this section. Of the six SAEs,
rash and pruritis were probably related to ceftobiprole.
•

Subject
had a reported an SAE of rash and pruritis causing prolonged
hospitalization. This was a 49-year-old male with no significant past medical history who
developed an erythematous papular pruritic rash over his trunk and extremities 10 days after
starting ceftobiprole for which ceftobiprole was discontinued. Concomitant medications
included paracetamol, omeprazole, and enoxaparin. Two days after discontinuing
ceftobiprole and receiving methylprednisolone and antihistamine therapy, the rash was
completely resolved without sequelae. Due to the lack of other concomitant medications that
have a high likelihood of causing the SAEs along with the temporal relationship, the FDA
reviewer agrees with the investigator that the SAE was probably related to ceftobiprole.

•

Subject
had a reported an SAE of bronchial obstruction causing prolonged
hospitalization. This was an 82-year-old female with a medical history of arterial
hypertension who developed bronchospasms, cough, tachypnea, and scarce expectoration
after 3 days of ceftobiprole treatment. She finished a 5-day regimen and ultimately, she
recovered from the broncho-obstructive syndrome. The FDA reviewer agrees with the
Applicant that the SAE was not related to ceftobiprole because despite the continuation of
ceftobiprole, the broncho-obstructive symptom did not worsen.

7.6.2.4. Adverse Events and FDA Medical Queries Leading to
Treatment Discontinuation, Trial BPR-CS-008

The incidence of AEs that led to treatment discontinuation was lower in the ceftobiprole arm
compared to the vancomycin and aztreonam arm (1.8% versus 2.9%). The AEs that led to
treatment discontinuation in the ceftobiprole arm included rash, pruritus, dysgeusia, deep vein
thrombosis, wound infection, and skin bacterial infection. The subjects with AEs of rash, pruritis,
and deep vein thrombosis leading to discontinuation are discussed in the Section 7.6.2.3.
The only AE that led to more than one discontinuation was skin bacterial infection (one is
discussed in the SAE section, and one is noted below):
• Subject
was a 36-year-old female with a medical history of intravenous
heroin use, diabetes mellitus type II, and hepatitis C who, after 6 days of ceftobiprole,
continued to have worsening of primary ABSSSI (started on Day 3). Ceftobiprole was
discontinued on Day 6 and the AE resolved on Day 35. No other concomitant antibacterial
drugs were given during Day 0 and Day 35 (when the subject was discontinued from the
trial). The worsening of primary ABSSSI could be interpreted as the lack of efficacy of
ceftobiprole in this subject rather than an AE per se; however, given that no additional
antibacterial drugs were initiated, it is difficult to comment on the association of this event
with ceftobiprole. The investigator considered it unrelated to trial drug.

7.6.2.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial BPR-CS008
AEs occurred in 148 of 334 subjects (44.3%) in the ceftobiprole arm and in 131 of 342 subjects
(38.3%) in the comparator arm. The AEs that occurred with a risk difference of ≥1% in the
ceftobiprole arm were gastrointestinal-related such as nausea (10.8% vs 5.6%), diarrhea (6.3% vs
4.7%), and dysgeusia (2.1% vs 0%). All AEs of nausea, vomiting or diarrhea were of mild to
moderate severity and the majority had dose interruption or modification. More than half of these
AEs were thought to be possibly/probably related to ceftobiprole by the investigator. As with the
009 trial, the GQ of bacterial infection was common in both arm but was not related to
ceftobiprole and likely related to underlying medical conditions and was therefore, not included
in the label.
There were no reports of diarrhea associated with Clostridioides difficile. Gastrointestinal
symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are often considered common adverse
reactions associated with antibacterial drugs, and are proposed by the Applicant in labeling.
Leukopenia
The AEs related to leukopenia were reported in three subjects in the ceftobiprole arm (0.9%) and
2 subjects in the vancomycin and aztreonam arm (0.6%). The TEAEs in the ceftobiprole arm
160
Reference ID: 5357793

the section discussing laboratory values.

aztreonam arm (1.2%) who experienced AEs related to the GQ of renal impairment (blood
creatinine increased occurred in 2 subjects receiving ceftobiprole and acute kidney injury
occurred in 4 subjects receiving vancomycin and aztreonam).The 2 subjects who experienced the

7.6.2.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial BPRCS-008
The analysis of drug-induced liver injury identified PTs related to liver injury in eight (2.4%)
subjects treated with ceftobiprole and eleven (3.2%) subjects treated with the comparator
(vancomycin and aztreonam). There were no Hy’s law cases detected.

AEs relating to hepatic injury:
The AEs reported in the ceftobiprole arm include gamma-glutamyl-transferase increased, alanine
aminotransferase increased, aspartate aminotransferase increased, and blood alkaline
phosphatase increased. None were categorized as severe TEAEs, SAEs, or TEAEs resulting in
treatment discontinuation.
The investigator considered that ceftobiprole was a possible cause of the elevated liver enzymes
(b) (6)
in four subjects (
in the ceftobiprole
arm. The cases are described below:
•

(b) (6)

Subject
is a 59-year-old male with a medical history of hepatitis C, and drug
abuse who had reported AEs of AST and ALT increased on Day 5, which was the last day of
ceftobiprole treatment. There were no concomitant medications and therefore it could have
been possible that ceftobiprole caused the elevated liver enzymes. However, elevated liver
enzymes secondary to infection cannot be ruled out.

In the other three cases involving increase in liver enzymes, alternative reasons for liver enzyme

treatment. These are noted below:
•

•

•

(b) (6)

Subject
, a 29-year-old female with a medical history of alcohol use and drug
abuse, reported an AE of AST and ALT increased on Day 32. The subject received
ceftobiprole only on Day 1 and liver enzymes obtained on Day 3 were within normal limits
(ALT 19 U/L, AST 23 U/L). The limited exposure to ceftobiprole and the timing of the AE
did not appear to correlate well with exposure to ceftobiprole.
(b) (6)
Subject
, a 31-year-old male with a medical history of drug abuse and alcohol
use, began having elevated ALT and AST on Day 3. While still on ceftobiprole, the subject’s
AST decreased from 141 U/L on Day 3 to 87 U/L on Day 5. Furthermore, after stopping
ceftobiprole on Day 5, the AST increased to 108 U/L on Day 16. Because of the inconsistent
LFT changes, the reviewer found it unlikely that ceftobiprole caused the elevated liver
enzymes, although it cannot be completely excluded.
(b) (6)
Subject
, a 40-year-old male with a medical history of hepatitis C and drug
abuse, had an elevated AST of 208 U/L on Day 3 (from 68 U/L on Day 1). The AST
decreased to 192 U/L while still on ceftobiprole and continued to decrease once discontinued.
Furthermore, the bilirubin was 13.68 µmol/L on Day -1 and decreased while on ceftobiprole
to 8 µmol/L on Day 5. Because of this, it was unlikely that ceftobiprole caused the elevated
liver enzymes.

7.6.2.8. Vital Signs’ Analyses, Trial BPR-CS-008
Heart Rate, Temperature, Respiratory Rate
The mean changes from Baseline to post-treatment in both arms were similar and within normal

7.6.2.9. Subgroup Analyses, Trial BPR-CS-008
Table 72 shows the incidence of common TEAEs by demographic subgroups of sex, age,
ethnicity, and race. The incidence of TEAEs in the ceftobiprole arm was higher in subjects
between the age of 18 to 34 years and the most common TEAEs are discussed below. There were
more TEAES in the subgroup of subjects ages 65-75 years in the ceftobiprole arm as compared
to the vancomycin and aztreonam arm, but the number of subjects was too small to draw any
meaningful conclusions. The majority of subjects were White, non-Hispanic or Latino, and from
the US; the incidence of TEAEs appeared to be overall similar to the safety population. In
addition, there did not appear to be imbalances in TEAEs by gender.
Age 18 to 34 years
In this age group, there was a higher percentage of subjects in the ceftobiprole arm (58.6%) who
experienced AEs compared to the percentage of subjects in the vancomycin and aztreonam arm
(40.3%). In addition, the percentage of TEAEs in the younger subgroup was higher than in the
older subgroups receiving ceftobiprole. The most commonly reported AEs in the ceftobiprole
arm were nausea (n = 14), headache (n = 5), diarrhea (n = 5), alanine aminotransferase increased
(5 subjects), and aspartate aminotransferase increased (5 subjects). The most commonly reported
AEs in the comparator arm were headache (6 subjects), diarrhea (5 subjects), nausea (4 subjects),
abscess limb (4 subjects), and pyrexia (3). It appears that nausea and increased liver tests may
have driven this difference between treatment arms in this subgroup of younger subjects. In this
(b) (6)
subgroup, there was one SAE each in the ceftobiprole arm (worsening of skin infection,
(b) (6)
) and vancomycin and aztreonam arm (cellulitis). There were no deaths in this subgroup.
Age 65-74 years
In this age group, there was a higher percentage of subjects in the ceftobiprole arm (48.1%) who
experienced AEs compared to the percentage of subjects in the vancomycin and aztreonam arm
(33.3%). The most commonly reported AEs in the ceftobiprole arm were blood creatinine
increased (2 subjects), headache (2 subjects) and injection site reaction (2 subjects) while the
most commonly reported AEs in the vancomycin and aztreonam arm were skin bacterial
infection (3 subjects), nasopharyngitis (2 subjects) and oedema peripheral (2 subjects). There
were 2 SAEs in the vancomycin and aztreonam arm (skin bacterial infection) and none in the
ceftobiprole arm. There were no deaths in either treatment arm in this subgroup.

7.6.3.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, Trial CAP-3001
Table 73 shows the overview of adverse events in Trial CAP-3001. SAEs were balanced
between the two treatment arms. The ceftobiprole arm had more subjects with AEs leading to
discontinuation of the study drug, dose modification, interruption, and reduction of the study
drug compared to the ceftriaxone arm although the differences were not large. The ceftobiprole
arm also had more subjects with AEs overall at 70% compared to 64.6% in the ceftriaxone arm.
This difference was driven mostly by more moderate AEs seen in the ceftobiprole arm. Severe
and mild AEs were balanced between the two arms.

7.6.3.2. Deaths, Trial CAP-3001
The deaths between the ceftobiprole arm and the ceftriaxone arm were balanced with 9 deaths in
each treatment arm (Table 74). There was one subject in the ceftobiprole arm and two subjects in
the ceftriaxone arm that had more than one AE leading to death. The majority of AEs leading to
death were different between the two arms. For the ceftobiprole arm, lung neoplasms and cardiac
failure were more common whereas in the ceftriaxone arm, pneumonia and sudden death were
most common. Cardiac and respiratory AEs were common AEs leading to death in the two
treatment arms which is consistent with the hospitalized Trial population.
Review of the narratives of subjects who had died confirmed the investigator assessment that
none of the deaths in the ceftobiprole treatment arm were related to the study treatment. For the
(b) (6)
ceftriaxone treatment arm, the investigator attributed subject
’s death to be likely related
to the treatment. Review of the narrative confirms this assessment as the subject’s pneumonia
course continued to worsen requiring intensive care management likely due to ineffective
treatment. The remaining deaths appear to be unrelated to study treatment.

7.6.3.4. Adverse Events Leading to Treatment
Discontinuation, Trial CAP-3001
The overall rate of AEs leading to discontinuation was low at less than 10% in each trial arm
(Table 76). The ceftobiprole arm had a higher rate of AEs leading to discontinuation compared to
ceftriaxone at 5.8% vs 3.7%. The higher rate of AEs leading to discontinuation in the
ceftobiprole arm was mainly due to gastrointestinal disorders with subjects experiencing
vomiting, abdominal pain, and nausea compared to 1 subject experiencing abdominal distension
leading to discontinuation in the ceftriaxone arm. Similar to SAEs, infections and infestations
disorders were also relatively common in both arms. These results suggest ceftobiprole is
relatively well tolerated with the drug leading to discontinuation in a relatively small percentage
of subjects. Of note, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain will be labeled as adverse reactions in
Section 6 of labeling.

7.6.3.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial CAP-3001
There were slightly more TEAEs in the ceftobiprole arm (70%) compared to the ceftriaxone arm
(64.6%; Table 77). However, there is a notable difference between the types of TEAEs in each
treatment arm. The TEAEs that occurred at a greater frequency in the ceftobiprole arm compared
to the ceftriaxone arm included nausea, vomiting, rash, phlebitis, and hemorrhage (≥2% risk
difference). Gastrointestinal related AEs were the most common AEs associated with the use of
ceftobiprole. In addition, there are TEAEs in both arms that were balanced (liver enzyme
177
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
increased, headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, insomnia, dizziness), which may be due to both
drugs being cephalosporins or due to underlying medical comorbidities. Pneumonia was also
balanced in both arms occurring at a high frequency however this is likely due to the underlying
illness of the subject. Please refer to Section 17.4 for the table of subjects with all AEs occurring
in the safety population.
Given the higher frequency of hemorrhage in the ceftobiprole arm, these subjects were evaluated
in greater detail. There were 4 cases of hemoptysis categorized under hemorrhage. Two of the
subjects may have developed hemoptysis that did not have an obvious cause aside from their
underlying pulmonary illness. Of the remaining two, one subject was on warfarin and aspirin and
the other developed hemoptysis 12 days after receiving the last dose of ceftobiprole and was also
diagnosed with lung cancer. For the other subjects who developed hemorrhage as an AE, three of
the subjects were on anti-coagulant medications and 4 subjects developed their AE several days
to weeks after receiving their last dose of ceftobiprole. There were two subjects that developed
hematoma and ecchymoses without a clear inciting event, however one of the subjects had only
received one day of treatment. Based on these evaluations, there does not appear to be a strong
signal that would indicate ceftobiprole is associated with hemorrhage as several of the AEs were
likely due to concomitant use of anti-coagulant medications or occurred after treatment.

7.6.3.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial CAP-3001
The number of subjects with either high or low chemistry analyte values were generally balanced
between the two treatment arms (Table 78). There were slightly more abnormalities in the
ceftriaxone arm with low sodium and elevated BUN. Elevated creatinine was also seen more
frequently in the ceftriaxone arm at 4.1% compared to 1.1% in the ceftobiprole arm (Table 79).
There were more cases of high potassium (6.5% vs 3.6%) and low glucose (5.5% vs 3%) in the
ceftobiprole subjects. Of note, hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia were reported as AEs less
commonly for ceftobiprole compared to ceftriaxone. The number of subjects with liver
abnormalities were balanced with no major differences between the two arms (Table 80). Total
cholesterol and triglycerides were also balanced between the two arms (Table 81). Regarding
hematology laboratory values, leukocytosis was observed more in the ceftriaxone arm at 31%
compared with 24% in the ceftobiprole arm (Table 82). The remainder of abnormal hematologic
values were otherwise balanced.
Overall, there does not appear to be any major difference between ceftobiprole and ceftriaxone
with respect to chemical, renal, cholesterol, hepatic, or hematologic laboratory values.

7.6.3.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Trial CAP3001
Figure 11 shows a screening assessment for potential cases of DILI. Overall, the number of
subjects in the four quadrants were generally balanced between the two arms (Table 83). There
(b) (6)
were two subjects in each treatment arm – subjects
in the ceftobiprole arm
(b) (6)
and subjects
in the ceftriaxone arm – that fit the criteria for potential Hy’s
Law.
•

•

(b) (6)

In the ceftriaxone arm, subject
was found to have elevated ALT at 45 U/L, AST at
114 U/L, and bilirubin at 2.22 mg/dL prior to receiving study medication for 3 days. Alkaline
phosphatase and GGT were also elevated. Repeat blood work on the third day showed
normalized ALT but increased alkaline phosphatase, AST at 127 U/L, and bilirubin at
2.81 mg/dL with a decrease in GGT. Repeat blood work to assess resolution of elevated liver
function tests was not done. The subject had elevated values prior to receiving the study drug
which may be due to initial illness and during treatment there was both improvement and
worsening of lab values. In this subject, it is unclear if the study treatment is related to the
liver dysfunction, but it is unlikely given the overall trend.
(b) (6)
Subject
did not have liver function tests prior to receiving ceftriaxone. After
receiving treatment for 9 days, liver function tests were obtained and the subject had normal
levels of ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT. Bilirubin was elevated at 4.39 mg/dL.
Study drug was stopped on day 11 and on day 13, subject had elevated ALT at 575 U/L, AST
at 1072 U/L, and increased bilirubin levels that peaked at 6.02 mg/dL. GGT and alkaline
phosphatase remained normal throughout the study. Lab work done at the end of the study
showed resolution of all liver function tests except a persistent mildly increased bilirubin.
Subject had developed a rib fracture on day 10 and cardiac failure on day 34. Subject had
also received ranitidine concurrently with study treatment. While rare, ranitidine has been
associated with liver injury with resolution upon stopping medication and it is possible that
concurrent use of ranitidine and other medications may have caused the hepatic injury.

184
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
•

•

(b) (6)

In the ceftobiprole arm, subject
was found to have elevated AST at 3861 U/L, ALT
at 883 U/L, bilirubin at 2.81 mg/dL, and elevated GGT prior to receiving treatment for 4
days. While on treatment, ALT decreased while the alkaline phosphatase and GGT increased
along with bilirubin which peaked at 5.79 mg/dL. AST was not done at the time. Repeat lab
work done at the end of the trial showed resolution of elevated laboratory values except for
GGT but that value of GGT had decreased to less than the initial elevated value. Given the
elevated values prior to receiving the study drug with a subsequent decrease in some of the
values while on treatment, it is less likely that the liver injury is due to the study drug. It is
likely that the initial abnormal laboratory values were due to the initial illness.
(b) (6)
Subject
had mildly elevated ALT, AST, and bilirubin prior to receiving ceftobiprole.
Alkaline phosphatase and GGT were within normal range throughout the trial. Subject
received 8 days of treatment and during treatment, ALT, AST, and bilirubin increased until
the last day of treatment. ALT and AST levels peaked at 68 U/L and 105 U/L respectively.
Repeat testing done days after stopping treatment showed decreasing ALT and AST however
bilirubin continued to increase to a peak of 2.51 mg/dL. There was no repeat testing to trend
resolution of the remaining elevated values. Approximately 47 days after last laboratory test,
the subject was reported to have hepatic cirrhosis. Given the diagnosis of hepatic cirrhosis
near the end of the trial, it is likely that the subject had underlying liver disease prior to
enrollment. This is supported in the initial elevated lab values prior to starting treatment. Any
association with ceftobiprole and DILI would be difficult to determine in this subject.

Based on these two subjects who met potential Hy’s Law criteria, there is no signal associating
ceftobiprole with DILI.

7.6.3.8. Vital Signs’ Analyses, Trial CAP-3001
Review of the vital signs data showed no clinical differences between the treatment arms. Over
the course of the trial there were changes in both arms consistent with resolution of bacterial
pneumonia including decreased heart rate, temperature, and respiratory rate along with increased
blood pressure.
7.6.3.9. Subgroup Analyses, Trial CAP-3001
Based on the sub-group analysis (Table 84), there were more subjects with reported AEs in the
ceftobiprole arm reported in each sex, race, ethnicity, and geographic subgroup which is
consistent with the higher rate of AEs in the general population. Of note, there were fewer
ceftobiprole subjects with AEs in the older age groups (>65 and >75 years). Overall, there does
not appear to be major differences in the incidence of AEs by subgroup beyond what was
observed in the general trial population. Some of the differences in AEs between the two
treatment arms may be due to low enrollment within that subgroup. For example, there were only
33 total subjects in the Black or African American subgroup.

7.6.4.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, Trial BPR-PIP-002
The proportion of subjects with TEAEs was similar in the ceftobiprole arm and the comparator
cephalosporin arm (31.9% vs. 29.5% respectively). The majority of TEAEs were mild in both
arms of the trial. The incidence of AEs leading to permanent discontinuation of the trial drug was
higher in the ceftobiprole arm than in the comparator arm (4.3% vs. 0) and is discussed in further
detail in Section 7.6.4.4. There was one subject with an AE leading to interruption of the study
drug, and one subject with a severe AE, both of which occurred in ceftobiprole arm. There were
seven SAEs in the ceftobiprole arm vs. two SAEs in the comparator arm during the study period
which are discussed below in Section 7.6.4.3

The narratives for the SAEs that occurred in the ceftobiprole arm are provided below. Two of
these SAEs - hypersensitivity and pneumonia - occurred during the IV treatment period and the
remainder (pleuropneumonia, pneumonia (2 events), tonsillitis streptococcal, pharyngitis
streptococcal, pleural effusion, and vomiting) occurred following transition to oral antibacterial
drugs:
•

Subject
experienced two SAEs of hypersensitivity and pleural effusion. This
17-year-old female with no significant medical history was admitted for treatment of CABP.
On Day 3 of ceftobiprole administration, during the infusion, she experienced facial and
extremity edema, a diffuse itchy rash, high fever and sweating. There was no associated
hypotension or bronchospasm. Ceftobiprole was discontinued and the subject was treated
with IV dexamethasone and oral chloropyramine. Symptoms resolved in an hour, and she
was transitioned to treatment with cefuroxime and levofloxacin. Two days later, a chest x-ray
demonstrated bilateral pneumonia and right-sided pleural effusion and her antibacterial
regimen was adjusted to cefuroxime and clindamycin. A follow-up chest x-ray 2 days later
revealed progression of pneumonia at which time vancomycin was initiated. CT chest
showed bilateral hydrothoraces which were categorized as an SAE due to prolongation of
hospitalization. Bilateral chest tubes were placed. Amikacin and amoxicillin/clavulanate
were started for persistent fever. She improved clinically, her chest tubes were removed and
she was transitioned to oral levofloxacin. The FDA reviewer’s evaluation supports the
relatedness of the SAE of hypersensitivity to ceftobiprole because it occurred during the IV
infusion. However, this reviewer agrees with the investigator that the SAE of pleural effusion
is likely due to complications of pneumonia and unrelated to study drug.

•

Subject
was a 1-year-old male with no significant medical history who was
hospitalized for CABP. He had an SAE of pneumonia on Day 1. He was noted to have
tachypnea during initial screening for the trial. On the same day, the subject received the first
dose of ceftobiprole but was transferred to the intensive care unit for worsening tachypnea
and was placed on mechanical ventilation later that day. Due to persistent fever following the
second dose of ceftobiprole, the study drug was discontinued, and the subject was started on
ceftriaxone and clarithromycin. Because his therapy was switched prior to Day 4, this subject
did not have a clinical response assigned on that day and was judged to have a category of
“worsened” at EOT. His clinical outcome was failure at the TOC visit. This reviewer agrees
with the investigator that the pneumonia is unlikely to be related to the study drug, given that
symptoms were present prior to his receiving the first dose of ceftobiprole and subsequent
clinical worsening occurred within 24 hours of the start of treatment. The narrative is

Subject
was a 6-year-old female with a history of atrial septal defect and
