(b) (6)
Subject
was a 2-year-old male who experienced an SAE of pneumonia. He
was originally hospitalized for CABP and treated with ceftobiprole for 5 days, followed by 5
days of oral amoxicillin clavulanate. The location of his pneumonia was not specified. His
clinical response at Day 4 was judged to be improved and cured at the EOT visit. Twelve
days after the EOT visit, he developed low grade fever and was diagnosed with a new left
lobar pneumonia for which he was hospitalized and transferred to the intensive care unit
within two hours of admission due to worsening tachypnea, dyspnea and persistent fever. He
was treated with ceftriaxone, meropenem, and clarithromycin during this hospitalization and
improved with treatment. Because the new pneumonia was diagnosed 12 days after his first
EOT visit, it could have represented failure of treatment of the initial pneumonia. His overall
clinical outcome was judged by the investigator to be failure at the TOC visit. This reviewer
agrees with the Applicant that it is likely not related to administration of the study drug.
(b) (6)

was a 3-year-old female treated for CABP with ceftobiprole for 3

developed fever and cough and was diagnosed with the SAEs of streptococcal pharyngitis
and tonsillitis streptococcal for which she was hospitalized and treated with amoxicillinclavulanate. Because there was approximately 3 weeks between completion of ceftobiprole
treatment for CABP and the onset of her tonsillopharyngitis, these SAEs were not judged to
be related to ceftobiprole.

Subject
was a 4-year-old male with no significant medical history who was

following day, ceftobiprole was discontinued, and amikacin, meropenem, and vancomycin
were started. Pleuritis was classified as an SAE as it resulted in prolongation of
hospitalization. In this reviewer’s opinion, the SAE is not a safety event per se, but rather
appears to represent worsening infection which may have been the result of failure of
treatment with ceftobiprole.

7.6.4.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial BPR-PIP002
TEAEs occurred with similar frequency in both treatment arms – 31.9% of subjects in the
ceftobiprole arm and 29.5% of subjects in the comparator cephalosporin arm (Table 88). The
most common TEAEs in the ceftobiprole arm were vomiting (7.4% of subjects), viral infection
(4.3%), headache (3.2%), pneumonia (3.2%), and alanine aminotransferase increased (3.2%), all
with a risk difference of >3.0 compared to the comparator arm while the most common AE in the
comparator cephalosporin arm was diarrhea (9.1% of subjects, risk difference -7.0). The
ceftobiprole arm had more AEs related to hypersensitivity, phlebitis, urticaria, and infusion site
reactions (6 subjects compared to 1 in comparator cephalosporin arm). The ceftobiprole arm also
had more AEs related to the lower respiratory tract including pleurisy, pleural effusion and
pneumonia (3 subjects compared to 0 in comparator cephalosporin arm) which are likely
reflective of the infection under study and the 2:1 enrollment in the ceftobiprole versus
comparator arms.
There were only 5 subjects in the ceftobiprole arm with HABP included in the trial. Among these
subjects, there were two AEs, chromaturia and pyrexia, neither of which were considered SAEs.

7.6.4.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial BPR-PIP-002
Chemistry analyte values between the ceftobiprole and comparator arms were generally similar
in this trial. Alterations in sodium levels were minor and balanced between treatment arms.
Hypokalemia occurred with a frequency of approximately 4-5.4% in both treatment arms,
however, there was an imbalance in favor of ceftobiprole in the occurrence of hyperkalemia with
a lower percentage occurring in the ceftobiprole arm versus the comparator cephalosporin arm
(4.3% versus 9.1% respectively, risk difference -4.7).

Hematology test values indicated similar trends in ceftobiprole and comparator cephalosporin
arms respectively in WBC counts, both Level 1 elevated (63% versus 54.5% respectively were
greater than 10,800 cells/mL) and Level 1 decreased (9.8% versus 9.1 % respectively were less
than 3,500 cells/mL). However, 41.3% vs. 25% of subjects in the ceftobiprole vs. comparator
arms respectively had Level 3 elevations in WBC counts. In keeping with the expected
physiological response to infection, WBC measurements were in general, abnormal at the start of
the trial and trended toward normal by the time of TOC visit. Clinically relevant Levels 2 and 3
neutropenia and thrombocytopenia were reasonably balanced between treatment arms. Other
hematology analytes including hemoglobin, lymphocyte, and eosinophil counts all had similar
changes in both treatment arms. Although pancytopenia is described in association with the
cephalosporin class of medications, pneumonia, severity of illness as well as the duration of
treatment may have contributed to changes in the hematology values seen in this trial.

Subject
was a 6-year-old male with no significant medical history who had

of concomitant medications, relatedness to ceftobiprole is possible. However, the etiology of
this subject’s pneumonia was not determined and may have been contributory as well to the
rise in liver enzymes.

7.6.4.8. Vital Signs’ Analyses, Trial BPR-PIP-002
Subjects in both treatment arms experienced tachycardia, tachypnea and higher body temperature
at Trial entry, which trended toward normal during the course of the Trial. These changes at trial
enrollment likely reflected appropriate physiological responses to pneumonia, and improvement
during the course of the trial is to be expected as pneumonia resolves. The trends in heart rate,
respiratory rate and body temperature are displayed in Figure 12 through Figure 14 below.

7.6.4.9. Subgroup Analyses, Trial BPR-PIP-002
Table 96 shows the incidence of AEs by demographic subgroups of sex and age. The incidence
of AEs in female subjects was higher in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the comparator
cephalosporin arm (29.3% and 17.4% respectively). Information from Dr. Ines Pagan, the
pharmacology/toxicology reviewer indicates that although there were no specific juveniles
included in the animal studies for ceftobiprole, there were no significant differences in the
toxicity profiles of females compared to males in these studies.
Fewer subjects in the 3 months to <2 years and the 2 years to <6 years age groups in the
ceftobiprole arm had TEAEs (35.1% and 25% respectively) compared to the same age groups in
the cephalosporin ± vancomycin arm (47.4% and 50% respectively). Conversely, more subjects
in the 12 years to <18 years age group in the ceftobiprole arm had TEAEs compared to the
comparator arm (33% versus 0). However, the number of subjects in each of these categories
was too small to draw any meaningful conclusions. There were no subgroup analyses performed
for ethnicity or race given that all but one subject enrolled in the trial were White. This lack of
ethnic diversity in the trial may limit generalizability of results to populations in the U.S.

7.6.5. Hospital-Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia and
Ventilator-Associated Bacterial Pneumonia, Trial
BAP 248/307
The BAP 248/307 Trial was submitted to augment the safety database of ceftobiprole. The
Applicant is not seeking an indication for HABP/VABP. This trial will be briefly described
below followed by a discussion of safety results.
BAP 248/307 was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, active-control, prospective, multicenter
trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of ceftobiprole compared to linezolid/ceftazidime in adult
subjects diagnosed with HABP and VABP. Pertinent inclusion criteria included subjects
clinically diagnosed with pneumonia after a minimum of 72 hours of hospitalization or residence
in a chronic care facility and who had clinical signs/symptoms of pneumonia. Subjects who were
pregnant or lactating, had renal impairment, hepatic dysfunction, who were HIV positive, or had
a known or suspected condition that may have jeopardized adherence to protocol requirements
were excluded from the trial. A total of 781 subjects were randomly assigned to the two study
arms with a total of 772 subjects included in the safety analysis, 386 subjects in each arm. There
were 567 subjects in the non-VABP subgroup (283 in the ceftobiprole arm and 284 in the
linezolid/ceftazidime arm) and 205 subjects in the VABP subgroup (103 in the ceftobiprole arm
and 102 in the linezolid/ceftazidime arm).
7.6.5.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, Trial BAP 248/307
Table 97 summarizes the AEs in Trial BAP 248/307. SAEs occurred in slightly more subjects in
the ceftobiprole arm at 36% compared to the linezolid/ceftazidime arm at 32%. More subjects
developed AEs leading to discontinuation of study drug with 14% of the ceftobiprole subjects
compared to 10% of the linezolid/ceftazidime subjects. There were also more subjects
experiencing AEs leading to dose modification in the ceftobiprole arm. Overall AEs were
balanced between the treatment arms at 78%. There were slightly more severe AEs in the
ceftobiprole arm at 38% compared to 35% of the comparator arm.

7.6.5.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial
BAP 248/307
There were slightly more subjects with SAEs in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the
linezolid/ceftazidime (Table 98). For ceftobiprole, the largest number of SAEs were noted in the
following SOC: infection/infestations at 13.5% followed by respiratory, thoracic, and

the ceftobiprole arm included cardiac failure, cardiac arrest, sepsis, septic shock, multiorgan
dysfunction, pneumonia, respiratory failure and distress, hyponatremia, and brain edema. A
significant portion of the SAEs were related to respiratory or infectious etiologies in both
treatment arms. This likely reflects underlying pulmonary disease and the disease process of
nosocomial pneumonia.

7.6.5.4. Adverse Events Leading to Treatment
Discontinuation, Trial BAP 248/307
The number of subjects with AEs leading to discontinuation is listed in Table 99. While the
ceftobiprole arm had more subjects with AEs leading to discontinuation (14%) compared to
linezolid/ceftazidime (10.4%), the difference was not driven by one particular SOC. The
respiratory, thoracic, and mediastinal disorders SOC had the highest number of subjects with
AEs leading to discontinuation in both treatment arms followed by infections and infestations
and nervous system disorders. Upon review of the AEs listed, many of the AEs appear to be
related to the underlying condition of the subjects. For example, pneumonia, sepsis, and acute
respiratory distress syndrome are expected conditions in this subject population. Of note,
hyponatremia was found to be associated with discontinuation of ceftobiprole in 4 subjects (1%)
compared to 1 subject in the comparator arm (0.3%). Low sodium values are discussed in the
“Laboratory Findings” subsection below.

7.6.5.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events, Trial BAP
248/307
TEAEs occurred in a similar proportion of subjects in the two treatment arms at 77.5% for
ceftobiprole and 77.7% for linezolid/ceftazidime (Table 100). The TEAEs that had the highest
incidence in the ceftobiprole arm were bacterial infection, diarrhea, respiratory failure, pyrexia,
hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and vomiting. Of these TEAEs, vomiting, bacterial infection,
pyrexia, and hyponatremia had a >2% risk difference in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the
linezolid/ceftazidime arm. There was also an imbalance in renal impairment and cardiac failure
in the ceftobiprole arm compared to the linezolid/ceftazidime arm. The high incidence of overall
TEAEs is likely due to the significant comorbidities of the subjects and their complicated disease
course. A significant portion of subjects in this trial required intensive care management with
extensive medical histories contributing to their illness. Of the TEAEs with an imbalance,
bacterial infection and cardiac failure were likely related to underlying medical conditions.
Hyponatremia was also noted in the laboratory findings (see section below). Vomiting was noted
in the other clinical studies as associated with ceftobiprole. Renal impairment was not observed
when examining the laboratory data (see Laboratory Findings section below). Please refer to
Section 0 for the table of subjects with all AEs occurring in the safety population.

7.6.5.6. Laboratory Findings, Trial BAP 248/307
The tables below summarize the laboratory data from Trial 248/307 (Table 101,Table 102,Table
103,Table 104,and Table 105). In the ceftobiprole treatment arm, there were more cases of
hyponatremia (19.4%) compared to the linezolid/ceftazidime treatment arm (14%). It appears
this difference in cases of hyponatremia was largely driven by mild cases (between 130 and 132
mEq/L). The remainder of the chemistry values were relatively balanced between the two
treatment arms. Of note, hyponatremia will be listed as an adverse reaction in section 6 of
labeling. Evidence of renal dysfunction in each arm was also overall balanced with elevated
creatinine occurring in 8.4% of subjects in the ceftobiprole arm vs. 7.5% in the
linezolid/ceftazidime arms. While in the ceftobiprole arm there were more cases of elevated
alkaline phosphatase at 24.1% compared to linezolid/ceftazidime at 15.5%, elevations in AST,
ALT, and bilirubin levels were overall balanced between the two arms and did not exceed more
than 10% of all subjects. Elevations in cholesterol levels were also balanced between the two
arms, however there were more cases of hypertriglyceridemia in the ceftobiprole arm (52.2%)
compared to the linezolid/ceftazidime arm (43.3%). Outliers in hematology values were also
overall balanced between the two arms, but lymphopenia occurred more in the ceftobiprole arm
(33.1%) than linezolid/ceftazidime (27.7%).
Overall, there does not appear to be major differences in the laboratory values between the
treatment arms. The subject population in the Trial was fairly ill with multiple medical
comorbidities that may be contributing to certain laboratory value outliers.

7.7. Key Safety Review Issues
7.7.1. Higher Mortality for Ceftobiprole Patients With
VABP in Trial BAP 248/307
Issue
Increased deaths were observed in the VABP subgroup of Trial BAP 248/307 in subjects in the
ceftobiprole arm compared to the linezolid/ceftazidime arm.

215
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Background
In Trial BAP 248/307, a subgroup analysis was done on the safety population based on their
pneumonia diagnosis. Of the total 772 subjects, there were 205 VABP subjects with 103 subjects
in the ceftobiprole arm and 102 in the linezolid/ceftazidime arm. It was noted that VABP
subjects in the ceftobiprole arm had a higher rate of death compared to the subjects in the
linezolid/ceftazidime arm. Although the trial was not submitted for an evaluation of efficacy, the
increased deaths may have represented a safety issue in this subgroup of subjects. An in-depth
analysis of the data was conducted to evaluate potential causes and reasons for the increased
deaths in the VABP subgroup.
Assessment
The total deaths in Trial BAP 248/307 were overall balanced between both arms (23%
ceftobiprole vs. 22% linezolid/ceftazidime). In the HABP (non-VABP) subgroup however, there
were fewer deaths in the ceftobiprole arm at 18.7% compared to 21.1% in the
linezolid/ceftazidime arm. This is contrasted by more deaths in the VABP subgroup among
ceftobiprole subjects (33%) compared to the linezolid/ceftazidime arm (23.5%). Given this
higher rate of death, the narratives for all the deaths in the BAP 248/307 trial were reviewed to
determine whether the study drug was related to death. The study drug and death were
considered unrelated by the FDA reviewer if the death occurred within 48 hours of receiving the
first dose of treatment, the death occurred after receiving the last dose of treatment, or another
cause of death was established in the narrative. If a subject who was diagnosed with VABP,
initiated treatment, and subsequently expired within a day, the study drug likely would have not
made a difference in the subject’s trajectory and the death was deemed unrelated to the
treatment. In addition, if a subject completed treatment of study drug with resolution of their
illness but expired afterwards, this was also considered unrelated as clinical cure was
documented and the death was not considered treatment failure. Study drug and death were
considered related if there was treatment failure characterized by worsening of VABP that led to
death after 48 hours of initiating treatment or if the subject’s death was due to an AE related to
the study treatment. There was one death related to an allergic reaction, presumably from the
trial treatment in the HABP subgroup in a subject receiving linezolid/ceftazidime.
Based on the narrative reviews, the death and study drug relatedness were balanced between the
two trial arms in the overall trial population with 12.6% of the deaths in the ceftobiprole arm and
14.3% of the deaths in the linezolid/ceftazidime arm deemed related to the study drug (Table
108). This balance in study drug relatedness is also seen within the subgroups. HABP subject
deaths related to the trial treatment was seen in 17% of the ceftobiprole deaths and 16.7%
linezolid/ceftazidime deaths. In the VABP subject subgroup, both treatment arms had 5.9% of
the deaths deemed related to the Trial drug.

Conclusion
Despite the increased deaths in the VABP subgroup who received ceftobiprole compared to
those who received linezolid/ceftazidime, most of the deaths do not appear to be related to the
study treatment itself. The increased deaths in the VABP subgroup may have been due to chance,
as there was a small number of subjects in the VABP subgroup relative to the entire trial. In
addition, the acuity and severity of illness in this subgroup may have led to increased deaths
overall, thereby confounding the association between deaths and trial treatment. However,
information on increased mortality in VABP subjects treated with ceftobiprole will be included
in the ceftobiprole labeling as a warning, emphasizing that ceftobiprole is not approved for the
treatment of VABP.

7.7.2. Imbalance in Adverse Events Related to
Thrombosis in Trial BPR-CS-009
Issue
An increased frequency of thrombosis was observed in the ceftobiprole arm as compared to
daptomycin arm in the BPR-CS-009 trial. This was evaluated further as a key safety issue due to
nonclinical signals of thromboembolic events discussed in Section 7.1 and summarized below.
Background
In the nonclinical/toxicology studies, there were findings of thrombi observed across species (at
the injection site in the rat, marmoset, and dog) and emboli noted in marmosets in the heart, lung,
kidney, mostly with administration of ceftobiprole for a duration of over 1 month. The Applicant
stated that in the 13-week studies in rats and marmosets, the thrombus formation was around the
tip of the infusion catheter. When examining the histological changes, it was consistent with
mechanical irritation by the infusion catheter, subsequently causing vascular-wall irritation and
subsequent thrombus formation. The mechanical irritation was attributed to the small size of the
veins relative to the large size of the implanted catheter. Ultimately, it was thought that the
thrombus formation was caused by local irritation and injury along with the higher
concentrations of ceftobiprole as compared with the clinical studies.
Assessment
When grouping the PTs using the narrow FMQ, there was a slightly higher incidence of
thrombosis in the ceftobiprole vs. the comparator arm.

(b) (6)

(b) (6)
).
Another information request was sent to the Applicant on February 23, 2024, requesting further

•

(b) (6)

was a 58-year-old female with a medical history of recently diagnosed DVT,
osteomyelitis and epidural abscess in T8-9, abscess drainage eight days prior to enrollment
and spinal decompression six days prior enrollment, who had a reported AE of thrombosis on
Day 11. The verbatim term was post-thrombotic disease of the lower extremities and in the
information request response, the Applicant clarified that the subject was diagnosed with
DVT 6 days prior to starting ceftobiprole and experienced a mild post-thrombotic syndrome
of the lower extremities on Day 11. The Applicant stated that these events were clearly
linked as the post-thrombotic syndrome (i.e., the chronic condition) was seen as favorable
progress of the pre-study deep vein thrombosis (i.e., the acute condition).
(b) (6)

was a 65-year-old female with a medical history of thrombophlebitis
(diagnosed 46 days prior to enrollment), aortic arteriosclerosis, and hypertension who had a
reported AE of DVT on Day 15. During the same time as the thrombophlebitis, the subject
also had a chronic wound on the right calf for which she had a necrectomy two days prior to
enrollment. The exact location of the initial acute thrombophlebitis on the right lower
extremity was not recorded, and the location of the DVT was at the right medial
gastrocnemius. The Applicant noted that it is possible that the exact location could have been
different and the two events were distinct, however, the chronic wound and necrectomy may
have predisposed for the development of a DVT. Additional risk factors for thrombosis
included not receiving DVT prophylaxis and the presence of an immobilization bandage.
Immobilization is a known risk factor for DVT (Samama 2000).
(b) (6)

was a 45-year-old female with a medical history of hemodialysis, chronic
kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, nontunneled central venous catheter placement 12 days
prior to enrollment who had an SAE of atrial thrombosis on Day 5 which was found on
transesophageal echocardiography. She was placed on heparin and a repeat echocardiography
219

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
showed reduced size of the thrombosis while she was still on ceftobiprole treatment. It is
unlikely that ceftobiprole contributed to the formation of atrial thrombosis as the thrombosis
improved during treatment.
•

•

•

•

(b) (6)

was a 48-year-old male with a medical history of diabetes mellitus, multiple
surgeries two months prior to enrollment (pancreatectomy 64 days prior, colectomy 62 days
prior, splenectomy 3 days prior), who had an AE of venous thrombosis limb on Day 8. The
verbatim term was right leg phlebothrombosis and the Applicant noted that the subject had
been diagnosed with a right lower extremity DVT 21 days prior to starting ceftobiprole. The
Applicant also noted that it is unclear whether the pre-study DVT and the AE of venous
thrombosis limb occurred at the exact same location and it is uncertain whether these were
related events.
(b) (6)

was a 34-year-old female with a medical history of intravenous drug abuse
who had an AE of venous thrombosis limb and a reported term of right basilic vein
thrombosis on Day 13. Prior to the AE, she had not been receiving any DVT prophylaxis,
had a peripherally inserted central catheter placed in the right basilic vein on Day 3 which
was removed once the DVT was diagnosed, and had a history of intravenous drug abuse
which are all associated with a risk of thrombi formation (McColl et al. 2001). The
association with ceftobiprole is unlikely, but not fully excluded.
(b) (6)

was a 45-year-old male with a medical history of chronic pancreatitis, distal
pancreatomy 11 days prior to enrollment, who had an AE of portal vein thrombosis on Day 8.
In a study involving 991 subjects who underwent distal pancreatomy, 2.1% were diagnosed
with portal vein thrombosis (Kamath et al. 2014). As portal vein thrombosis is a very specific
type of thrombosis and may have been due to prior surgery, it is less likely that there was an
association with ceftobiprole.
(b) (6)

is a 58-year-old female with a medical history of arteriovenous fistula,
hemodialysis, and type 2 diabetes mellitus experienced an SAE of arteriovenous fistula
thrombosis on Day 45 which was 23 days after ceftobiprole was discontinued. Because of the
prolonged time between the onset of the thrombosis and the last dose of ceftobiprole, an
association between the thrombosis and ceftobiprole is unlikely.

Conclusion
Out of the 7 subjects discussed above, 4 had events that appeared to be unrelated to ceftobiprole
(one had pre-existing DVT and post-thrombotic syndrome, one had portal vein thrombosis in the
setting of pancreatic surgery, and 2 had no clear temporal association with ceftobiprole).
However, in 2 subjects, it was not clear if the DVT or venous thrombosis was the same as the
(b) (6)
episode occurring several days before treatment with ceftobiprole
(b) (6)
). Another subject had an upper extremity DVT in the setting of a peripherally inserted
(b) (6)
central catheter line
). The remaining 3 subjects in the ceftobiprole arm who
experienced venous thrombosis had other risk factors for venous thrombosis such as
immobilization, multiple surgeries, or IV lines, however, the contribution of ceftobiprole could
not be fully excluded. Given the nonclinical findings of thromboemboli in multiple animal
species, a similar finding in humans may be possible, but overall less likely given confounding
factors in the study population (e.g., multiple comorbidities, prolonged hospitalization, prior
surgical procedures, and inconsistent DVT prophylaxis).

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Notably, no significant imbalance in thrombosis events was noted in the other clinical trials
discussed in this review. Additionally, thromboembolic disease has not been reported with
ceftobiprole in the post market setting (from countries where it is approved for indications of
HABP and CABP). However, ceftobiprole will be administered to subjects with SAB who may
be prone to valvular insufficiency, peripheral vascular disease, and potentially prolonged
hospitalization predisposing them to venous thrombosis. Therefore, thrombosis will be included
in section 6 of the labeling under the subsection “Selected Adverse Reactions of ZEVTERA in
Adult Patients” occurring at a rate < 2% in the clinical trials and will be further monitored by
routine surveillance in the post-market setting.

8. Therapeutic Individualization
8.1. Intrinsic Factors
8.1.1. Renal Impairment
Renal impairment had a significant effect on ceftobiprole exposure. Following a single infusion
of ceftobiprole 250 mg over 30 minutes, systemic exposure (area under the concentration-time
curve [AUC]last) was 29% higher in subjects with mild renal impairment, and 2.5-fold, and 3.3fold higher in subjects with moderate and severe renal impairment, respectively, compared to
subjects with normal renal function. Urinary recovery was approximately 74% to 32% in
subjects with mild to severe renal impairment, respectively (see Section 14.2.3.
Dose adjustment for renal impairment is recommended as depicted in Table 111 based on 1)
FDA analyses and PK simulations 2) the Applicant’s population PK analyses 3) evaluation of
target attainment rates for the proposed doses in subjects with moderate and severe renal
impairment and 4) safety and efficacy data from the pivotal phase 3 efficacy trials using the
proposed dose adjustments.

8.1.2. End-Stage Renal Disease and Patients Receiving
Intermittent Hemodialysis
Dosage in subjects with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) (defined as a CrCL < 15 mL/min) and
subjects receiving intermittent hemodialysis (iHD) is supported by simulated ceftobiprole
exposures derived using a population PK model fit with data from nine phase 1 studies and three
phase 3 studies, including 20 subjects with SAB who received ceftobiprole after iHD (see
Section 14.5.2.3). These simulations, in combination with adequate target attainment, support a
ceftobiprole dosage of 250 mg every 24 hours in subjects with CrCL <15 mL/min and subjects
receiving iHD, when dosed after the iHD session (see Section 14.5.2.3). The Applicant
conducted a PK study in subjects with ESRD requiring hemodialysis, where six ESRD subjects
requiring hemodialysis were matched by age and weight with six healthy subjects. The PK of
ceftobiprole was compared between healthy subjects and ESRD subjects dosed after dialysis
(post-dialysis) or dosed before dialysis (pre-dialysis). In ESRD subjects receiving a 4-hour
dialysis session after a 2-hour 250 mg ceftobiprole intravenous infusion, 28% of the dose was
removed by hemodialysis.
The clinical pharmacology reviewer noted that plasma data used for PK analysis by the
Applicant was not consistent with the raw data provided in the assay report. Specifically, the
plasma concentrations at 30 min for ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, ceftobiprole, and the openring metabolite from all the ESRD subjects during the period 2 (i.e., postdialysis) of the study
were switched with their respective concentrations at 90 min in the Applicant’s report.
Upon further analysis the reviewer also noted questionable concentration-time profiles for four
out of six ESRD subjects when dosed after hemodialysis. As illustrated in Figure 17, ceftobiprole
(b) (6)

during the infusion phase. Furthermore, the plasma concentration time profiles were considered
(b) (6)
abnormal for Subjects

over. Taken together, the questionable data in 4 out of the 6 ESRD subjects studied precluded
reliable estimation on ceftobiprole PK characteristics in the ESRD subjects dosed after
hemodialysis.

CABP, the Day 1 AUC and Cmax values were approximately 1.3- and 1.6-fold lower than
subjects with normal renal function.
Based on the lower exposures observed on Day 1 in ESRD subjects, PK/PD target attainment
analyses were conducted for each indication to support the proposed dosage. The overall
percentage probabilities of PK/PD target attainment on Days 1 in subjects with SAB was >
99.9% for S. aureus. In ABSSSI subjects, overall target attainment on Day 1 was >99.9% for
S. aureus, 100% for Streptococcus species, and 87.2% for Enterobacterales. In CABP subjects,
overall target attainment on Day 1 was 100% for S. pneumoniae, >99.9% for S. aureus, and were
87.0% or 87.1% for Enterobacterales.
An additional analysis for visual inspection revealed similar plasma concentrations in phase 3
subjects on and off iHD based on pooled PK data of phase 3 ABSSI, CAP, SAB subjects (Figure
18). In addition, a subgroup analysis conducted by the Agency suggests that hemodialysis
did not impact overall success or ACM in SAB subjects with a CrCL <15 mL/min enrolled in
Trial BPR-CS-009 compared to subjects receiving daptomycin at the PTE visit (Table 114 and
Table 115, respectively). Taken together, the proposed dosage of 250 mg IV q24h for ESRD
subjects is acceptable given the similar steady state exposures compared to subjects with normal
renal function, high rates of target attainment on Day 1 and similar efficacy noted in the phase 3
SAB Trial.

8.1.3. Patients With Augmented Renal Clearance
In a covariate analysis conducted by the Applicant, the subgroup with the greatest difference in
predicted ceftobiprole exposures was subjects with augmented renal function. The Applicant
simulated ceftobiprole AUC0-24h on Day 1 in subjects with various degrees of renal impairment
228
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
relative to a population of healthy male subjects who have a body weight of 75 kg and normal
renal function (BSA-indexed CLCR of 100 mL/min/1.73 m2) using the final population PK
model. In subjects with CLCR above 150 mL/min/1.73 m2, a point estimate of 44% reduction in
exposures (i.e., 24-hour AUC) compared to subjects with normal renal function Figure 19. These
results suggest a ceftobiprole dosage of 500 mg (equivalent to 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril
sodium) every 6 hours in subjects with increased renal clearance is likely to achieve
approximately the same exposures achieved with a dosage of 500 mg every 8 hours in subjects
with normal renal function in SAB.
For ABSSSI and CAP, a dosage adjustment to 500 mg every 6 hours also demonstrated adequate
target attainment in subjects with CLCR of 150 mL/min to <240 mL/min (see Section 14.5).
Hence, this dosage adjustment is recommended in adult subjects with a CLCR >150 mL/min.
Despite incorporating BSA-indexed CLCR in the final population PK analysis for ABSSSI, CAP,
and SAB in adults, the renal dose adjustment described in the ceftobiprole labeling is based on
CLCR without indexing to BSA. This is because the model-predicted exposure comparisons and
PTA analyses across renal function groups were conducted using subject level CLCR without
BSA indexing. The effect of augmented renal clearance (CLCR >150 mL/min) on ceftobiprole PK
in pediatric subjects is unknown.

8.1.5. Hepatic Impairment
The effects of hepatic impairment on the PK of ceftobiprole have not been evaluated.
Ceftobiprole does not undergo significant hepatic metabolism and has low plasma protein
binding. As such, hepatic impairment is not expected to alter the elimination of ceftobiprole.
Dosage adjustments are not necessary in patients with impaired hepatic function.

8.1.6. Body Weight
A single-dose study was conducted to investigate the PK of ceftobiprole in subjects with morbid
obesity in comparison to non-obese subjects. Exposure to ceftobiprole was lower in morbidly
obese subjects attributed to a larger volume of distribution and a higher CL, resulting in ~17%
lower exposure which is unlikely to be clinically relevant. No doses adjustment based on body
weight were made in the phase 3 studies.
The effect of weight was also evaluated in the adult population PK (PopPK) analysis and in the
PK/PD target attainment analysis. Although body weight was a statistically significant predictor
of interindividual variability in CL, central and peripheral volumes of distribution in the PopPK
analysis, ceftobiprole dose adjustments based on body weight are not required to ensure
sufficient PK/PD target attainment.

8.1.7. Gender
The effects of gender on ceftobiprole PK were evaluated in two phase 1 studies, as a primary
objective of study BAP00036 and a secondary objective of Study CSI-1004. Systemic exposure
to ceftobiprole was higher in females, with 21% higher Cmax and 15% higher AUClast in
BAP00036 and 24% higher Cmax and 14% higher AUC0-inf in CSI-1004, compared to males.
The higher systemic exposure in females observed in these studies was attributed to a lower body
weight in females.
The effect of gender was also evaluated in the PopPK analysis. In the adult PopPK model,
gender identified as statistically significant predictor of the interindividual variability observed in
the peripheral volume of distribution but was not found to be clinically relevant. Dose
adjustment is not indicated based on gender.

8.1.8. Other Intrinsic Factors
The effects of adult age and race were evaluated in the PopPK analysis and were not identified as
statistically significant covariates. Accordingly, dose adjustments based on age or race are not
indicated.

Reference ID: 5357793

8.2. Extrinsic Factors
8.2.1. Pharmacokinetics Based Drug-Drug Interactions
Ceftobiprole as a Victim of Drug-Drug Interactions
In hepatocytes, ceftobiprole was slowly metabolized to the open-ring hydrolysis product
BAL1029 and does not appear to undergo significant hepatic metabolism.
In vitro studies showed that ceftobiprole is not a substrate of P-glycoprotein (P-gp), breast cancer
resistance protein (BCRP), multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP2), bile salt export pump, organic
anion-transporting polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1 in vitro. Ceftobiprole was a
substrate of the renal uptake transporters organic anion transporter 1 (OAT1) and organic cation
transporter 2 (OCT2) but not OAT3 in vitro. Ceftobiprole was not evaluated as a substrate of
multidrug and toxin extrusion protein 1 (MATE1), or MATE2-K as active secretion does not
contribute to ceftobiprole elimination.
Ceftobiprole as a Perpetrator of Drug-Drug Interactions
In vitro studies showed that ceftobiprole did not inhibit or induce cytochrome P450 (CYP) 1A2,
2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, or 3A4/5 at therapeutic plasma concentrations. Hence, ceftobiprole
is unlikely to result in clinically relevant CYP-mediated DDIs.
In vitro studies showed ceftobiprole was an inhibitor of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 but was not an
inhibitor of P-gp, BCRP, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, or OCT2.
The in vitro transporter inhibition assessment based on calculated R values is outlined in Table
118. A drug has the potential to inhibit a transporter in vivo if the R value is >1.1. Since the in
vitro studies indicate that a drug is an OATP1B1 or OATP1B3 inhibitor, we recommend the
Applicant conduct an in vivo drug interaction study evaluating ceftobiprole as an inhibitor of
OATP1B1 and OATB1B3 transporters as a post-marketing requirement (see Section 14.1.5).

8.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of
Reproductive Potential
Nonclinical Reproductive and Developmental Toxicology and Lactation Data
Intravenous administration of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to pregnant rats and monkeys
during organogenesis showed no evidence of adverse fetal developmental outcomes at doses
approximately 1.4 times and 0.9 times the MRHD, respectively, based on BSA comparison.
Intravenous administration of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to rats 2-weeks prior to mating,
during organogenesis, and through lactation resulted in no significant adverse fertility or fetal
development effects in offspring at doses approximately 1.4 times the MRHD, based on BSA
comparison. Slight reductions in number of pups born per litter and decreased postnatal survival
up to day 4 after birth were associated with maternal toxicity (mortality, reduced food
consumption and body weight gain in surviving females during gestation). No offspring adverse
effects were observed in surviving pups during the postnatal postweaning development period
(Days 5 through 22) at doses up to 360 mg/kg.
Pregnant rats were administered ceftobiprole at doses of 175, 250, and 360 mg/kg/day from 14days pre-mating through lactation/postpartum day 21. Ceftobiprole was excreted in rat milk at
levels of approximately 20% of the corresponding maternal plasma ceftobiprole levels. The
concentration of ceftobiprole in animal milk does not necessarily predict the concentration of
drug in human milk.

The Office of Pharmaceutical Quality (OPQ) review team assessed NDA 218275 with respect to

which need to be reconstituted and further diluted for intravenous infusion. Each drug product
vial contains 667 mg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole) and
is supplied in a carton containing 10 single-dose vials. The majority of CMC information
provided in the NDA to assure and demonstrate the identity, strength, purity, and quality of the
proposed drug product, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection, was found to be adequate.
However, since the proposed drug product is an injectable powder for reconstitution, it needs to
comply with applicable guidances and regulations to ensure that the excess solid in a vial is
sufficient to allow for withdrawal and administration of the net container content of the drug
product. Therefore, additional finished drug product and in-process controls are needed. In
addition, the currently established drug product assay and impurity limits are considered
acceptable on an interim basis and should be reassessed based on the stability testing results for
three new drug product batches manufactured using a revised drug substance assay calculation.
These issues will be addressed through two PMC studies (the PMC descriptions and draft
timelines are included in Section 24, below). All manufacturing and testing facilities were found
acceptable. An exception to the FDA/USP salt policy guidance was made for the drug name,
strength and equivalency statement in consultation with OND.

The Applicant has provided attestation that all trials submitted for this NDA were conducted in

on the interpretation of the safety and efficacy of the trials.
A review of the clinical sites was conducted by OSI to ensure data quality and protocol safety.
Seven clinical sites were chosen for inspection based upon their high enrollment in their
respective pivotal trials (6 clinical investigators and the Applicant). Two sites (Site 044 in
Bulgaria and 067 in California, USA) were selected for BPR-CS-008, two sites (Site 203 and
205 both in Bulgaria) were selected for BPR-CS-009, and two sites (886005 in Taiwan and
001003 in Georgia, USA) were selected for CAP-3001. The seventh site inspected was Basilea
Pharmaceutical International LTD in Switzerland and this was directed to investigate specific
concerns about good clinical practice regarding the three trials. Of note, under NDA 22132,

12. Summary of Regulatory History
Basilea Pharmaceutica, Ltd., (Applicant) submitted a Pre-Investigational New Drug Application
for BAL 5788 for injection on July 24, 2002, for the treatment of Complicated Skin and Skin
Structure Infections (cSSSI).
On September 16, 2002, the Division held a meeting with the Applicant to discuss the drug
development program, leading into phase 2 studies. The Division recommended that the
Applicant provide data from repeat dose toxicity studies and full reports for toxicology,
nonclinical, and pharmacokinetic (PK) metabolic studies, along with full assay validation data
from plasma samples obtained, as part of their forthcoming investigational new drug (IND)
submission.
On November 7, 2002, the Applicant submitted their investigational new drug application (IND
064407) which was deemed safe to proceed by the Division on December 9, 2002.
On June 30, 2005, the ownership of the IND was transferred to Johnson and Johnson
Pharmaceutical Research & Development, L.L.C. On January 24, 2011, IND ownership was
transferred back to Basilea Pharmaceutica, Ltd.
On June 24, 2014, a type C, Guidance meeting was held to discuss the drug development
program for the CABP indication.
The Applicant submitted requests for Qualified Infectious Disease Product (QIDP) designations
under the GAIN Act, on April 09, 2015, for CABP and ABSSSI. These indications were granted
QIDP designation on July 20, 2015, and August 7, 2015, respectively.
On November 17, 2015, a type B, End of Phase 2 meeting was held to discuss the phase 3 drug
development program for the indications ABSSSI, CABP, and Staphylococcus aureus
bacteremia (SAB). Issues discussed included the NI margin, primary efficacy endpoint,
concomitant antibiotic use, number of studies, and treatment duration.

13.1.1. Pharmacology
Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is a 5th generation cephalosporin antibacterial with bactericidal
activity against gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens.
Further details regarding in vitro and in vivo efficacy of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium can be
found in Section 19, Clinical Microbiology.

Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, Pharmacokinetics
The absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of ceftobiprole medocaril (BAL5788)
and ceftobiprole (active metabolite, BAL9141) was investigated in multiple species.
Pharmacokinetics were assessed in the mouse, rat, rabbit, cynomolgus monkey, marmoset and
dog. Excretion was primarily investigated in the rat.
Absorption
Nearly all studies have been conducted via the intravenous route, except for juvenile toxicology
study conducted in rats by the subcutaneous route.
Distribution
Low-to-moderate plasma protein binding (18 to 40%) was detected in mouse, rabbit, dog,
monkey, and human plasma, across a concentration range of 30-300µM. A comparative study of
mouse and human showed that protein binding in both species is low.
In a rat exploratory quantitative whole body autoradiography study following a single
intravenous administration of 14C radiolabeled ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (20 mg/kg),
quantifiable levels of radioactivity (>0.29 mcg-equiv/g) were detected in all tissues with a low
overall distribution into most organs and tissues. The highest concentrations of radioactivity 15
minutes post-dose were found in the kidney (34.2 and 32.3 mcg-equiv/g in the cortex and
medulla, respectively), skin (19.63 mcg-equiv/g), tooth pulp (19.17), liver (18.96 mcg-equiv/g),
lung (17.3 mcg-equiv/g), blood (17.04 mcg-equiv/g), connective tissue (15.73 mcg-equiv/g),
aorta (11.61 mcg-equiv/g) and stomach mucosa (11.98 mcg-equiv/g). Lower levels (below
10 mcg-equiv/g) were detected in mandibular and mesenteric lymph nodes, adrenal gland,
thyroid, adrenal gland, pituitary gland, salivary glands, lacrimal gland, harderian gland, pineal
body and muscle with lowest levels detected in the brain and spinal cord (0.38 and 0.58 mcgequiv/g, respectively). Elimination of radioactivity was rapid (declining over 10-fold in 7 hours)
except for the kidney with an estimated half-life of over 24 hours. Elimination of radioactivity
was predominantly by the renal route (82% of the dose within 48 hours). In a similar distribution
study in mice, the highest concentrations of radioactivity across tissues were found in the
coagulating gland (78.29 mcg-equiv./g), the excretory organs kidney (30.43 and 24.24 mcgequiv./g in cortex and medulla, respectively) and liver (26.26 mcg-equiv./g), as well as in skin
and aorta. Elimination from tissues was rapid (declining concentrations by 10fold in 2 hours)
with detectable levels only in the kidney cortex and liver by 24 hours.

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Metabolism
The parent pro-drug compound BAL5788 is rapidly metabolized to BAL9141. BAL941 is
further metabolized to the open lactam ring form (BAL2070, up to 10% of the urinary
compounds in this form). Further metabolism of BAL9141 into open ring forms were seen in
multiple species (up to 4 other metabolites, ~5%).
The metabolism of BAL5788 (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium) was investigated in vitro using
primary cultures of hepatocytes from livers of humans, rats, mouse, dog, marmoset, and
cynomolgus monkeys and rat and mouse brain homogenates and rat liver and kidney
homogenates. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (pro-drug) was rapidly metabolized to Ro 63-9141,
which in turn metabolized to the open beta-lactam ring form, BAL 65-2070. The percentage of
metabolism at 48 hours is shown below.

In an Applicant report (BAP00069), the comparative metabolism of ceftobiprole medocaril
sodium was investigated in vivo after administration of a single dose of radiolabeled (14C)
ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (13.3 mg/kg). The report included the metabolic profiles in rat
plasma, urine, bile and kidney, rat brain and marmoset urine. The majority of the drug was
shown to be eliminated in the urine. Within 5 to 10 minutes, the majority of the drug was
converted from ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (pro-drug to ceftobiprole). Approximately
10% of the compound detected in urine was the open ring form (Ro 65-2070) with other 4
metabolites detected (below 5%). Small amounts of ceftobiprole were detected in the
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of rats (1 to 2%). There did not appear to be significant differences
in the metabolic profiles of males and females.

Excretion
Urinary excretion accounted for the majority of BAL5788 elimination in all species. Excretion
was primarily investigated in the rat with 95% of the dose administered recovered in the urine
after four days post dose. Cumulative excretion in rat showed 73% eliminated in the urine, 17%
in the feces, 3% in the cage wash and 1% left in the carcass.

Interactions
In vitro studies ceftobiprole (active metabolite) did not appear to be a substrate or cause
inhibition of several human proteins that may have a role in drug-drug interactions including
human efflux transporters (P-glycoprotein, BCRP, bile salt export pump [BSEP] and MRP2) or
human uptake transporters (organic anion-transporting polypeptide [OATP]1B1, OATP1B3,
OCT1, OCT2, OAT1 and OAT3).

13.1.2. Toxicology

Studies
For reference, the following compound identifiers have been used for ceftobiprole medocaril
sodium (pro-drug): BAL5788-001, BAL0005788-001, BAL5788, JNJ-30982081, JNJ(b) (4)
30982081, Ro 65-5788, Ro 65-5788/001 and for its active metabolite
ceftobiprole (Ro 63-9141/000, 63-9141, BAL9141)
BAP00230. A Two-Week Toxicity Study of BAL5788 (Prodrug of BAL9141) Via
Intravenous Infusion in Dogs Followed by a Two-Week Recovery Period
Key Study Findings
•

•
•

Histaminergic reaction (reddening of the skin, face edema, injection of the oral mucosa,
vomiting and salivation) primarily associated with the shorter infusion time (30 minutes).
Findings significantly decreased with a longer infusion time for the high and medium dosed
animals (2 hours). These finding correlated with a dose dependent increase in plasma levels
of histamine that returned to control levels after infusion (approximately 4 hours from start of
infusion).
Injection site hemorrhage (slight) of the subcutis observed in all animals, hyperplasia of the
tunica intima was observed at 50 and 100 mg/kg/day in males and females.
No observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) considered at 100 mg/kg/day (1.2-fold the
MHRD based on body surface area [BSA] comparisons).

the reddening of the conjunctiva and oral mucosa were no longer
observed. Although occasional vomiting and reddening of the auricles
and conjunctiva were observed, incidence and severity of findings
decreased over time.

Toxicokinetic parameters
Toxicokinetics
•

Blood plasma levels (2/sex/group) of BAL5788 and BAL9141 (mcg/mL) were evaluated on
Days 0 and 27 at 10 minutes prior the end of infusion and 2 hours post infusion. Overall,
there did not appear to be significant differences of exposure between males and females,
dose proportional increases or significant exposure accumulation when comparing Days 1 to
27 of either BAL5788 or BA L9141.

Table 140. Toxicokinetics Analysis

Source: Reviewer generated table

•

Urine levels of BAL5788 and BAL9141 were evaluated on days 0 and 13 [high dose only], at
0-2, 2-4, 4-6 h after the start of infusion. The urinary levels of BAL5788 were highly variable
and ranged from 0-277 mcg/mL. Levels of BAL9141 were slightly less variable and
showed some dose dependence. On Study Day 0, the highest measured urinary
concentrations of BAL9141 were 15170 mcg/ml (male, 360 mg/kg, 0-2h) and 17280 mcg/ml
(female, 250 mg/kg, 4-6 h). On day 13, the highest urinary concentration of BAL9141 was
23160 mcg/mL (male, 360 mg/kg, 4-6 h). On day 27, the highest urinary
concentrations of BAL9141 were 15070 mcg/mL (male, 175 mg/kg, 2-4h) and
16330 mcg/mL (female, 360 mg/kg, 4-6 h). There was no indication of drug precipitation in
the distal tubules or collecting tubules.

TOX-7154/ A Thirteen-Week Toxicity Study of BAL5788 (Prodrug of BAL9141) Via
Intravenous Infusion in Common Marmosets Followed by a Four-Week Recovery Period
Key Study Findings
•
•
•
•
•

Mortality was observed at all doses tested (≥50 mg/kg). The cause of death was attributed to
thrombosis/emboli in the lung and heart, potentially originating from the injection site
thrombi.
Clinical signs in early death animals included clonic/tonic seizures, decreased activity, vomit
and hind leg paralysis. Lymphoid depletion and atrophy were observed in the spleen, thymus
and lymph nodes.
Liver findings (only in males) included hepatocellular vacuolization and hypertrophy.
Lung findings included fibrosis and thrombosis.
No NOAEL was established in this study due to mortality observed at all doses tested.

Table 145. Observations and Results
Parameters
Major Findings
Mortality
Death or euthanasia prior to scheduled sacrifice at all doses tested
(low dose: 2/4 males and 1/5 females; mid-dose: 2/5 males and 1/5
females; high dose: 2/8 males and 3/9 females). Prior to death or
euthanasia, animals showed similar clinical signs including decreased
activity with lateral recumbency, clonic or tonic convulsions, edema,
hind limb paralysis and vomiting.
Unscheduled death animals: One high dose animal died one day after
the first dose; however, the rest of animals were found dead between
days 27-62 or euthanized due to signs of overt toxicity between days
48-64. One animal was euthanized on day 64 due to lack of patency in
the catheter.
Clinical signs
Animals surviving to scheduled sacrifice: High dose males and
females showed abnormal urine color (5/6) and occasional vomiting
(2-3/6 males and females, 1 to 23 times) and low incidence soft stools
in females (2/6, 1 to 2 time; most findings observed after week 4 of the
study (not significant findings observed at recovery).
Body weights
No remarkable changes observed
Feed consumption
No remarkable changes observed
Ophthalmoscopy
No remarkable changes observed
Hematology
No remarkable changes observed
Clinical chemistry
Early death males: increased BUN (2 to 3-fold) and creatinine (1 to 3fold).
Urinalysis
No remarkable changes observed
Gross pathology
Early death animals: thickening of the vascular wall and
yellowish/white material at the injection site (drug material suspected
but not confirmed by testing). Sporadic observations included
edema/ascites/hydrothorax, hydropericardium and lymph node
enlargement.
Scheduled sacrifice: nearly all animals (including control) had injection
site thickening of the vascular wall and deposition of yellowish white
material at the tip of the catheter and in the vena cava and femoral/
iliac veins. Only injection site damage persisted through recovery.

Local Tolerance
TOX7588. A Local Irritation Study of BAL5788 by Intravenous Injection to Rabbits
Methods
The purpose of this study was to test the irritation potential of 2 ceftobiprole medocaril sodium
formulations made from slightly different synthesis routes (BAL5788 A, intended for dilution in
saline and B intended for dilution in 5% dextrose). BAL5788-A (drug product [DP] formula,
batch # 30-4EXP, 91.6% purity); BAL-5788-B (New DP formula, batch # I050605, 100.9%
purity) in 5 % dextrose was administered by IV injection to male Kbt rabbits (2.9-3.4 kg, 15
weeks old, 3/group) into the ear vein (0.05 mL/site/day) once daily for 8 consecutive days.
Positive control bromosulfalein (BSP) diluted into saline. Clinical signs (daily), body weight
(prior to administration), observations of the injection site, and histopathology of the injection
site (Day 8) were conducted/observed.
Results
There were no clinical signs. Body weights did not change significantly from controls. At
10 mg/mL very slight to slight inflammation was observed in most rabbits (including controls)
around the injection site between Days 3 and 5. Positive control rabbits showed slight or
moderate inflammation along with thrombi throughout the dosing period. With the exception of
the positive control animals where cell infiltration, desquamation edema, fibrosis, hemorrhage
and thrombus were noted, there were no noteworthy findings. There were no significant
differences in local irritation between the BAL5788 formulations A and B; BAL5788 was no
more irritating than normal saline this 8- day study in rabbits.
TOX7904. A Local Irritation Study of BAL5788 by Intravenous Injection to Rabbits-2
Methods
BAL-5788-B (formula, batch # I050605, 100.9% purity), vehicle (5% dextrose) or positive
control BSP were administered intravenously into the ear vein at 0, 2 and 10 mg/mL either as
fresh solution or aged for 30-hour period to male Kbt:JW rabbits (2.9-3.3 kg, 16 weeks old,
3/group) for 8 consecutive days.
Clinical signs (daily), body weight (prior to administration), observations of the injection site,
and histopathology of the injection site (Day 8) were conducted/observed.
Results
There were no abnormal clinical signs or changes in body weight. There were no dose dependent
changes in inflammation as compared to physiological saline at the injection site. The BSP
animals showed slight to moderate inflammation and small thrombi. No significant differences in
microscopic observations were made with BAL5788 or physiological saline. The positive
controls showed cell infiltration, desquamation edema, fibrosis, hemorrhage and thrombi. Aging
BAL5788 did not result in greater local irritation potential.

13.1.2.5. Other Toxicology
13.1.2.5.1. Other Studies
TOX 7589. An Antigenicity Study of BAL5788 in Guinea Pigs
Methods
For passive sensitization, male Hartley guinea pigs were injected subcutaneously (6 sites on the
dorsal skin of 2 animals) with serum from the actively sensitized animals, then 4 hours later
challenged with 25, 50 or 100 mg/kg of intravenously administered BAL5788 and Evan’s blue
dye. The dorsal skin was then examined for dye leakage. Actively sensitized animals were
challenged with 100 mg/kg BAL5788 (pro-drug) and the reactions observed. Intravenous
sensitization was evaluated at 1) 10 mg/kg/ BAL5788 (5 times week for 3 weeks, 2) 50 mg/kg/
BAL 5788 (5 times a week for 1 week) and 20 mg/kg (5 times week for 2 weeks, 3) 10 or
50 mg/kg, emulsified with Freund’s complete adjuvant (FCA) or Freund’s incomplete adjuvant
(FIA) once weekly for 3 weeks. Positive control was 1 mg/kg subcutaneous ovalbumin
emulsified with FCA once weekly for 3 weeks. The negative control was 5% dextrose IV or
subcutaneous with FCA or FIA once weekly for 3 weeks. A 100 mg/kg challenge dose of
BAL5788 (batch 30-4EXP, 93.8% purity) was used.
Results
One animal in the 50 mg/kg intravenous sensitization group died at day 4. No significant changes
were noted in body weight. No abnormalities were seen in the sensitization with 5% dextrose or
10 mg/kg BAL with or without FCA/FIA. In the 50/20 mg/kg BAL alone groups, scratching and
piloerection were observed in 1/5 guinea pigs (ASA grade 1). In the 50 mg/kg group with
FCA/FIA, anxiety, tremor, piloerection, dyskinesia, dyspnea were seen in all animals within 60
minutes of challenge and 1/5 animals died (ASA reaction scores were 1/5 at 1, 2/5 at 2, 1/5 at 3
and 4). In the positive control group, one animal died within 6 minutes of challenge (ASA 4)
while the remaining 4 animals had an ASA reaction grade of 2. No reactions were noted in the
BAL5788 passively challenged animals. The positive control had 5/5 animals positive. BAL5788
was shown to have moderate antigenic potential.
Report 10016. Ro 63-9141/001: Phototoxicity Study (In Vitro)
Methods
The potential phototoxic potential of Ro 63-9141/001 (ceftobiprole, batch # 18116B2, 3704500 mcg/mL) was evaluated an in vitro assay with Balb/c 3T3 mouse fibroblasts by incubating
the test article in the cell culture system with or without exposure to a non-cytotoxic dose of
ultraviolet light (ultraviolet A [UVA] wavelength of 240-4500 nanometers) or kept in the dark.
Cytotoxicity was expressed as a dose dependent reduction of the growth rate of cells as
determined by uptake of the vital dye Neutral Red one day after treatment. Negative control was
the vehicle, PBS/ 3% dimethyl sulfoxide [DMSO]) and chlorpromazine was used as positive
control.

NDA 218275

Results
There were no changes in cell viability at any concentration of drug tested or changes after
exposure to UVA radiation as compared to cultures kept in the dark. Chlorpromazine, the
positive control for UVA, behaved as expected (with a Dark/UVA discrimination factor for
cytotoxicity of 66-fold). The study was valid and the test article was considered negative for
phototoxicity.
Report 1004008. Ro 65-5788/001: In Vitro Assessment of Hemolysis, Plasma Turbidity and
Plasma Precipitation in Dog Blood
Methods

The potential of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (13.3% or 133.3 mg/mL pro-drug,
batch# 90402B2171202) to induce hemolysis and plasma turbidity was evaluated in vitro using
venous dog blood. Vehicles used were saline and 5% glucose. Hemolysis was measured by
spectrophotometer (hemoglobin %) and turbidity was evaluated visually.
Results
No significant hemolysis or plasma turbidity or precipitation were seen in dog blood under in
vitro conditions in a 13.33% test solution of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium pro-drug
(corresponding to 10% or 100 mg/ml of the active drug Ro 63-9141/000) at concentrations
corresponding to 1.25% (12.5 mg/ml pro-drug). At higher concentrations, hemolysis of up to
7.3% and moderate to marked plasma turbidity and precipitation were observed.
Tox7587. Haemocompatibility Test with Human, Rat, and Marmoset Blood
Methods
Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was evaluated at 5 concentration levels (1, 5, 12.5, 25 and
50 mg/mL) for hemocompatibility with rat, marmoset, and human blood at a volume ratio of 0.2,
0.4 and 0.8 (1:5, 2:5 and 4:5) test material:blood. Reportedly, in the human, this ratio
corresponds to administration of 1.6, 3.2 and 6.4 mL/min intravenous infusion rates. Hemoglobin
release was determined following a 3-minute incubation at 37°C. For the plasma compatibility
evaluation rat, marmoset, and human plasma were mixed with ceftobiprole medocaril sodium
solutions at a ratio of 0.8 (4:5) test material:plasma. Samples were observed for flocculation,
precipitation, and coagulation after 0.16, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 30 and 60 minutes at room
temperature.
Results
No test article related hemolysis was observed at any dose tested in rat, marmoset. or human
blood. When ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was mixed with human, rat, or marmoset plasma at
a ratio of 0.8 (equivalent to an infusion rate of 6.4 mL/minute), dose dependent adverse reactions
were observed (flocculation, precipitation, and coagulation) with increasing ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium concentrations and increasing time. In all three species the adverse reactions
(primarily precipitation) were observed ≥2.5 mg/mL concentration level. At ≥25 and with
increasing time periods, flocculation and coagulation were also observed.

13.1.2.5.3. Safety of Impurities
Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection (pro-drug (BAL5788) for ceftobiprole, BAL9141)
will be given as an intravenous infusion and will be marketed as a sterile lyophilized powder for
reconstitution (inactive ingredients are citric acid monohydrate in sodium hydroxide). There are
no pharmacology/toxicology concerns for the excipients. The unit dose is 667 mg of ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium per vial (equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole). The MRHD is 2.67 g/day
(equivalent to 2.0 g ceftobiprole). The animal data supports safety of ceftobiprole medocaril
sodium for up to 1 month duration, however, based on clinical data treatments for up to six
weeks were permitted. We deferred to the clinical review team on the safety of ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium administered for this extended duration.
The genotoxicity profile of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was mixed including a negative Ames
assay, a positive mouse lymphoma assay, a negative forward mutation assay, and positive
chromosomal assays for both the pro-drug and active metabolite suggesting clastogenic potential.
However, in vivo ceftobiprole medocaril sodium was negative in both the micronucleus assay
and rat liver unscheduled DNA synthesis reducing concern for potential clastogenic activity.
In considering potential and actual impurities in the drug substance (DS) and DP, the Applicant
assessed genotoxic potential of several impurities using Derek quantitative structure-activity
relationship (QSAR) analysis (a second tool was not expected since initial phase 3 clinical trials
were conducted prior to the publication of the ICH M7 Guidance). Expert analysis based on
available scientific literature or data from studies conducted by the Applicant and purging
assessments were also considered. In general, the Applicant followed ICH M7, particularly in
assigning a classification of mutagenic potential to the impurities. The Applicant considered 155
compounds, classified 94 of them as class 4 or 5 (can be treated as nonmutagenic), and used
purging calculations or direct analytical methods to demonstrate absence of 57 compounds.
There were 5 impurities classified in classes 1, 2 or 3 and these were amongst the compounds
demonstrated to be absent in the drug substance. The Applicant also provided a rationale for
(b) (4)
levels of
guided by ICH Q3C Guidance, with special consideration of the shortterm use of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection. For limit setting of impurities based on
manufacturing experience and commercial process capabilities, the Applicant proposed the use
of alternative thresholds higher than ICH Q3A and Q3B Guidance, including a reporting

Conclusion of the Review of Impurities not Fully Qualified in Toxicology Studies
The impurity qualification review indicates that the select individual impurities in the DS and DP
are not adequately qualified based on the toxicology studies considered. However, the levels of
these impurities in ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for the intended clinical treatment durations
and indications are considered acceptable based on the following considerations: 1) The
impurities specified below share significant structural similarities with ceftobiprole medocaril
sodium and represent a small fraction of the DP, therefore, these individual impurities are not
likely to cause greater toxicities than those observed with exposure to the DP. 2) The overall
analysis of the mutagenic potential of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (prodrug), which shares
similar structural alerts with the individual impurities evaluated, indicates that ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium and associated impurities are not likely to have mutagenic potential. 3)
Although mixed results have been observed with ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole
in in vitro mutagenicity tests (negative in a limited Ames test, positive in the mouse lymphoma
assay, but negative in a more recent HPRT forward mutation assay), primarily associated with
(b) (4)
the presence of
further in silico QSAR analysis based on
application of expert knowledge and comparison to the most structurally similar analogs indicate
that both compounds are predicted to be negative for bacterial mutagenicity. The analysis
performed by FDA’s Computational Toxicology Consultation Service experts included three
QSAR state of the art models: Derek Nexus six 6.3.0 (DX), Leadscope Model Applier 2022.0.2.3
Bacterial Mut V2 model (LMA) model and CASE Ultra 1.9.0.8 GT1_BMUT model 1.9.0.2 (CU)
and was consistent with ICH M2(R7) Guideline (i.e., prediction of bacterial mutagenicity using
multiple complementary methodologies).
Although there are limitations in the qualification of impurities based on toxicological studies,
the levels of impurities in ceftobiprole medocaril sodium are considered acceptable and no
further evaluations of impurities for safety is warranted.

14. Clinical Pharmacology
14.1. In Vitro Studies
14.1.1. Preclinical Studies to Determine the PK/PD
Target of Ceftobiprole
Identification of PK/PD Index
The percentage of time during a dosing interval when the unbound drug concentration exceeds
the minimum inhibitory concentration (%fT>MIC) has been identified as the PK/PD index that
best correlates with the bactericidal activity of most β-lactam drugs.
Dose fractionation studies conducted with S. aureus American type culture collection (ATCC)
33591 confirmed the PK/PD index best correlated with in vivo efficacy was %fT > MIC (Figure
23).

304
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Figure 23. Correlation of Ceftobiprole PK-PD Indices With Efficacy Against Staphylococcus
aureus ATCC 33591.

Source: Craig WA, Andes DR. In vivo pharmacodynamics of ceftobiprole against multiple bacterial pathogens in murine thigh and
lung infection models. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 2008 Oct;52(10):3492-6.
Each Circle Represents the Mean Data Per Mouse From Two Thighs.
Abbreviations: AUC, area under the concentration-time curve; ATCC, American type culture collection; CFU, colony forming unit;
Cmax, maximum plasma concentration; MIC, minimum inhibitory concentration; PD, pharmacodynamic; PK, pharmacokinetic; T, time

Identification of PK/PD Target
The activity of ceftobiprole was evaluated in a mouse neutropenic thigh-infection model. Mice
were given single subcutaneous doses (0.2 mL/ dose) of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (10, 40,
and 160 mg/kg). A sigmoid dose-response model derived from the four-parameter Hill equation
was used to calculate the dose of ceftobiprole producing a net bacteriostatic effect and 1-log10
kill over 24 hours. The %fT > MIC values for each static and 1-log kill dose were estimated from
PK and MICs. Ceftobiprole was tested against a total of 14 gram-positive strains (n = 8 S. aureus
and n = 6 S. pneumoniae) and five strains of gram-negative bacteria, including E. coli, K.
pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa, and E. cloacae. The results of %fT > MIC to achieve net bacterial
stasis, 1-log10 kill and 2-log kill are presented in Table 197.
Since free-drug plasma %fT>MIC targets from this study were only reported for net bacterial
stasis and a 2-log10 colony forming unit (CFU) reduction from baseline, free-drug plasma
%fT>MIC targets associated with a 1-log10 CFU reduction from baseline were linearly
interpolated by averaging the targets for net bacterial stasis and a 2-log10 CFU reduction from
Baseline.
Overall, these pharmacodynamics studies suggested that bactericidal (1-log kill) %fT>MIC
values of approximately 30% and 50% would provide efficacious dosing for ceftobiprole for
treatment of infections caused by gram-positive and gram-negative pathogens, respectively.

PK/PD Target in Acute Pneumonia Model
Additional PK/PD studies in the neutropenic mouse lung infection model demonstrated that
antibacterial effects were induced with %fT>MIC values at 15 – 25% of the dosing interval for
S. pneumoniae and S. aureus, including MRSA.
In the first study, neutropenic mice were infected with four strains of S. pneumoniae (including
one penicillin-sensitive strain, one penicillin-resistant strain and two highly penicillin-,
ceftriaxone- and cefotaxime-resistant strains) and administered either ceftobiprole or ceftriaxone.
For the four tested strains of S. pneumoniae, the %fT>MIC as a percent of the dosing interval
ranged from 9 to 18% for ceftobiprole. This study evaluated total-drug, rather than free-drug,
time over MIC.

A third study conducted by the same group employed the same model and eight strains as in

14.1.2. Protein Binding
Initial studies investigated the plasma protein binding of ceftobiprole by ultrafiltration in mouse,
rat, rabbit, dog, marmoset, Cynomolgus monkey, and human (BAP00112, BAP00566). Results
from both studies indicated that plasma protein binding was low, ranging from approximately
10% to 45% across species, and independent of drug concentrations (10 or 100 μg/mL). In
humans, plasma protein binding ranged from 22.1% to 40.8%. These initial studies used a small
sample size and showed a high intra- and inter-experimental variability for human plasma
protein binding.
Table 201. Plasma Protein Binding of Ceftobiprole in Animal Species and Human

Source: Study BAP00556; Study BAP00112

Due to the variability noted in studies BAP00112 and BAP00566, two additional studies were
conducted to investigate human plasma protein binding. The first study utilized ultrafiltration to
investigate ceftobiprole binding to human plasma protein (FK5789). Protein binding was
measured at concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 100 μg/mL in pooled plasma samples from male
and female healthy normal volunteers. Results indicated that plasma protein binding was low and
concentration independent, with the mean percent binding equaling 17.3%.
A second study (FK6157) was conducted to confirm the extent of plasma protein binding
observed, due to differences noted in the later study versus the preliminary studies. The study
used freshly obtained (i.e., within 72 hours), non-pooled human plasma samples, which were
incubated with ceftobiprole at concentrations of 3.5 and 35 μg/mL. Results again indicated that
plasma protein binding was low and concentration independent, with a mean percent binding of
15.4%.

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275

Table 202. Plasma Protein Binding of Ceftobiprole in Humans

Source: Study FK5789; Study FK6157

Taken together, the average protein binding of ceftobiprole is noted to be 16% and independent
of ceftobiprole concentration across the range of 0.5 to 100 μg/mL.

14.1.3. Metabolism
Conversion of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to ceftobiprole is very rapid in human plasma (38
seconds; study BAP00072). Inhibition studies with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid suggested
that type A plasma esterases are involved in the cleavage of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium to
ceftobiprole (study BAP00207). A mechanistic study investigating the enzymes involved in the
hydrolysis of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium demonstrated a lack of specificity of this conversion
which occurred both enzymatically (by paraoxonases and other hydrolytic enzymes) and nonenzymatically (Study FK6700).
In vitro hepatocyte studies indicated the primary metabolite is the open-ring hydrolysis product
(study BAP00070). The prodrug ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is rapidly hydrolyzed, in contrast
to the active moiety ceftobiprole, which is slowly metabolized. At least three additional,
unidentified metabolites were present in trace amounts. Thus, ceftobiprole does not appear to be
a substrate of CYP enzymes. The proposed metabolism of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is
presented in Figure 24.

14.1.4. Potential for CYP Enzyme-Mediated Drug-Drug
Interactions
No clinical drug-drug interaction studies of ceftobiprole have been performed.
In vitro CYP inhibition data (ceftobiprole concentration up to 200 μM; 107 μg/mL) are
summarized in Table 203. Only a slight (6% to 28%) inhibitory potential was apparent in the
highest concentration range tested (50 to 200 μM; 26.7 to 107 μg/mL; 1009572, FK6366, and
FK6604). Ceftobiprole was not a time-dependent inhibitor of prototypical CYP substrates at the
highest concentrations tested (200 μM; 107 μg/mL; studies FK6366 and FK6604). Due to
solubility constraints, subsequent attempts to evaluate the direct and metabolism-dependent in
vitro inhibition of human CYP enzymes at higher concentrations of ceftobiprole were
unsuccessful (Study FK5807).
