Source: Study FK6366; Study FK6604; Study FK5807

In cultured human hepatocytes treated with vehicle, ceftobiprole (up to 200 μM; 107 μg/mL) or
human cytochrome P450 enzyme inducers (i.e., omeprazole, phenobarbital, and rifampin),
ceftobiprole did not induce CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, or CYP3A4/5 (Studies
FK5831/XT053012, FK6603/XT083004, and XT223040).

14.1.5. Potential for Transporter-Mediated Drug-Drug
Interactions
Ceftobiprole as a Substrate Of P-Glycoprotein and Breast Cancer Resistance Protein
In vitro experiments were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of drug
(efflux) transporters P-gp and breast cancer resistance protein in a bidirectional permeability
assay across MDCKII cells (studies FK5942, XT138008, and XT228043). The bi-directional
permeability of ceftobiprole (1, 10, and 100 μM; 0.535, 7.14, and 53.5 μg/mL) across MDCKIIMDR1, MDCKII-BCRP and control cells was low at all conditions (less than 3 x 10-6 cm/sec,
similar to the control). The net efflux ratio of ceftobiprole was ≤2 at all concentrations and on all
cell lines suggesting that ceftobiprole is not a substrate of either P-gp or BCRP.
Ceftobiprole as a Substrate of the Hepatic Transporters Organic Anion Transporter P1B1,
Organic Anion Transporter P1B3, and Organic Cation Transporter 1
In vitro studies in transporter-expressing and control HEK293 cells were conducted to determine
whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of the hepatic uptake transporters OATP1B1, OATP1B3, and
OCT1 (Studies XT138008 and XT228043).
In Study XT138008, ceftobiprole (1, 5, and 10 μM; 0.535, 2.68, and 7.14 μg/mL) was incubated
with transporter (OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1) expressing cells and control cells.

312
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Ceftobiprole did not accumulate in transporter-expressing cells or control cells to a great extent
and did not appear to be a substrate for OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1.
In Study XT228043, ceftobiprole (0.084, 0.24, 0.84, 2.4, 8.4, 28 and 84 μM) was incubated with
OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 transporter expressing cells and control cells. Ceftobiprole did not
show accumulation of probe substrate in transporter-expressing cells or control cells to a great
extent with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) above 84 μM. The uptake ratio of 84
μM (44.5 μg/mL) ceftobiprole was less than two in the absence of OATP1B1 or OATP1B3
inhibitors. These results indicated that ceftobiprole is not a substrate of OATP1B1 or OATP1B3
at 84 μM but results at lower concentrations were inconclusive.
Ceftobiprole as a Substrate Of The Renal Transporters Organic Cation Transporter 1,
Organic Cation Transporter 3, and Organic Cation Transporter 2
In vitro studies in transporter-expressing and control HEK293 cells were conducted to determine
whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of the renal transporters OAT1, OAT3, and OCT2 (Study
XT138008). The highest concentration feasible to be tested in these assays was 10 μM (7.14
μg/mL). Ceftobiprole accumulated in OAT1 and OCT2 expressing cells at higher levels than
control cells, suggesting it may be a possible substrate of those two transporters. However, the
results should be interpreted with caution, as the amount of compound that accumulated in the
cells was very low, which can have a large impact on the results.
Ceftobiprole as a Substrate of the Transporters BSEP, and MRP2
In vitro studies in transporter-expressing and control vesicles in the presence and the absence of
ATP were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is a substrate of the efflux transporters
BSEP and MRP2. Ceftobiprole (1, 5, and 10 μM; 0.535, 2.68, and 7.14 μg/mL) did not
accumulate in MRP2 or BSEP expressing vesicles in the presence of ATP at levels greater than
in the absence of ATP suggesting it is not a substrate of either MRP2 or BSEP (Study
XT138008).
Ceftobiprole as an Inhibitor of Transporters
In vitro experiments were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is an inhibitor of drug
efflux transporters P-gp and BCRP in a bidirectional permeability assay across Caco-2 cells
and/or MDCKII cells (Studies FK5942, XT138008, and XT228043). The potential for
ceftobiprole to inhibit P-gp was evaluated in a MDR-MDCK cell assay using digoxin as the
probe substrate. The permeability of digoxin in the presence and absence of ceftobiprole did not
show any increase in the presence of 40 μM (21.4 μg/mL) ceftobiprole. The efflux ratios did not
change significantly. As such, the results indicated that ceftobiprole is not a P-gp inhibitor.
Similarly, ceftobiprole did not reduce the net efflux ratio of prazosin across MDCKII-BCRP and
control cells, suggesting it is not an inhibitor of BCRP in vitro.
In vitro experiments (Studies XT138008, XT228043) were also conducted to determine whether
ceftobiprole is an inhibitor of uptake transporters OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, OCT2, OAT1,
and OAT3 and of efflux transporters MATE1 and MATE2-K by measuring the accumulation of
a probe substrate in a transporter-expressing and control HEK293 cells.
At the concentrations tested (0.3 to 200 μM; 0.16 to 107 μg/mL) (XT138008), ceftobiprole
inhibited the accumulation of estradiol glucuronide in the OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 expressing

313
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
cells with IC50 values of 67.6 and 44.1 μM (36.14 μg/mL and 23.57 μg/mL), respectively. In a
second study (study XT228043), ceftobiprole IC50 for OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 inhibition were
determined to be above 84 μM (44.5 μg/mL, maximum achievable concentration). An
investigational drug has the potential to inhibit OATP1B1/3 in vivo if the R value is >1.1. The
R values for OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 were 1.50 and 1.76, respectively. Thus, ceftobiprole may
increase concentrations of drugs eliminated by OATP1B1 and OATP1B3. Since the in vitro
studies indicate that a drug is an OATP1B1 or OATP1B3 inhibitor, we recommend the Applicant
conduct an in vivo drug interaction study evaluating ceftobiprole as an inhibitor of OATP1B1
and OATB1B3 transporters as a post-marketing requirement (see Section 8.2.1).
Ceftobiprole was not an inhibitor of MATE1, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, or OCT2 as it did not show
accumulation of probe substrate in transporter-expressing cells or control cells to a great extent
with IC50 were above 84 μM (44.5 μg/mL) (Studies XT138008 and XT228043).
It was not possible to determine the inhibition potential of ceftobiprole on MATE2-K due to
possible solvent-related issues with the in vitro assay (Study XT228043).
In vitro experiments were conducted to determine whether ceftobiprole is an inhibitor of efflux
transporters BSEP and MRP2 by measuring the accumulation of a probe substrate (taurocholic
acid or estradiol glucuronide) in vesicles in the presence of ceftobiprole (Study XT138008). The
transport of taurocholic acid was reduced to less than 25% of the control in the presence of all
concentrations of ceftobiprole (0.3 to 200 μM; 0.16 to 107 μg/mL) indicating that the IC50 could
be lower than 0.3 μM. The Applicant attributes this inhibition to the acetic acid in the incubation
that could have had an effect on the activity. Ceftobiprole did not inhibit the MRP2 mediated
transport of estradiol 17-β-D-glucuronide.

14.2. In Vivo Studies
14.2.1. Single Ascending Dose
Study NP16104
NP16104 was a phase 1 single-center, single-dose, open-label, intra-subject, dose-escalation
study in three healthy male volunteers aged 18 to 30 years. Each subject received single 30-min
infusions of 250 mg, 500 mg, and 750 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium with a washout
period of 72 hours between treatments.
Blood samples were collected prior to each drug administration and up to 24 hours after start of
infusion. Urine was collected pre-dose and up to 24 hours post-dose. Ceftobiprole and
ceftobiprole medocaril sodium were quantified using a validated high-performance liquid
chromatography method and PK parameters were derived by non-compartmental and 2compartmental methods. Plasma and urine PK parameters of ceftobiprole are summarized in
Table 204 and Table 205, respectively.
Plasma concentrations of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium at the end of the infusion amounted to
only 2% to 4% of those of the active principle, ceftobiprole. Thus, the PK of ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium could not be determined.

Study BAP00006
BAP00006 was a phase 1, single-center, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled single,
ascending dose study involving five sequential dose levels of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium. In
total, 40 healthy, male subjects between the ages of 20 and 40 years old were randomly assigned
to one of the following five dose groups: 125, 250, 500, 750, or 1000 mg ceftobiprole medocaril
sodium. Each dose group included 8 subjects (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, n = 6; placebo, n =
2).
Blood samples were collected immediately before infusion start and at up to 24 hours after the
start of infusion. Subjects were asked to void urine immediately before starting the first urine
collection interval, 2 hours before dosing. Subsequently, urine was collected at –2 to 0 h
(control) and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and
ceftobiprole were quantitated by use of a validated LC/LC-MS/MS method and PK parameters
were derived by non-compartmental and two-compartmental methods. A one-way analysis of
variance was used to assess dose-proportionality. The mean (standard deviation [SD]) %fT >

Reviewer Comments
Pharmacokinetic analyses were conducted after the clinical study report was issued to either
further characterize the PK of ceftobiprole (accumulation index), correct a data discrepancy
(urine volume), or incorporate new information (protein binding). The overall mean predicted

14.2.2. Multiple Ascending Dose
Study BAP00010
BAP00006 was a phase 1, single-center, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled multiple
ascending dose study involving two dose levels of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (500 mg and
750 mg of ceftobiprole equivalents).
Sixteen subjects were randomly assigned to one of the two dose groups. Each dose group
included 8 subjects (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium, n = 6; placebo, n = 2). A third dose group
(1000 mg) was planned but no subjects received this dose, due to the occurrence of elevated liver
transaminase levels in approximately 50% of subjects dosed with placebo or ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium. Adverse changes were noted in 2 of 4 subjects receiving placebo and in 7 of
12 subjects receiving BAL5788 at 500 mg (3 of 6 subjects) or 750 mg (4 of 6 subjects).
On Study Days 1 and 8, blood samples were collected immediately before infusion start and up
to 24 hours after the start of infusion. To determine the trough levels of ceftobiprole, blood
samples were collected before the morning infusion on Study Days 3, 5, and 7. Urine was
collected at –2 to 0 hours (control) and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion on Study Days 1
and 8.
Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium and ceftobiprole were quantitated by a validated LC/LC-MS/MS
method and PK parameters were derived by non-compartmental and two-compartmental
methods. Drug accumulation, RACC, was estimated by AUC0-12h on Day 8 divided by AUC0-12h
on Day 1. Time above the minimum inhibitory concentration (T > MIC) was determined (MIC90
for MRSA = 2 μg/mL). A one-way analysis of variance was used to assess dose-proportionality.
Pharmacokinetic parameters and cumulative urinary recovery for ceftobiprole following multiple
intravenous administration of 500 and 750 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium in healthy, male
subjects are summarized in
Table 215. The mean (SD) %fT>MIC for subjects receiving 500 mg was 47.9 (4.2) on Day 1 and
49.9 (5.3) on Day 8. The mean (SD) %fT>MIC for subjects receiving 750 mg was 61.2 (5.4) on
Day 1 and 62.5 (4.4) on Day 8.

14.2.3. Renal Impairment
BAP00018 was a phase 1, single-center, open-label, non-randomized parallel group study.
Twenty male subjects (5 per group) were enrolled into the following groups according to their
creatinine clearance (CLCR) determined at screening:
•
•
•
•

Group A (normal renal function: CLCR >80 mL/min),
Group B (mild renal impairment: CLCR = 51-80 mL/min),
Group C (moderate renal impairment: CLCR = 30-50 mL/min), and
Group D (severe renal impairment: CLCR <30 mL/min)

On study Day 1, each subject received a single dose ceftobiprole medocaril sodium 30 minutes.
Blood samples were collected immediately before infusion start and up to 24 hours after the start
of infusion. Urine was collected at –2 to 0 hours (control and last portion of the 24-hour urine
collection on Study Day –1) and up to 24 hours after the start of infusion.

method. Pharmacokinetic parameters were derived by non-compartmental and twocompartmental methods. Time above the minimum inhibitory concentration (T > MIC) was
determined; in these calculations, the dosing interval was defined as 12 hours (corresponding to
twice daily administration), and the MIC value defined as 4 μg/mL, since this is the highest MIC
for ceftobiprole in the case of MRSA.

hours after the start of infusion in all subjects and all periods. Venous blood samples were also

samples were also collected every 30 minutes. Additional pre-dose, 2-hour blood, and 24 hours
post-start of the infusion blood samples were taken on Day 1 for the determination of plasma
protein binding by ultra-filtration.

14.2.4. Obesity
CSI-1008 was an open-label, single-dose, parallel-group PK study of ceftobiprole in morbidly
obese and non-obese subjects. Twenty-five (12 morbidly obese, defined as a BMI of ≥40 kg/m2,
and 13 demographically-matched non-obese, defined as a BMI between 18 and 30 kg/m2)
subjects were enrolled in the study and received a single 2-hour infusion of 500 mg ceftobiprole.
The mean weight and BMI were 130.9 kg and 45.5 kg/m2 for morbidly obese subjects and
73.5 kg and 24 kg/m2 for non-obese subjects, respectively.
Blood and urine were collected pre-dose and up to 24 hours following the end of infusion. An
additional 2-hour blood sample was taken for the determination of plasma protein binding by
ultra-filtration. Plasma, ultra-filtrate, and urine samples were analyzed for ceftobiprole medocaril
sodium, ceftobiprole and the open-ring metabolite using a validated LC-MS/MS method.
Ceftobiprole AUC was approximately 17% lower among morbidly obese compared to non-obese
subjects (Table 219).

14.2.5. Drug Penetration
Soft Tissue Penetration
CSI-1002 was an exploratory study to evaluate the penetration of ceftobiprole into soft tissue
determined by in vivo microdialysis in healthy subjects.
This Study was conducted in two sequential parts: a pilot study and a main study. The pilot study
was conducted in 3 control subjects. Ceftobiprole was locally administered via microdialysis
followed by a washout period of 3 hours during which dialysate samples were taken every
30 minutes for 4 hours.
The main study was conducted in 12 healthy subjects. Ceftobiprole was administered locally via
microdialysis followed by a washout period of 3 hours. After the washout period, each subject
received a single 2-hour IV infusion of 500 mg ceftobiprole medocaril sodium. Dialysate
samples were collected pre-dose and every 20 min from start of infusion through 12 hours poststart of dosing. Blood samples were collected at time 0 (pre-dose) up to 24 hours after the start of
the infusion.
Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium concentrations were only assessed in plasma. Protein binding in
plasma was determined by ultra-filtration at pre-dose, 2, and 12 hours after the start of the
infusion. Concentrations of ceftobiprole in dialysate were quantified using a validated highperformance liquid chromatography/ultraviolet method.
Individual PK parameters for ceftobiprole in plasma, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue are
summarized in Table 221. Penetration of ceftobiprole into soft tissues was demonstrated and was
69% of the unbound plasma exposure for skeletal muscle and 49% of the unbound plasma
exposure for adipose tissue.

Lung Penetration
CSI-1005 was an exploratory, open-label study to assess the bronchoalveolar distribution and PK
of ceftobiprole administered as 500 mg every 8 hours to healthy adult subjects.
Twenty-eight healthy subjects were enrolled to receive ceftobiprole and undergo bronchoalveolar
lavage (BAL) sampling. Of these, 25 were evaluable for PK and 24 subjects underwent the BAL
procedure. Two control subjects were enrolled to undergo the BAL procedure only to validate
the bioanalytical assay and did not receive ceftobiprole. All subjects, except for the control
subjects, received four 2-hour infusions of ceftobiprole (500 mg) 8 hours apart. Following the
fourth infusion, a single BAL sample was collected in each subject at either 2.5, 4, 6, or 8 hours
after the start of the infusion.
Blood samples were also collected in all pre-dose and up to 8 hours after the start of the infusion.
Ceftobiprole concentrations in plasma and BAL fluid was quantified using a validated LCMS/MS method.
Overall penetration in ELF and alveolar macrophages (as measured by the AUC ratio of the
tissue concentration to the unbound plasma concentration) was 16% and 2%, respectively.
Plasma and BAL ceftobiprole concentrations are outlined in Table 222 and Table 223,
respectively.

14.5. Pharmacometrics Assessment
14.5.1. Population PK Analysis
14.5.1.1. Review Summary
In this submission, the Applicant performed population PK (PopPK analyses including phase 3
studies in adult subjects with SAB, ABSSSIs, and CABP). PopPK analyses were also performed
for pediatric subjects.
In general, the Applicant’s PopPK analyses (for SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP in adult subjects and
for CABP in pediatric subjects) are considered acceptable for the characterization of ceftobiprole
disposition and evaluation of covariate impacts. The PopPK models were also acceptable for the
generation of exposure metrics for exposure-efficacy analyses, clinical scenario simulations, and
PTA analyses. Overall, the PopPK, PK/PD, and PTA analysis results support dosage selections
for the indicated general and special populations requiring dosage adjustments. The Applicant’s
analyses were verified by the reviewer, with no significant discordance identified. Specifically,
the developed models corresponding to the indications were used to support the current
submission as outlined in Table 225. Of note, the labeling language reflects review team
conclusions at the time of writing this review but may not reflect the finalized labeling language.

Section 8.5 Geriatric Use
No dosage adjustment is required for elderly patients. Dosage
adjustment for elderly patients should be based on renal function.
Section 8.6 Renal Impairment
Adult Patients
The ZEVTERA dosage is reduced in adult patients with CLCR <
50 mL/min, including patients with a CLCR < 15 mL/min either
receiving or not receiving hemodialysis.
Renal impairment (CLCR < 50 mL/min) increases ceftobiprole AUC in
adult patients, which may increase the risk of ZEVTERA adverse
reactions.
Pediatric Patients
The ZEVTERA dosage is reduced in pediatric patients 2 years of age
and older with renal impairment (eGFR 15 to < 50 mL/min/1.73 m2).
Use in pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with renal
impairment (eGFR 15 to < 50 mL/min/1.73 m2) is predicted to
increase ceftobiprole AUC, which may increase the risk of ZEVTERA
adverse reactions. The effect of any degree of renal impairment in
pediatric patients younger than 2 years of age or in pediatric patients
2 years of age and older with an eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 either
receiving or not receiving hemodialysis on ceftobiprole PK is
unknown.
8.7 Augmented Renal Clearance
Increase the ZEVTERA dosing frequency in adult patients with
augmented renal clearance (CLCR > 150 mL/min).
Use in adult patients with augmented renal clearance
(CLCR > 150 mL/min) is predicted to decrease ceftobiprole exposure,
which may reduce ZEVTERA efficacy. The effect of augmented renal
clearance function (CLCR > 150 mL/min) on ceftobiprole PK in
pediatric patients is unknown.
Section 12.3 Pharmacokinetics
Specific Populations
No clinically significant differences in the PK of ceftobiprole were
observed in adults based on age (18 to 91 years), gender (36%
female), or race/ethnicity (88% White, 3% Black, 5% Asian). The
effect of hepatic impairment on ceftobiprole PK is unknown.

Base Model
The final base model was a 3-compartment PK model with linear elimination from the central
compartment, and baseline creatinine clearance (CLcr) was included on CL a priori. Additive
error models (in the log domain) were separate for phase 1 and phase 3 studies. The model
structure is shown in Figure 26.
Interindividual variability (IIV) was modelled assuming a log-normal distribution for patient
level random effects. Residual variability was tested as additive, proportional, or combined.
Model evaluation and selection of the base model were based on standard statistical criteria of
goodness-of-fit (GoF) such as a decrease in the minimum objective function value (OFV),
accuracy of parameter estimation (i.e., 95% confidence interval excluding 0), successful model
convergence, and diagnostic plots.

function and categorical covariates were parameterized as a fractional change.

however, when the prediction-corrected VPC plot is limited to SAB subjects, some underpredictions are shown and are more prominent beyond 8 hours. This is likely due to the

attainment analysis (i.e., PTA) in adult subjects with SAB.

the hemodialysis session.” The uncertainty regarding iHD effect in ESRD subjects is further
complicated by the unreliable results of the dedicated phase 1 study in ESRD subjects (see

Base Model
The original PopPK model structure was fitted to the pooled pediatric and adult dataset. The final
base model (from pediatric data alone) was a linear 3-compartment with a direct relationship
between renal clearance (CL) and GFR based on Rhodin and fat-free mass (GFRRhodin, FFM). Body
weight was included on volume (estimated exponent) and clearance related terms (fixed
exponent of 0.75). IIV was included on central volume of distribution (Vc) only.
For the final base model, IIV was modelled assuming a log-normal distribution for subject level
random effects. Residual variability was tested as additive, proportional, or combined. Model
evaluation and selection of the base model were based on standard statistical criteria of GoF such
as a decrease in the OFV, accuracy of parameter estimation (i.e., 95% confidence interval
excluding 0), successful model convergence, and diagnostic plots.
Covariate Model
Covariate screening was undertaken via plots in the original pediatric only PopPK model, but no
obvious relationships were observed. As such, no formal stepwise covariate modeling was
364
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
conducted (i.e., forward selection and backwards elimination) when the model was fitted to the
pooled dataset.
14.5.1.5.2. Final Model
The final PopPK model (revised with pooled data) has the same model structure as the final base
model. The parameter estimates of the original and revised pediatric PopPK model are
summarized in Table 238. The relationship between CL and GFR was estimated to be quite
similar when fit to the pooled dataset (slope of 0.0555 vs. slope of 0.0548 from the pediatric
model), and the population mean estimates for Q1 (intercompartmental flow from Vc to Vp1,
volume of distribution for peripheral compartment 1) and Q2 (intercompartmental flow from Vc
to Vp2, volume of distribution for peripheral compartment 2) were similar as well. The
Applicant acknowledged that the addition of adult phase 1 data resulted in marked decreases in
the population mean Vc and V1 estimates such that the population mean volume of distribution
at steady-state (Vss) (i.e., sum of all volume of distribution terms) is calculated to be 17.3 L
versus 71.7 L when the model was fit to the pediatric data alone. Prediction-correct VPC plots
are shown in Figure 40, Figure 41, and Figure 42. A comparison of the two models is illustrated
in Figure 43.

Reviewer Comments
The distributions of free-drug %T>MIC in the two analysis populations for ABSSSI and CABP
being at or close to high end of the range likely indicate that the subjects were at the plateau of
the exposure-efficacy relationships for ABSSSI and CABP infection types. When evaluated
against nonclinical targets of %T>MIC (Table 243), fewer subjects with gram-negative
pathogens achieved the stasis, 1-log kill, and 2-log kill targets (range, 77.8% to 100%) when
compared to those with gram-positive pathogens (range, 100%-100%). This is further evaluated
in PTA analysis section to support dosing selection.
14.5.2.1.3. PTA
Because the renal route is a major elimination pathway for ceftobiprole (and as described in the
PopPK modeling section), the target attainment analysis utilized renal-based dosing groups to
simulate ceftobiprole exposures to support dosing selection for ABSSSI and CABP. To simulate
in a clinical scenario, virtual subjects resembling the respective subject populations (i.e., ABSSSI
and CABP) were generated, and exposure metrics were derived from the virtual subjects. Note
that given the lack of information on renal replacement modality impact on ceftobiprole PK (i.e.,
percent of drug being removed from iHD in the ceftobiprole development program), the
Applicant’s simulations were conducted without incorporating the extraction ratio (see Section 8
and Pharmacometric Assessment Appendix Section 14.5.1.4.2). Ceftobiprole dosing regimens
for exposure derivation (via simulations) and PTA analyses are summarized in Table 244. For
the PTA analysis, the nonclinical PK/PD targets are summarized in Section 5. The randomly
assigned targets were derived based on an estimated log normal distribution of %T>MIC targets
associated with a given endpoint (truncated within 2 standard deviations of the mean value).

Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Reviewer Comments
For pathogens causing ABSSSI or CABP, the PTA analyses (based on median and random
targets) demonstrate that the proposed dosing regimen (across renal function groups) provides
sufficient coverage up to an MIC of 4 µg/mL for 1-log kill across MIC distributions for
respective gram-positive pathogens; for gram-negative pathogens, the exposures cover up to an
MIC of 2 µg/mL for 1-log kill.

14.5.2.2. Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia PK/PD Analysis
14.5.2.2.1. Introduction
The Applicant performed PK/PD analyses for the SAB populations with the following objects:
•
•

To evaluate exposure-efficacy relationships using the refined PopPK model for SAB
To conduct PTA to support ceftobiprole dosing regimens and susceptibility testing
interpretive criteria against S. aureus
14.5.2.2.2. Exposure-Efficacy Analysis

Exposure-efficacy relationship was evaluated for SAB using PK and clinical data from Trial
BPR-CS-008. Dosing regimens administered in SAB subjects are summarized in Table 262. The
primary endpoint was overall success in the treatment of SAB, including infective endocarditis,
at the post-treatment evaluation (PTE) visit (Day 70 +/- 5 post-randomization) in the mITT
population (defined as the subset of subjects in the intent-to-treat (ITT) population who received
any amount of study medication, and who had a blood culture positive for S. aureus at baseline
based on a central microbiology laboratory assessment). Overall success is defined if the
following criteria were met:
•
•
•
•
•
•

Subject was alive at PTE visit;
No new metastatic foci or complications of the SAB infection;
Resolution or improvement of SAB-related clinical signs and symptoms; and
Two negative blood cultures for S. aureus
At least one while subject was on active study treatment, and
confirmed by at least one subsequent negative blood culture for S. aureus (either in the
period between 7 days after the end-of-treatment (EOT) visit and PTE visit or at the PTE
visit)

The Applicant employed two analysis populations for the exposure-efficacy analysis: 1) mITT
population with baseline pathogen, microbiological data, and sufficient PK data and 2) a
subpopulation of the first analysis population with S. aureus isolated at baseline. A total of 174
and 172 subjects were included in the mITT and mITT S. aureus analysis populations,
respectively. Refer to the Applicant’s PK/PD report (Tables 10 and 11 in the submitted report)
for a summary of baseline characteristics of the analysis populations. The response for efficacy
endpoints by visits in two analysis populations are summarized in Table 263. Ceftobiprole MIC,
free-drug AUC, and Day 1 free-drug plasma %T>MIC for both analysis populations are
summarized in Table 264. Percent of subjects in each analysis population achieving nonclinical
targets is summarized in Table 265. Given that individual %T>MIC aggregate at the high end of
respective ranges, the exposure-efficacy analyses (univariable or multivariable) were not
performed by the Applicant.
Of note, two subjects had A. baumannii and C. striatum selected as baseline pathogens with
MICs of >64 and >16 µg/mL, respectively. For these two subjects, the free-drug %T>MIC were
of 0% on Days 1 and 10 and were categorized as failures regarding overall success endpoints at
EOT and PTE. While the free-drug plasma %T>MIC with respect to the baseline S. aureus

398
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
pathogens for these two subjects was 98.8%, the Applicant postulated that the clinical failure was
potentially due to the other pathogens or other subject variables.

14.5.2.3. Assessment of End-Stage Renal Disease Dosing
Regimen for Adults
For adult subjects with ESRD (on or not on iHD), 250 mg IV q24h is the recommended dosing
regimen (for all indications); however, model-based simulations show that the
exposure (i.e., Day 1 AUC) may be suboptimal in ESRD subjects (not on iHD) with
renal function of 0-15 mL/min when compared to those with normal renal function (defined as
90-150 mL/min) in ABSSSI (Figure 45). Numerically lower model-predicted exposures on Day
1 are also seen with CABP and SAB infection types. As such, an Information Request was
communicated to the Applicant to compare ESRD dosing (not on iHD) at q12h vs. q24h dosing
frequencies and provide safety assessment for the q12h dosing regimen.
While the q12h dosing may seem reasonable based on Day 1 exposure metrics, the exposures
(after multiple-day administrations) on Day 5 for SAB and Day 7 for ABSSSI and CABP are
higher than those observed to date in clinical and nonclinical studies (Table 275). Additionally,
the Applicant stated that there has been no clinical safety experience at the predicted exposures
that would be reached based on the q12h dosing regimen in ESRD subjects.

412
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
Despite lower exposures at the proposed dosing regimen at q24h on Day 1, the accumulation
observed in simulated ESRD subjects after 5 days of ceftobiprole administrations for the
proposed dosing regimen led to exposures in a similar range to that observed in simulated
subjects with normal renal function. Furthermore, the PTA results (representative PTA results for
SAB based on the median target for 1-log kill is provided in Table 276) demonstrate that the
q24h still provide sufficient exposure (>90% probability of target attainment) across SAB,
ABSSSI, and CABP infection types (refer to the Applicant’s response to Information Request for
additional PTA results).

Reviewer Comments
In the setting of iHD, the exact exposures are difficult to predict due to a lack of dedicated
phase 1 study data to confirm the extraction ratio. As such, no modeling and simulations can be
conducted with the extraction ratio from iHD to predict the concentrations over time. If a
conservative measure of assuming 100% of ceftobiprole is removed during iHD sessions, the
ceftobiprole administered post-dialysis would have been similar to the exposures derived on Day
1 as shown in Table 275 . Moreover, these model-predicted exposures achieved similar
probability target attainments values of >90%. In general, the ESRD dosing of 250 mg IV q24h
in the setting of iHD (administered post-dialysis) is acceptable. Refer to Section II.8.1.2 for
discussions.
14.5.2.4. Pediatrics CABP PK/PD Analysis
The Applicant performed Monte Carlo simulations and dose optimization with the original
pediatric only PopPK model (Report 00616-3). In this review, the emphasis is placed upon the
optimized dosing regimen for pediatric subjects of 3 months to <18 years using the revised
pediatric PopPK model. To perform Monte Carlo simulation in pediatric subjects, a dataset of
5,000 virtual subjects aged <18 years with appropriate body size and renal function was created.
The characteristics of the virtual subjects are illustrated in Figure 59.
To evaluate ceftobiprole dosing regimens in pediatric age groups, including those of 2 year of
age or older with renal impairment, the 24-hour AUC and Cmax from the healthy adults serve as
the reference exposure (receiving 500 mg q8h for 5 days; Study CSI-1004). For detailed
methodology and results of the initial dose selection and optimization (i.e., exposure matching),
refer to the Applicant’s PopPK Report 00616-3.
Model-based predictions of 24-hour AUC and Cmax of ceftobiprole according to the weight-based
dosing regimens (proposed by the Applicant) by age group are shown in Figure 60 and Figure 61
and are summarized in Table 277. Target attainment based on predicted exposures are
summarized in Table 278. Because the submission includes study data for pediatric subjects
under 3 months of age, this subgroup was evaluated and included in the technical reports by the
Applicant. The analysis results of this pediatric subgroup are irrelevant to the proposed pediatric
indication of 3 month to <18 years of age.

Reviewer Comments
Based on model-predicted exposures, the AUC and Cmax of the pediatric age subgroups generally
align with those from the healthy adult subjects from Study CSI-1004. Because the healthy adult
exposures are known to be higher than adult subjects from the phase 3 studies, an additional plot
was generated by the reviewer to compare the exposures from pediatric subgroups to adult
subjects. As shown in Figure 62, the AUCs of the pediatric subgroups generally fall within those
of the adult subjects with CABP from phase 3. While the Cmax may be slightly higher for the 2 to
<6-year-old and 6 to <12-year-old groups, the Cmax is contained within the healthy adult
exposures for safety. The exposures in adolescent subjects (i.e., 12 to <18 year-olds) are
numerically lower when compared to those in healthy adults (Figure 60 and Figure 61);
however, most adolescents received 500 mg dosages based on body weight, and the exposures
generally align with those in the adult subjects.
Overall, the predicted exposures in pediatric subgroups are comparable to those in adult
subjects (from Phase 3 studies) while not exceeding those in healthy adults (i.e., safety
consideration). Furthermore, the PTA results demonstrate appropriate target attainments across
age groups, indicating that the dosing recommendations are acceptable for pediatric age groups.
14.5.2.4.1. Moderate or Severe Renal Impairment
Dosing recommendations in renally impairment pediatric subjects was previously assessed and
proposed with the original pediatrics only PopPK model. After modeling refitting with the
pooled PK data, the Applicant re-evaluated the dosing regimen. Overall, the exposures of the
pediatric renal impairment subgroups are predicted to be mostly within the reference healthy
adults exposure range (Figure 63 and Figure 64), and the dosing regimens are supported by the
PTA results as shown in Table 281. Of note, the dosing recommendation for adolescents with
severe RI has been modified to be 7.5 mg q12h (up to 250 mg). This is further discussed in
Section 14.5.2.5.

14.5.2.5. Assessment of Severe Renal Impairment Dosing
Regimen for Adolescents
Based on the submitted PK/PD report for pediatric subjects for the CABP indication (Report
00616-3), a dose of 7.5 mg/kg q24h (up to 500 mg) was recommended for adolescents 12 to
<18 years of age; however, the Applicant proposes the same weight-based dosing at q12h dosing
frequency (i.e., 7.5 mg/kg q12h, up to 250 mg) in the severe RI category. As such, an
Information Request (dated 5 FEBRUARY 2024; link) was communicated to the Applicant.
Briefly, the Applicant stated that the decision to modify from q24h to q12h was to align with
adult dosing regimen for severe RI through interactions with the European Health Authorities.
Additionally, the Applicant provided further simulations to support the q12h dosing regimen in
this population as summarized in Table 282. At a dosing frequency of q12h (capped at 250 mg
per dose), the exposures based on AUC would be slightly higher and the Cmax slightly lower in
adolescent subjects with severe RI (AUC = 259 μg*h/mL; Cmax = 20.7 μg/mL) than the
exposures predicted in subjects with q24h dosing frequency (AUC = 240 μg*h/mL; Cmax = 24.6
μg/mL). Overall, the change in dosing frequency results in an improvement in PTA results.
Table 282. Summary of Predicted Ceftobiprole AUC and Cmax for Q24H and Q12H Dosing Interval
for Adolescents With Severe Renal Impairment

Source: Applicant’s response to Information Request [dated 5FEBRUARY2024; link], Table 1, page 4
Note: 667 mg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 500 mg of ceftobiprole. For pediatric patients: 13.3 mg/kg is
equivalent to 10 mg/kg of ceftobiprole. 26.7 mg/kg of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium is equivalent to 20 mg/kg of ceftobiprole. Dosing
adjustments for each indication are based on renal function

Reviewer’s Comments
Considering an increase in dosing frequency, the PTA is expected to be similar or improved as
shown in results above. Because the ceftobiprole dose is capped at 250 mg for the q12h dosing
frequency (as opposed to 500 mg q24h), this dosing strategy likely will optimize the PK/PD
target of %T>MIC given that the 250 mg single dose leads to an effective exposure for respective
pathogens. Overall, the proposed 7.5 mg/kg q12h dosing for adolescents with severe RI is
acceptable.

17. Clinical Safety
17.1. Phase 1 Studies
The Applicant submitted eighteen adult phase 1 and two pediatric phase 1 studies for
ceftobiprole. The population of these studies include healthy subjects, subjects on hemodialysis,
subjects with impaired renal function and end-stage renal disease, morbidly obese subjects,
subjects who underwent elective hip replacement surgery, and subjects who were hospitalized in
intensive or intermediate care units. These studies covered a dose range of 125 mg to 1000 mg.
There were no deaths in the phase 1 healthy adult studies. However, there were two adult
subjects in the intensive care unit phase 1 studies who died due to the unrelated adverse events
(AEs) of septic shock and intracranial hemorrhage. SAEs were reported for eight subjects (none
in healthy adults). The only SAE which was considered related to the study drug was acute
kidney injury. The most common AEs experienced in this population were nausea (29.6%), taste
disorder (21%), headache (16.6%), and vomiting (11.2%). Additional AEs that occurred in >2 %
of the subjects include dysgeusia, infusion site pain, diarrhea, hypotension, abdominal pain,
nasopharyngitis, feeling hot, phlebitis, pyrexia, constipation, dizziness, fatigue, and injection site
pain. The AEs experienced in phase 1 studies were similar to the AEs seen in the subsequent
phase 3 studies. There are no significant safety issues or concerns based on the phase 1 data.

423
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
The pediatric phase 1 studies BPR-PIP-001 and CSI-1006 were multicenter, open-label, singledose, add-on studies of ceftobiprole in pediatric subjects undergoing treatment with IV
antibacterial drugs with the aim of evaluating the single-dose PK and safety of ceftobiprole. Trial
BPR-PIP-001 included 15 neonates and infants aged up to 3 months; 6 treatment-emergent
adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 6 subjects and only one TEAE of diaper dermatitis occurred
in more than one subject. Neither the TEAEs nor the two SAEs of cerebral infarction and
diaphragmatic hernia were considered to be related to the study drug. Study CSI-1006 included
64 subjects aged 3 months to less than 18 years. Eight subjects experienced 14 SAEs, none of
which were considered treatment-related by the investigator. TEAEs were reported in 48.4% of
subjects and vomiting was the most common (9.4%). TEAEs of vomiting, diaper dermatitis,
pruritis, headache, increased eosinophil count, diarrhea, catheter-related site reaction, urine
crystals, increased alanine aminotransferase (125 U/L), and increased aspartate aminotransferase
(121 U/L) were considered potentially related to ceftobiprole; the latter two laboratory-based
TEAEs occurred in the same subject. No deaths were reported and no subjects discontinued
either Study due to a TEAE.

18. Clinical Virology

19. Clinical Microbiology
19.1. In Vitro Activity
The in vitro ceftobiprole MIC range and concentrations required to inhibit 90% of isolates
(MIC90) against the target pathogen isolates collected in the JMI SENTRY surveillance studies
from 2016 to 2020 and isolates collected in the European Union surveillance studies from 2016
to 2019 is shown in Table 288. Ceftobiprole is active against MSSA (MIC90 = 0.5 mcg/mL),
MRSA (MIC90 = 2 mcg/mL), S. pneumoniae (MIC90 = 0.25-0.5 mcg/mL), S. pyogenes
(MIC90 = 0.015 mcg/mL), S. agalactiae (MIC90 = 0.03 mcg/mL), H. influenzae (MIC90 =
0.12 mcg/mL), and H. parainfluenzae (MIC90 = 0.25 mcg/mL). The ceftobiprole MIC90s for the
penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae subset was higher (MIC90 = 0.5 mcg/mL) than for the
penicillin-susceptible subset (MIC90 = 0.015 mcg/mL) but were within the proposed susceptible
breakpoint of ≤0.5 mcg/mL for ceftobiprole.
The ceftobiprole MIC90 for E. faecalis and E. faecium were 2 mcg/mL and >4 mcg/mL,
respectively. The ceftobiprole MIC90 against M. catarrhalis was 0.25 mcg/mL. Against 12
vancomycin-resistant/ampicillin-susceptible E. faecalis, the ceftobiprole MIC90 was 2 mcg/mL.
Ceftobiprole is active against some gram-negative bacteria producing AmpC cephalosporinases
or non-ESBL Class A enzymes with MIC90 values of ≤1 mcg/mL. Ceftobiprole has limited
activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter species with MIC90 values of
≥16 mcg/mL. The ceftobiprole MIC90 values against P. aeruginosa are above the PK-PD
target achievable by proposed dosing regimen. Ceftobiprole is not active against ESBL or
metallo -lactamases producing bacteria. The ceftobiprole MIC90s for key pathogens, S. aureus,
S. pneumoniae, E. coli, and K. pneumoniae isolates from the European Union surveillance were
similar to that observed for the US isolates. Ceftobiprole, like other cephalosporins, is not active
against the atypical intracellular bacterial CABP pathogens, Mycoplasma pneumoniae or
Chlamydophila pneumoniae. The ceftobiprole MIC against 30 Legionella pneumophila isolates
by broth microdilution ranged from 0.03 – 0.12 mcg/mL (MIC90 = 0.06 mcg/mL) (Sahm 2007a).
Ceftobiprole activity against intracellular forms of L. pneumophila has not been investigated.
Ceftobiprole has limited activity against anaerobes.

19.2. Interaction With Other Antimicrobials
In the in vitro checkboard broth and/or time kill assays, ceftobiprole was tested in combination
with daptomycin, vancomycin, gentamicin, or rifampin against 20 MRSA strains with varying
degrees of vancomycin susceptibility. Ceftobiprole was also tested in combination with
doripenem, levofloxacin or colistin against strains of P. aeruginosa (N = 24), A. baumannii
(N = 19) or fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli (N = 19). Ceftobiprole in combination with
ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, amikacin, and tobramycin was evaluated in 61 clinical P. aeruginosa
isolates. No antagonism was observed in these studies. Majority of the combination were
indifferent.

19.3. In Vivo Activity
The in vivo activity of ceftobiprole was evaluated in multiple animal models of infection. These
include the murine septicemia model, the murine peritonitis model, the neutropenic thigh
infection model (PK-PD studies), the murine acute pneumonia model, the rat and rabbit
endocarditis model, the rabbit meningitis model, the rat and rabbit osteomyelitis model, and the
murine urinary tract infection model.
Murine Septicemia Model
Ceftobiprole (ED50 values <5 mg/kg) was effective in treating experimental septicemia in mice
due to S. aureus strains (ceftobiprole MIC values ≤2 mcg/mL) (Table 290). Against MRSA I-6
and MRSA 8525, ceftobiprole was more active than vancomycin (vancomycin ED50 = 6.7 mg/kg
and 12.1 mg/kg). Ceftobiprole also demonstrated activity against three penicillin-resistant strains
of S. pneumoniae, including a strain S. pneumoniae 23 F-CTR (ceftobiprole MIC 1 mg/mL),
however, the ceftobiprole ED50 for the S. pneumoniae penicillin resistant strains were higher than
the S. pneumoniae penicillin sensitive strain. Similar ceftobiprole doses (ED50 <5 mg/kg) were
effective against E. coli, K. pneumoniae, C. freundii, S. marcescens and P. mirabilis. Against the
TEM-1 containing E. coli OC4367, the ceftobiprole ED50 was higher (2.7 mg/kg/day) than
against the parent E. coli strain (0.5 mg/kg/day) but ceftobiprole was more active than
ceftazidime or cefepime and as active as meropenem. The presence of the ACT-1 AmpC
cephalosporinase did not affect the in vivo activity of the ceftobiprole and comparators in this
animal model. The strain Proteus vulgaris 1028 with in vitro resistance to ceftobiprole was also
resistant in vivo (ED50 >12 mg/kg). Cefepime (ED50 = 1 mg/kg) and meropenem (ED50
<0.4 mg/kg) had greater activity against the P. aeruginosa BA strain compared to ceftobiprole
(ED50 = 4 mg/kg).

Murine Peritonitis Model
In the murine peritonitis model, female mice were infected intraperitoneally with E. faecalis (10X the 50% lethal dose) and then
immediately treated subcutaneously with ceftobiprole medocaril sodium or ampicillin. Against the rare -lactamase-producing strain
TX0921, ceftobiprole was more active than ampicillin (Table 291). It is likely that the activity of ceftobiprole against lactamaseproducing E. faecalis is due to the inherent stability of the drug to hydrolysis by this enzyme (similar to class A staphylococcal
penicillinase PC1). Ceftobiprole PD50 (dose that protects 50% of the animals) values at 96 hours were lower than ampicillin for E.
faecalis strains TX2484, and OG1RF, respectively.

Murine Acute Pneumonia Model
In the immunocompromised murine model of acute pneumonia, the ten-day cumulative survival rates for infected mice (all strains)
receiving ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (total daily doses of ceftobiprole equivalents, 2.1 to 75 mg/kg) ranged from 57 to 100%,
whereas with ceftriaxone (total daily doses, 10 to 400 mg/kg), the survival rates varied between 13 and 100% (Table 292). In the
immunocompetent murine model of acute pneumonia, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium reduced bacterial burden in the lungs. Against
the wildtype strain ATCC 6301, and the two macrolide-resistant isolates, the ceftobiprole ED50 was 2.5- to 4-fold lower than that
determined for ceftriaxone. Against H. influenzae, E. cloacae and the non-ESBL producing K. pneumoniae ceftobiprole, ceftriaxone
and cefepime all reduced bacterial burden in the lungs compared to no treatment. The reason for the activity of ceftriaxone
(MIC=16 mcg/mL; Intermediate susceptibility) against the non-ESBL producing K. pneumoniae is not clear. For the ESBL-positive K.
pneumoniae strain where the MICs were all greater than or equal to 128 mcg/mL, there was no difference between treated and
untreated animals. Emergence of resistance studies conducted on bacteria recovered after therapy (except for ESBL-positive K.
pneumoniae) found post-treatment MIC values within 2-fold of pre-treatment MIC values.

Neutropenic murine thigh infection model
The neutropenic murine thigh infection model was used for PK-PD assessments and ceftobiprole exposures for a 1 log kill for S.
aureus (MRSA and MSSA), S. pneumoniae, E. coli, K. pneumoniae, E. cloacae were determined (see section 19.4).
Endocarditis Model
The activity of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium against S. aureus was examined in a rat and rabbit model of endocarditis (Table 293). In
the rat model of endocarditis, the three ceftobiprole medocaril sodium dosing regimens (72 mg/kg, 144 mg/kg, and 288 mg/kg that
achieved steady-state levels in serum of 2.5, 5, and 10 times the MIC for the test organisms) cleared >90% of vegetations in rats with
experimental endocarditis caused by penicillinase-producing MRSA COL (Bla+) and the MRSA P8-Hom strain. Blood and spleen
cultures from all animals were negative. No resistant mutants were isolated from infected vegetations from any group of treated

animals. In another study, treatment with standard dose-ceftobiprole simulating human kinetics of 500 mg every 12 hours (q12h)
cleared 93% and 77% of vegetations infected with strains PC3 and Mu50, respectively, and reduced the vegetation counts by >6 log10

In the rabbit model of endocarditis, the activity of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (25 mg/kg (equivalent to 19 mg of ceftobiprole per

vegetations, spleen and kidneys of MRSA in 6/7, 5/7, and 7/7 rabbits with aortic catheter infected with 1.5 x 107 CFU of MRSA strain
COL. In contrast, vancomycin (30 mg/kg intravenous q12h for 4 days) and daptomycin (18 mg/kg intravenous q24h for 4 days)
cleared MRSA from these tissues in fewer animals.

Rabbit Meningitis Model
In the rabbit model of experimental meningitis, the activity of ceftobiprole (40 mg/kg IV once) was similar to cefepime (100 mg/kg at

extent than cefepime.

Rat and Rabbit Osteomyelitis Model
In the rat model of MRSA mediastinitis and sternal osteomyelitis (Table 294), ceftobiprole (70
and 100 mg/kg for 5 days) decreased the MRSA load in the sternum by 1 log10 and 1.4 log10
compared with untreated controls and the vancomycin-treated group. MRSA was recovered from
the spleen in 5/7 saline-treated animals but in none of the antibacterial drug-treated animals.
Following 14 days therapy, 5/8 ceftobiprole-treated rats and 6/8 vancomycin-treated rats cleared
MRSA from the sternum compared with none of the saline-treated animals. In those animals that
did not clear MRSA, only rare colonies were recovered. In rabbits with localized osteomyelitis
due to MRSA 168-1, ceftobiprole medocaril sodium (40 mg/kg ceftobiprole equivalent, q8h, 4
weeks) administered subcutaneously was more active than vancomycin (30 mg/kg, q12h, 4
weeks, subcutaneous) or oral linezolid (60 mg/kg, q8h, 4 weeks) at 2 weeks after end of
treatment.
Murine Urinary Tract Infection Model
In the murine urinary tract infection model, mice were treated with single doses of ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium (equivalent to 4.3 to 34.2 mg/kg of ceftobiprole and concentrations achievable
in humans with standard human dosing) or vancomycin (2-fold range from 6.25 to 50 mg/kg of
body weight), 1-hour post-infection. Two doses of ampicillin (2-fold range from 12.5 to
200 mg/kg) were administered subcutaneously 1- and 2-hour post-infection (previously shown to
simulate ampicillin human doses of 3 gm). The minimum detection limit of bacteria in these
experiments was 102 CFU/gm. Protection was defined as no recovery of bacteria from kidney or
bladder homogenates at 48 hours post-infection. The authors state that ceftobiprole was active
against the Bla+ and Bla- E. faecalis OG1 strains, while ampicillin (depending on the inoculum)
was less effective against Bla+ than Bla- OG1 strains in this murine urinary tract infection model
based on 50% protective dose (Table 295). However, it should be noted that treatment was
initiated 1-2 hours post-infection making it difficult to assess if urinary tract infection was
established. Hence, data from this Study should be interpreted with caution.

In summary, ceftobiprole was shown to be active against MSSA and MRSA in the murine
septicemia model and rat and rabbit endocarditis and osteomyelitis models. Ceftobiprole was
active against S. pneumoniae, including penicillin resistant strains in the murine septicemia and
the murine acute pneumonia models. Ceftobiprole was also shown to be active against E. coli
expressing TEM-1 and Act-1 AmpC cephalosporinase, K. pneumoniae, C. freundii,
S. marcescens, and P. mirabilis in the murine septicemia model. In a rabbit model of meningitis
ceftobiprole was effective at reducing bacterial burden in the CSF in rabbits infected with strains
of E. coli, K. pneumoniae and β-lactamase positive and negative H. influenzae. In both a rat and
rabbit model of endocarditis, ceftobiprole did not sterilize but was effective in reducing cardiac
vegetations of MRSA including a vancomycin intermediate strain. Similarly, in both a rat and
rabbit model of osteomyelitis, ceftobiprole was effective in reducing bacterial burden in MRSA
infected sternal bones.

19.4. PK/PD Studies
Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic studies in the neutropenic mouse thigh infection model
identified %fT>MIC as the PK/PD index that correlated with in vivo activity. An exposure target
of %fT>MIC = 30% for 1-log kill was selected based on the animal studies with gram-positive
bacteria (Table 296 and Table 297).

19.5. Clinical Studies
Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia
BPR-CS-009 was a randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial conducted to establish the
efficacy and safety of ceftobiprole medocaril sodium compared to daptomycin in the treatment of
SAB, including infective endocarditis. The trial assessed microbiological eradication rates
(negative blood culture for S. aureus) at Day 4, Day 8, and the EOT and PTE visits in the mITT
population. The mITT population comprised of 387 subjects (ceftobiprole: n = 189; comparator:
n = 198). In the ceftobiprole group, 74.6% of subjects (141/189) had an MSSA infection at
baseline, and 23.8% of subjects (45/189) had an MRSA infection at baseline. In the comparator
group, 73.7% of subjects (146/198) had an MSSA infection, and 24.7% of subjects (49/198) had
an MRSA infection.
The microbiological eradication rates at various visits in the mITT population in subjects with
SAB due to MSSA and MRSA are shown in Table 299. The microbiological eradication rates
appear to be slightly lower in the MRSA subgroup compared to the MSSA subgroup but could
be due to the small number of subjects with MRSA.

Relapse of S. aureus bacteremia was assessed by the data review committee in two subjects

isolates with MICs that were four-fold higher than the baseline MICs and were clinical failures.
No development of resistance on therapy was observed in subjects treated with ceftobiprole.
In the ceftobiprole group, MICs were determined for 141 baseline MSSA isolates and 43
baseline MRSA isolates (Table 300). For the MSSA isolates, the ceftobiprole MIC range was
0.12 – 1 mcg/mL with an MIC90 of 0.5 mcg/mL. For the MRSA isolates, the ceftobiprole MIC
range was 0.5 – 2 mcg/mL with an MIC90 of 2 mcg/mL. There was no apparent correlation
between baseline ceftobiprole MICs and clinical failure.

Characterization of the clonal strain type of the baseline MRSA isolates (ceftobiprole n = 43,

USA300 clonal complex. Clinical outcome per treatment group for the pooled U.S. and U.S.
LAV clonal types, representing 49% of strains typed, was assessed. Overall success at the PTE
visits was observed in 76.2% of subjects (16/21) in the ceftobiprole group, and 69.6% (16/23) in
the comparator group (Table 301) for the US strain type.

The trial demonstrates that ceftobiprole is effective in the treatment of SAB due to methicillinresistant and methicillin-sensitive S. aureus.
ABSSSIs
Trial BPR-CS-008 was a double-blind, non-inferiority, active-controlled trial, which randomized
679 adult subjects with qualifying ABSSSI and who fulfilled the requirement to receive
intravenous antibacterial drugs in a hospital setting. The mITT population consisted of 506
subjects (ceftobiprole N= 244; vancomycin plus aztreonam N =262) and was a subset of subjects
in the ITT population who had causative pathogens identified by the central microbiology
laboratory from skin lesions or blood cultures. Local laboratory results were included only if
isolate could not be cultured at the central laboratory. Nine gram-negative and 27 gram-positive
baseline pathogens isolated from subjects in the mITT population were only analyzed by local
laboratories. The ME population consisted of 426 subjects (ceftobiprole N= 203; vancomycin
plus aztreonam N =223) and was the subset of subjects in the mITT population who were also in
the clinically evaluable population. Gram- positive pathogens were isolated at Baseline in 442
subjects while gram-negative pathogens were isolated in 34 subjects and mixed gram positive
and gram-negative pathogens were isolated in 30 subjects at Baseline. The early clinical response
and investigator’s assessment of overall clinical success at TOC by Baseline pathogen are shown
in Table 302. Ceftobiprole was active against S. aureus (methicillin sensitive and methicillin
resistant), Streptococcus pyogenes, and K. pneumoniae. There were no ABSSSI subjects with
baseline E. coli in the mITT population. It should be noted that the number of subjects with
Enterobacter cloacae was small (n = 3), but all 3 subjects were a clinical success, including a
subject with E. cloacae isolate with MIC>64 mcg/mL (Table 303).

Bacteremia Subjects
Of the 506 subjects in the mITT population, 17 (3.4%) had concomitant bacteremia and had
pathogens isolated from baseline blood cultures. Of the 17 subjects with positive blood cultures,
7 were in the ceftobiprole arm and 10 were in the comparator arm). All subjects with positive
blood cultures in the ceftobiprole arm (n = 7) were responders, while 9 out of 10 subjects were
responders in the comparator arm (Table 304).

microbiological persistence at EOT, the subject met the definition of clinical cure. The isolate
was not further characterized.
CABP
Common typical bacterial pathogens that cause CABP include Streptococcus pneumoniae,
Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Atypical bacterial
pathogens such as Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Legionella
pneumophila also cause CABP. Data from two multiregional phase 3 trials, CAP-3001 and BPRPIP-002 were included to support the CABP indication. Evidence of efficacy and safety in
HABP from trial BPR 248/307 was included to provide additional information on the pneumonia
population. The Applicant is not requesting an indication for the treatment of HABP and data
from this trial were not reviewed for efficacy.

The analysis of clinical success by pathogen in the Day3-mITT population suggests that
ceftobiprole has similar activity as ceftriaxone except that ceftobiprole appears to have greater
efficacy against S. pneumoniae (Table 45). The analysis of microbiological eradication by
pathogen, and clinical success by pathogen, per the original prespecified analysis is shown in
Table 308. Microbiological Eradication at the TOC Visit by Causative Pathogen (mITT and ME
Populations, Pre-Specified Analysis), CAP-3001 and Table 309, respectively. For the majority of
the subjects, microbiological outcome at TOC was presumed eradication or presumed persistence
and derived from clinical outcome. Ceftobiprole was active against methicillin sensitive
Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, E. coli, K. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and H.
parainfluenzae. Although both subjects with CABP due to MRSA were a clinical success, only
one of the two subjects had eradication of MRSA. The number of subjects with CABP due to
MRSA was small (n = 2). Similarly, only one subject had E. cloacae but was a clinical success.
No microbiological relapse was noted in either treatment arm at the late follow-up visit. The
analysis of clinical outcome by baseline pathogen and ceftobiprole MIC is shown in Table 311.

BPR-PIP-002
This was a phase 3 investigator-blind trial which enrolled pediatric subjects with CABP or
HABP requiring intravenous antibacterial treatment in a hospital setting. The BPR-PIP-002
phase 3 trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of ceftobiprole versus standard-of-care
cephalosporin treatments, with or without vancomycin, in pediatric subjects (3 months to 17
years) with HABP or CABP requiring hospitalization. The mITT population comprised of only
six subjects: five in the ceftobiprole arm and one in the comparator arm. Table 312.

19.6. In Vitro Susceptibility Test Method
The MIC values for ceftobiprole were determined by broth microdilution method in accordance
with the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines (M07-A6). Tier 1 studies
evaluated the effect of media (cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth, Iso-Sensitest broth), media
supplementation (25 mg/L calcium, 0.002% Tween 80), temperature (30oC or 35oC), presence of
2% NaCl, inoculum size, incubation conditions (5%CO2), pH, and serum. A 2-fold increase in
ceftobiprole MICs against the two P. aeruginosa strains occurred with increase of inoculum
density from 104 to 105 to 106 CFU/mL Increases in ceftobiprole MIC were also made when high
inoculum β-lactamase-positive strains were tested. Ceftobiprole MIC values from dry-form broth
microdilution MIC panels were within 1log2 dilution of the reference frozen-form MIC values.
Overall, the ceftobiprole MIC obtained under various of testing conditions were within 1log2
dilution of the standard CLSI broth microdilution method.

Ceftobiprole Disk Diffusion Method
The 30 mcg ceftobiprole disk, similar to other cephalosporin disk masses, was originally
developed according to CLSI M23 guidelines and QC ranges were established by CLSI
(CLSI M23). Since the original disk development studies, a new 5 mcg ceftobiprole disk was
found to reduce the size of the inhibition zones and was commercialized in the European regions.
Disk Optimization
The activity of the 5 (lot#322789), 10 (lot# 322790), and 30 (lot# 322793) mcg ceftobiprole
disks against seven QC strains (E. coli ATCC® 25922, H. influenzae ATCC® 49247, H.
influenzae NCTC 8468, P. aeruginosa ATCC® 27853, S. aureus ATCC® 25923, S. aureus
(b) (4)
ATCC® 29213, S. pneumoniae ATCC® 49619) was examined using
disk (Technical
report CT-041). All 3 disk masses resulted in an acceptable zone size range (i.e., a variation of
not more than 3 mm) for all QC strains tested. A study conducted by the EUCAST laboratory
(b) (4)
examined 5 mcg (from
) and 30 mcg ceftobiprole disks against 40 – 42 clinical
isolates each of S. aureus, S. pneumoniae (including a penicillin non-susceptible subset), and
different species of the Enterobacterales. Scatterplots comparing the 30 mcg and 5 mcg disks
using the raw data provided by the EUCAST laboratory was submitted. The 5 mcg ceftobiprole
disks was stated to result in a better differentiation for non-wildtype isolates than the 30 mcg
disks.

Breakpoint Assessment
The in vitro surveillance, PK-PD cut-off and clinical outcome data were used to arrive at
breakpoints for the target pathogen.
Staphylococcus aureus (Methicillin Sensitive and Methicillin Resistant)
The assessment supports a ceftobiprole susceptible breakpoint of 2 mcg/mL for S. aureus
(methicillin-susceptible and methicillin-resistant) based on MIC90 values, PK-PD cut-off, overall
success or clinical cure rates in the clinical studies for SAB, ABSSSI, and CABP (Table 316).
Note that there is insufficient clinical data from CABP subjects with MRSA. The intermediate
(4 mcg/mL) and resistant (8 mcg/mL) breakpoints are set as 2-fold and 4-fold dilution higher
than the susceptible breakpoint as the maximum MIC observed for S. aureus in surveillance
studies was 4 mcg/mL. The corresponding ceftobiprole 5 mcg disk breakpoints are S ≥16 mm;
I = 14-15 mm; R ≥13 mm based on acceptable error rates.

Streptococcus pneumoniae
The assessment supports a ceftobiprole susceptible breakpoint of 0.5 mcg/mL for S. pneumoniae
based on MIC90 values, animal studies with isolates with MIC of 1 mcg/mL, PK-PD target
attainment, clinical cure rates in the CABP trial (Table 317). Limited clinical data at MIC of
1 mcg/mL. The intermediate (1 mcg/mL) and resistant (2 mcg/mL) breakpoints are set as 2-fold
and 4-fold dilution higher than the susceptible breakpoint as the maximum MIC observed for S.
pneumoniae in surveillance studies was 2 mcg/mL, while the maximum MIC in CABP trial was
1 mcg/mL. No disk breakpoints are proposed by the Applicant as clinical isolates from CABP
trial were not tested with the 5 mcg ceftobiprole disk.

Streptococcus pyogenes
The assessment supports a ceftobiprole susceptible only breakpoint of ≤ 0.5 mcg/mL for S.
pyogenes based on MIC range and MIC90 values, PK-PD cut-off, clinical cure rates in the
ABSSSI trial (Table 318). No clinical data is available for isolates with MIC > 0.03 mcg/mL. A
susceptible only breakpoint of ≤0.5 mcg/ml is acceptable based on the Applicant’s rationale and
MICs observed with other Streptococcus species that are susceptible to ceftobiprole, ceftaroline
and ceftriaxone. No intermediate or resistant breakpoints are set as the maximum MIC observed
for S. pyogenes in surveillance studies was 0.12 mcg/mL. The corresponding ceftobiprole 5 mcg
disk susceptible only breakpoint is ≥ 24 mm.

Haemophilus influenzae and Haemophilus parainfluenzae
The assessment supports a ceftobiprole susceptible breakpoint of 0.25 mcg/mL for H, influenzae
and H. parainfluenzae based on MIC90 values, clinical cure rates in the CABP trial (Table 320).
Limited clinical data is available for MIC >0.12 mcg/mL. The wildtype H. influenzae lactamase positive and negative populations have an epidemiological cut-off of 0.25 mcg/mL.
The H. parainfluenzae population is similar to the H. influenzae population. A susceptible
breakpoint of 0.25 mcg/mL would not cut the MIC distribution for H. influenzae and cover the
wildtype population. The intermediate (0.5 mcg/mL) and resistant (1 mcg/mL) breakpoints are
set as 2-fold and 4-fold dilution higher than the susceptible breakpoint, as the maximum MIC
observed for H. influenzae in surveillance studies was 1 mcg/mL. No disk breakpoints are
proposed by the Applicant as H. influenzae and H. parainfluenzae clinical isolates were not
tested using the 5mcg ceftobiprole disks.

20. Mechanism of Action/Drug Resistance
20.1. Mechanism of Action
Ceftobiprole exerts its antibacterial activity by binding to multiple penicillin-binding proteins
(PBPs) and inhibiting their transpeptidase activity, which is essential for the synthesis of the
bacterial cell wall. The concentrations required to inhibit 50% binding to PBPs (IC50s) from
various gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria were determined using fluorescein-labeled
penicillin, [H3}-penicillin, biocillin fluorescein-labeled, or fluorescein isothiocyanate labeled
ampicillin (Table 322 and Table 323). The studies showed that ceftobiprole has a high affinity
for S. aureus PBPs 1 – 4, including PBP2a in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (Table 322).
Ceftobiprole has high affinity for all six S. pneumoniae PBPs in penicillin-susceptible strains,
including PBP2b. Ceftobiprole’s PBP binding affinity is reduced for PBP1b and PBP2b in
penicillin-resistant strains, but ceftobiprole still has good affinity for PBP1a, PBP2a, PBP2x, and
PBP3 in these strains. Ceftobiprole has a high affinity for S. epidermidis PBP 2’, compared to all
other -lactams measured. Ceftobiprole has good affinity for wildtype PBPs 1-5 of E. faecium
but does not have measurable affinity for the mutated PBP5 from ampicillin-resistant E. faecium,
resulting in elevated -lactam MICs in E. faecium strains that have these variants of PBP5.

20.2. Mechanism of Resistance
Single-step resistance frequencies were determined for 10 S. aureus strains using agar plates
containing ceftobiprole at 2x to 8x MIC and an inoculum of 5 x 108 to 5 x 109 CFU. Resistance
frequencies observed for ceftobiprole were low in S. aureus and ranged from ~9.6 x 10-8 at 2x
MIC to <1.5 x 10-10 at 8X MIC (Table 326). In serial passage studies, a 4-fold increase in MIC
was observed in 3 out of 5 S. aureus isolates after 50 passages. In the case of coagulase negative
525
Reference ID: 5357793

NDA 218275
Zevtera (ceftobiprole medocaril sodium for injection)
staphylococci, the ceftobiprole resistance frequencies were 1.1 x 10-8 to <7.7 x 10-10 and 4 of the
5 strains had a 4-fold increase in MIC after 50 passages. In most cases, the transiently elevated
ceftobiprole MICs decreased when the strains were cultured in the absence of drug, suggesting
the resistance mutations were not stable.
When a high inoculum of S. aureus strains (109 CFU/mL) was serially passaged in subinhibitory
concentrations of ceftobiprole for 28 days, resistance due to rare mutations developed in 20-21
days. For the strain carrying mutated mecA gene on a plasmid with an initial ceftobiprole MIC of
16 mcg/mL, the MIC increased to 256 mcg/mL after 20 passages. For the strain carrying
wildtype mecA gene on a plasmid in a mecA– background, ceftobiprole MIC increased from
4 mcg/mL to 128 mcg/mL after 21 passages. In the third strain that lacked the mecA gene,
ceftobiprole MIC increased from 1 mcg/mL to 256 mcg/mL after 20 passages. The mecA gene
acquired mutations which lie close to the ceftobiprole binding site (Banerjee et al. 2008). The
mutations in the mecA– strain that led to an increased ceftobiprole MIC were in three genes: two
substitutions were in the gene encoding the low molecular weight PBP4, one in a gene encoding
a predicted signaling protein, GdpP, and one in the gene encoding an efflux protein, AcrB, which
is implicated in resistance to cationic compounds.
Single-step resistance frequencies for ceftobiprole in 10 S. pneumoniae (including penicillin
sensitive and penicillin resistant) strains ranged from 2 x 10-7 at 2x MIC to <6.7 x 10-9 at 8X
MIC. Three strains showed a 2-fold increase in MIC after 50 passages.
Single-step resistance frequencies for ceftobiprole in 8 H. influenzae (including  lactamase
positive and  lactamase negative) and 2 M. catarrhalis strains resulted in very low resistance
frequencies of <4.3 x 10-11 to 1.3 x 10-10 at 2x MIC and 8x MIC. A 4-fold increase in MIC was
seen in one strain after 50 passages.
Single-step mutants were obtained by exposing clinical isolates of Morganella morganii,
Citrobacter freundii, Providencia stuartii, Enterobacter cloacae, Serratia marcescens,
Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa to 2x-, 4x- and 8x- ceftobiprole MICs. Singlestep resistance frequencies for five Enterobacterales strains and one P. aeruginosa strain were
10-6 to 10-8 at 2x MIC for ceftobiprole and comparable to the values obtained for cefepime and
ceftazidime. The resistant mutants in C. freundii and E. cloacae occurred at frequencies of 10-6 at
2x MIC and 4x MIC of ceftobiprole. The mutants appeared to have become resistant through
over-expression of the chromosomal Class C β-lactamase. Mutants of P. aeruginosa were
obtained at a frequency of 10-6 and <10-9 at 2x MIC and 4x MIC, respectively. None of the
mutants over-expressed the chromosomal Class C β-lactamase but were found to over-express
the MexXY efflux pump (Queenan et al. 2010). The mutation frequencies for Enterobacterales
and P. aeruginosa were higher than those observed for S. aureus and S. pneumoniae.

Resistance in Isolates From Ceftobiprole Clinical Trials
In the CAP-3001 (CABP) trial, K. pneumoniae isolates from 1 subject had a ≥ 4-fold increase in
the ceftobiprole MICs between baseline (0.12 mcg/mL) and post-baseline (>16 mcg/mL). The
organism acquired an ESBL (TEM-4 with 4 amino acid changes) (Queenan 2009d). The
Applicant concluded that ceftobiprole resistance did not develop over the course of therapy and
the subject was infected with a new strain of K. pneumoniae which had a higher ceftobiprole
MICs and expressed more resistance mechanisms.
Subject isolates from the BAP248/307 HABP clinical trial with a ≥4-fold increase in ceftobiprole
MIC values were characterized by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (Queenan 2009b). Eleven
subjects had related or identical isolates post-baseline with increased ceftobiprole MICs analysis.
All 11 baseline isolates were gram-negative (P. aeruginosa, n=4; A. baumannii, n=2; E. cloacae,
n = 2; E. coli, n = 1; S. marcescens, n = 1; and K. pneumoniae, n = 1). The pulsed-field gel
electrophoresis results suggest that resistance to ceftobiprole developed while on therapy for
these isolates. Subject isolates from the BAP248/307 HABP clinical trial with ceftobiprole MIC
values ≥16 mcg/mL were evaluated for the expression of β-lactamases. Three principal
resistance profiles were discovered: (1) ESBL-positive, with CTX-M or SHV family Class A
extended-spectrum β-lactamases, (2) ESBL-positive, combined with an AmpC Class C βlactamase, (3) ESBL-negative, having an AmpC Class C β-lactamase, either plasmid-encoded or
chromosomally located. Ceftobiprole is not active against gram-negative bacteria producing
ESBLs from TEM, SHV or CTX-M families, serine carbapenemases (such as KPC), class B
metallo-β-lactamases, or class C (AmpC cephalosporinases) expressed at high levels and Ambler
class D β-lactamases including carbapenemases.
In summary, resistance in some bacteria is due to poor binding to PBPs, expression of 
lactamases including AmpC  lactamases, and expression of efflux pumps. In E. faecium, βlactam resistance is mediated by low affinity binding to PBP5, which may be expressed at higher
levels in ampicillin-resistant isolates. Ceftobiprole is resistant to hydrolysis by S. aureus
penicillinases and is hydrolyzed slowly by some Class C and Class A β-lactamases found in
gram- negative bacteria. Like most cephalosporins, ceftobiprole is hydrolyzed by ESBLs, serine
carbapenemases and metallo-β-lactamases. It is also hydrolyzed by the Class A
cephalosporinases from Proteus vulgaris, which has inherent resistance to ceftobiprole.
Cross-Resistance
Analysis of drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus subset of the 2016-2020 SENTRY surveillance
isolates demonstrated that ceftobiprole was active against isolates non-susceptible to
clindamycin, daptomycin, erythromycin, gentamicin, levofloxacin, linezolid,
tetracycline, tigecycline, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (ceftobiprole susceptibility ranged
from 97.7%–100.0% based on the proposed ceftobiprole breakpoint of S ≤2 mcg/mL for
S. aureus). Ceftobiprole MIC50/90 values (e.g., 0.5/2 mcg/mL) were identical for the S. aureus
subsets with vancomycin MIC values of ≤1 mcg/mL and >1 mcg/mL. Ceftobiprole maintained
activity against 88.0% of the ceftaroline non-susceptible isolates.

Rationale for Major Changes to Finalized PI2 Compared to
Applicant’s Draft PI
In the Dosage Forms and Strengths Section (3) of the PI, the
strength was presented in terms of the salt (ceftobiprole
medocaril sodium instead of the prodrug (ceftobiprole medocaril)
and the active metabolite (ceftobiprole). This was an exception to
the salt policy in the Guidance for Industry: Naming of Drug
Products Containing Salt Drug Substances. This strength
presentation was also included in Section 11 Description and
Section 16 How Supplied/Storage and Handling of the PI.
In the Description Section (11) of the PI, the sodium content
stated as “Each vial of ZEVTERA contains approximately 32 mg
of sodium” was added as per the labeling recommendations in
the Draft Guidance for Industry: Quantitative Labeling of Sodium,
Potassium, and Phosphorus for Human Over-the -Counter and
Prescription Drug Products.
Refer to the Office of Product Quality Assessment (in DARRTS
dated 3/28/2024) for additional details regarding the labeling
changes to the product quality sections.
